definition: To lower in rank, dignity, or esteem; to humiliate or degrade.
etymology: From Old French abaissier "to lower," from Late Latin bassus "low."

examples.text: He had concealed nothing, and even, in his self-abasement, he had striven to make himself more despicable than he had really been.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: If anything was needed to put the last touch to her self-abasement it was the sense of the way her old life was opening its ruts again to receive her.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: If they would serve their fellowmen, let them do it by making manifest the power and reality of conscience, in constraining them to penitential self-abasement!
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

definition: To make someone feel embarrassed, ashamed, or disconcerted.
etymology: From Old French esbaïss-, stem of esbaïr "to astonish, dismay."

examples.text: She wished Beth could hear him, but she did not say so, only praised him till he was quite abashed, and his grandfather came to his rescue.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: Prince Andrew was watching these men abashed by the Emperor's presence, and the women who were breathlessly longing to be asked to dance.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Abashed boys slunk into the rear pews and giggled, while milky little girls, up front with their mothers, self-consciously kept from turning around.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To become less intense or widespread; to lessen or reduce something.
etymology: From Old French abatre "to beat down," from Latin ad- "to" + battuere "to beat" (also the source of "battle" and "batter").

examples.text: Turkey pulled warships back from close escort of its Sismik 1 survey ship as the threat of conflict with Greece over oil rights in the Aegean Sea abated.
examples.source: Reuters, “Turkey Lifts Survey Ship Escort As Tension Abates”

examples.text: Wherever the sentiment of the majority is still genuine and intense, it is found to have abated little of its claim to be obeyed.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: Our institutions will not deteriorate by extension, and our sense of justice will not abate under tropic suns in distant seas.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: To formally give up a throne or position of power; to fail to fulfill a duty or responsibility.
etymology: From Latin abdicare "to disown, renounce," from ab- "away" + dicare "to proclaim."

examples.text: The poll also found that the majority of Britons would prefer the monarchy to miss a generation, with the Queen handing the throne to her grandson Prince William, 22, on her death or abdication.
examples.source: BBC News, “Royal couple watch nation's mood”

examples.text: Would he have to abdicate his precentorship, as he had his wardenship, and to give up chanting, as he had given up his twelve old bedesmen?
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: But there is no comfort or security for us in evasion, no solution in abdication, no relief in irresponsibility.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: A departure from what is normal, usual, or expected, often an unwelcome one.
etymology: From Latin aberrare "to wander away," from ab- "away" + errare "to stray."

examples.text: Meanwhile, the Indian Government said the prospects for the country's booming economy remained "very bright" despite a "temporary aberration" this year.
But he added that would be a statistical aberration and not a significant shift in economic activity.
examples.source: Reuters, “Japan Economy May Be Near Bottom, Economists Say”

examples.text: But apart from temporary aberration, the doctor diagnosed mania, which premised, in his words, to lead to complete insanity in the future.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: A state of temporary disuse or suspension.
etymology: From Anglo-French abeiance "expectation," from Old French abeer "to gape after, aspire to."

examples.text: The commission then took the pair to the European Court of Human Justice - which ruled EU countries could not put the pact "in abeyance", and confirmed the EC's right to launch "excessive debt procedures".
examples.source: BBC News, “EC calls truce in deficit battle”

examples.text: Animated by this reflection, he stumps faster, and looks a long way before him, as a man with an ambitious project in abeyance often will do.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Whilst the question of specie payments is in abeyance the prudent business man is careful about contracting debts payable in the distant future.
examples.author: Ulysses S. Grant

definition: To regard with disgust and hatred; to detest.
etymology: From Latin abhorrere "to shrink back from in dread," from ab- "away" + horrere "to bristle, shudder."

examples.text: My vices are the children of a forced solitude that I abhor, and my virtues will necessarily arise when I live in communion with an equal.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: But since she felt that he understood her also, his business would be to make her see Beaufort as he really was, with all he represented—and abhor it.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Come hither! bury thyself in a life which, to your now equally abhorred and abhorring, landed world, is more oblivious than death.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Extremely bad, miserable, or hopeless; (of a person or behavior) completely lacking pride or dignity.
etymology: From Latin abjectus "cast away," past participle of abicere, from ab- "away" + jacere "to throw."

examples.text: That was the first thing that struck him, an abject, miserable fool, and he repeated it to himself a dozen times in a rush of angry feeling.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: If so, it was, in view of his contemplated action, an abject sign of a still imperfect callousness for which he must be given all due credit.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: When warned that abject submission offered the only salvation against overwhelming power, hope showed the way to victory.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: To solemnly renounce a belief, cause, or claim; to reject formally.
etymology: From Latin abjurare "to deny on oath," from ab- "away" + jurare "to swear."

examples.text: The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: On receiving this the victim might either openly abjure his former ways, or might fly from the country.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: "Ces gens-la don't divorce, you know, any more than they emigrate or abjure—they think it impious and vulgar"; a fact in the light of which they seemed but the more richly special.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: To detest intensely; to loathe.
etymology: From Latin abominari "to shun as an ill omen," from ab- "away" + omen.

examples.text: Now can we be right in praising and admiring another who is doing that which any one of us would abominate and be ashamed of in his own person?
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: I lived in an infernal mess of rust, filings, nuts, bolts, spanners, hammers, ratchet-drills—things I abominate, because I don't get on with them.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: It is a belief that God not only abominates the act of the misbeliever, but will not hold us guiltless if we leave him unmolested.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

definition: Failing to produce the intended result; unsuccessful.
etymology: From Latin abortivus, from aboriri "to miscarry," from ab- "away" + oriri "to arise, be born."

examples.text: I proceed, then, from the morning which followed our abortive chase of the convict and our other strange experiences upon the moor.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: After several abortive attempts to get Affery to look at him while she cleared the table and washed the tea-service, Arthur thought of an expedient which Flora might originate.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The earth was lumpy, the stubble prickly and lined with grass, thistles, abortive stumps of clover.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To leave hurriedly and secretly, typically to escape detection or arrest, often with something stolen.
etymology: From Latin abscondere "to hide away," from abs- "away" + condere "to put, store."

examples.text: And, indeed, the merchants tell many a true tale of shiftlessness and cheating; of cotton picked at night, mules disappearing, and tenants absconding.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: There he was before me, in motley, as though he had absconded from a troupe of mimes, enthusiastic, fabulous.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: It was rather hard on Maggie that Tom always absconded without letting her into the secret, but the weaker sex are acknowledged to be serious impedimenta in cases of flight.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Formal release from guilt, obligation, or punishment; forgiveness.
etymology: From Latin absolutio "acquittal," from absolvere "to set free."

examples.text: If there be no such minister present, the congregation can have the benefit of no absolution but that which each may succeed in administering to himself.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: For to accuse, requires lesse Eloquence (such is mans Nature) than to excuse; and condemnation, than absolution more resembles Justice.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: I confessed, that I might obtain absolution; but now that falsehood lies heavier at my heart than all my other sins.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: To declare free from guilt, blame, or responsibility.
etymology: From Latin absolvere "to set free," from ab- "from" + solvere "to loosen."

examples.text: But she says the findings absolve the media of some blame as it is not just presentation of thin images that results in body dissatisfaction but the way body-dissatisfied people view images.
And remember, moreover, that it is often he who comes off victorious from the strife, absolved of all crime in the eyes of the world.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: "And yet," said I, smiling, "I cannot quite hold myself absolved from the charge of sensationalism which has been urged against my records."
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Moderate or restrained, especially in eating and drinking; not self-indulgent.
etymology: From Latin abstemius, from abs- "from" + temetum "strong drink."

examples.text: And it was others who looked abstemious and he who looked greedy; it was he somehow who finally paid, and it was others who mainly partook.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: His daily living being very plain, he had a peculiar taste for sudden and isolated luxuries; he was an abstemious epicure.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: But for all this, the great negro was wonderfully abstemious, not to say dainty.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: The practice of refraining from indulging in something, especially alcohol, food, or sex.
etymology: From Latin abstinentia, from abstinere "to hold back," from abs- "from" + tenere "to hold."

examples.text: To Dorothea this was adorable genuineness, and religious abstinence from that artificiality which uses up the soul in the efforts of pretence.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Though not required by their religion, the double abstinence has had time to grow into a custom of their tribe; and custom, in the East, is a religion.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: Wise policies, such as welfare reform and drug education and support for abstinence and adoption have made a difference in the character of our country.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Difficult to understand; obscure.
etymology: From Latin abstrusus "concealed," past participle of abstrudere "to thrust away, hide."

examples.text: In a thousand ways he smoothed for me the path of knowledge and made the most abstruse inquiries clear and facile to my apprehension.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: The Golden Dustman seeming to be engaged in some abstruse calculation, Mr Wegg assisted him with the following additional items.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And this is incident to none but those, that converse in questions of matters incomprehensible, as the Schoole-men; or in questions of abstruse Philosophy.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

definition: A deep or seemingly bottomless chasm; a vast, immeasurable depth or a catastrophic situation.
etymology: From Greek abyssos "bottomless," from a- "without" + byssos "bottom."

examples.text: The shark, though, seems to be excluded from life in the abysses because of a lack of food down there and the relatively high buoyancy of its liver, says the paper, by Professor Imants Priede of Scotland's University of Aberdeen.
I feel as if I were walking on the edge of a precipice, towards which thousands are crowding and endeavouring to plunge me into the abyss.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Through all this ordeal his root horror had been isolation, and there are no words to express the abyss between isolation and having one ally.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: To agree to a demand, request, or treaty; to assume an office or position.
etymology: From Latin accedere "to approach, assent," from ad- "to" + cedere "to go, yield."

examples.text: Alyosha reflected that it was better to accede to the mamma's request, or else she would be sending down to Lise's room every minute that he was there.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: As usual, sixteen implicitly acceded to the dictum of seventeen in such a matter, and said that he certainly was not nice.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: I acceded to this the more readily, because I now reproached myself with having treated her former letter rather lightly.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To praise enthusiastically and publicly; enthusiastic public praise.
etymology: From Latin acclamare "to shout at," from ad- "to" + clamare "to shout."

examples.text: He also won acclaim in the country arena with his interpretations of Hank Williams standards such as Your Cheating Heart and You Win Again.
examples.source: BBC News, “Lasting influence of legend Charles”

examples.text: It breeds as quickly as the yeoman, and as soundly; strong is the temptation to acclaim it as a super-yeoman, who carries his country's virtue overseas.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: And to the Congress and to all Americans, I say it is time to acclaim a new consensus at home and abroad, a common vision of the peaceful world we want to see.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: An award or expression of praise or admiration.
etymology: From French accolade "embrace," from Italian accollare "to embrace around the neck," referring to the embrace given when conferring knighthood.

examples.text: The US movie also picked up four other accolades including best director for Alexander Payne and supporting actor for Thomas Haden Church.
examples.source: BBC News, “Wine comedy wins critics' award”

examples.text: The highest accolade in veterinary science has been awarded to a man partly responsible for the success of brahman cattle in northern Australia.
Last month, they were the big winners in Ireland's top music honours, the Meteor Awards, picking up accolades for best band and album.
examples.source: BBC News, “Snow Patrol bassist exits group”

definition: To approach and address someone boldly or aggressively.
etymology: From French accoster, from Latin ad- "to" + costa "rib, side," originally "to come alongside."

examples.text: The Englishman, with the coolness of his nation, addressed him in terms nearly similar to those with which he had accosted the mayor of Marseilles.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: When Jeff arrived, Tom accosted him; and "led up" warily to opportunities for remark about Becky, but the giddy lad never could see the bait.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: I had meant to be gay and careless, but the powerlessness of the strong man touched my heart to the quick: still I accosted him with what vivacity I could.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Gradual growth or increase by the addition of new layers or parts; something added in this way.
etymology: From Latin accretio, from accrescere "to grow," from ad- "to" + crescere "to grow."

examples.text: It's another bit of evidence for the now widely accepted cannibal, or accretion, theory of galactic evolution, Parker says.
The mass would be likely to remain nearly the same, assimilating constantly to itself its gradual accretions.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Few women had tried more earnestly to pierce the accretions in which body and soul are enwrapped.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: The point at which someone or something is best, most successful, or most perfect.
etymology: From Greek akmē "highest point, prime."

examples.text: The acme of bliss, which would have been a marriage with the tragedian, was not for her in this world.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: Mine has been a tale of horrors; I have reached their acme, and what I must now relate can but be tedious to you.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Just as "Uncle's" pickled mushrooms, honey, and cherry brandy had seemed to her the best in the world, so also that song, at that moment, seemed to her the acme of musical delight.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: To accept or comply with something reluctantly but without protest.
etymology: From Latin acquiescere "to rest, be at ease," from ad- "to" + quiescere "to rest."

examples.text: Archer acquiesced, and she turned the ponies down Narragansett Avenue, crossed Spring Street and drove out toward the rocky moorland beyond.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: He acquiescing, we followed at a distance: never losing sight of her, but never caring to come very near, as she frequently looked about.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: How the public debt is to be paid or specie payments resumed is not so important as that a plan should be adopted and acquiesced in.
examples.author: Ulysses S. Grant

definition: Unpleasantly sharp, pungent, or bitter to smell or taste; harsh or bitter in temper or speech.
etymology: From Latin acer, acris "sharp, pungent," formed on the model of "acid."

examples.text: London traders said the Asian cocoa was considered unsuitable for western palates because of an acrid odour and a high level of free fatty acids.
examples.source: Reuters, “Asian Cocoa Producers Expand Despite Critics”

examples.text: There was no need to think them dead, for their stertorous breathing and the acrid smell of laudanum in the room left no doubt as to their condition.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: As I entered, however, my fears were set at rest, for it was the acrid fumes of strong coarse tobacco which took me by the throat and set me coughing.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Bitterness or ill feeling, especially in speech or debate.
etymology: From Latin acrimonia "sharpness," from acer "sharp."

examples.text: Babyshambles, which he formed after his acrimonious departure from the Libertines, played a warm-up show at The Garage, north London, on Monday.
examples.source: BBC News, “Rocker Doherty in on-stage fight”

examples.text: It may have been that Mrs Lammle tried in some manner to excuse her conduct to herself by depreciating the poor little victim of whom she spoke with acrimonious contempt.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He said: "It is wrong to waste the precious gift of time, on acrimony and division."
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: To cause a machine or device to operate; to motivate someone to act in a particular way.
etymology: From Medieval Latin actuare "to carry out," from Latin actus "a doing, act."

examples.text: But there are higher considerations than either of those, and I hope I shall be forgiven if I now allow myself to be actuated solely by them.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: When actuated by selfish and vicious motives, I asked you to undertake my unfinished work, and I renew this request now, when I am only induced by reason and virtue.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: These opinions have been adopted in the firm belief that they are in accordance with the spirit that actuated the venerated fathers of the Republic, and that succeeding experience has proved them to be humane, patriotic, expedient, honorable, and just.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: The ability to make good judgments and quick, accurate decisions, especially in a particular field.
etymology: From Latin acumen "a point, sharpness," from acuere "to sharpen." The same root gives "acute" and "acupuncture."

examples.text: For a man who was never in the country, and who did not evidently do much in the way of business, his knowledge and acumen were wonderful.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: When they went down, uncle Pullet observed, with some acumen, that he reckoned the missis had been showing her bonnet,—that was what had made them so long upstairs.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But when St. John had mused a few moments he recommenced as imperturbably and with as much acumen as ever.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: A short, traditional saying expressing a general truth.
etymology: From French adage, from Latin adagium "proverb."

examples.text: "There is an old adage, 'get straight back on the horse that threw you,'" Richards told BBC Sport.
That experience is the parent of wisdom, is an adage the truth of which is recognized by the wisest as well as the simplest of mankind.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Charley verified the adage about little pitchers, I am sure, for she heard of more sayings and doings in a day than would have come to my ears in a month.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind; unyielding.
etymology: From Greek adamas "untamable, invincible," later the name of a legendary hard stone, from a- "not" + daman "to tame."

examples.text: I grieve for the future of my children, it's no wonder they're adamant they don't ever want any of their own.

Shultz was said to be adamantly against the U.S. wheat offer last year and has been reported to be one of the major obstacles in making another subsidy overture to the Soviet Union, grain industry sources said.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Grain Trade Calls Shultz Remark Significant”

examples.text: A force within them, and yet quite beyond them, seemed slowly and pitilessly washing away the adamant of their oath.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: To warn or reprimand someone firmly, often gently but earnestly; to advise against something.
etymology: From Latin admonere "to remind, warn," from ad- "to" + monere "to warn" (compare "monitor").

examples.text: Last week, the firm was admonished by the Securities and Exchange Commission which said it had made major errors in its financial reporting.
examples.source: BBC News, “Senior Fannie Mae bosses resign”

examples.text: The President again briefly, but impressively, admonished him to answer only what was asked, and not to go off into irrelevant exclamations.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Other considerations of the highest importance admonish us to cherish our Union and to cling to the Government which supports it.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: A firm warning or reprimand; cautionary advice.
etymology: From Latin admonitio, from admonere "to remind, warn," from ad- "to" + monere "to warn."

examples.text: She remembered having submitted to his admonition on a different occasion when she was expected to like a very different prospect.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: She was disheartened by Lady Bertram's silence, awed by Sir Thomas's grave looks, and quite overcome by Mrs. Norris's admonitions.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: These interests are exposed to invasion in the wars between other powers, and we should disregard the faithful admonition of experience if we did not expect it.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Clever or skillful in using the hands or mind; deft in handling situations.
etymology: From French à droit "according to right, properly," from Latin directus "straight."

examples.text: A few adroit words, one or two knowing tender glances of the eyes, and his heart was inflamed again and his doubts and suspicions forgotten.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Then he descended with cautious and slow step, for he dreaded lest an accident similar to that he had so adroitly feigned should happen in reality.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: He told her about the election, and Anna knew how by adroit questions to bring him to what gave him most pleasure—his own success.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Excessive admiration or praise.
etymology: From Latin adulatio, from adulari "to fawn upon, flatter."

examples.text: "There's no point in him demanding praise and adulation for setting a whole new raft of targets when he has so woefully failed to meet the ones he already has," added Mr Duncan.
examples.source: BBC News, “Brown to outline presidency goals”

examples.text: He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave, and is obliged to practise the greatest adulation and servility, and to be the flatterer of the vilest of mankind.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: Their nauseous adulation of princely patrons was more prominent to me and chained my attention more surely than the charms of color and expression which are claimed to be in the pictures.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To make something poorer in quality by adding another, inferior substance.
etymology: From Latin adulterare "to corrupt, falsify," from ad- "to" + alter "other."

examples.text: I suppose one reason why we are seldom able to comfort our neighbours with our words is that our goodwill gets adulterated, in spite of ourselves, before it can pass our lips.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He was in the same plight as the manufacturer who has to adulterate and misrepresent his product.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: She offered to them good, honest household cake made of currants and flour and eggs and sweetmeat, but they would feed themselves on trashy wafers from the shop of the Barchester pastry-cook, on chalk and gum and adulterated sugar.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Difficulties or misfortune; a state of hardship.
etymology: From Latin adversitas, from adversus "turned against," from ad- "to" + vertere "to turn."

examples.text: By encouraging hope, called "positive illusions," our distant ancestors could cope with adversity, strengthen their resolve and bluff their opponents.
It comes with sickness, it comes with sorrow, it comes with the loss of the dearly loved, it is one of the most frequent uses of adversity.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I see America today crossing a threshold, not just because it is our Bicentennial but because we have been tested in adversity.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: Concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty; (noun) a set of principles underlying an artistic style or taste.
etymology: From Greek aisthētikos "of sense perception," from aisthanesthai "to perceive."

examples.text: But now a new vision is surfacing, where smart fabrics and textiles will be exploited to enhance functionality, form, or aesthetics.
Hitherto he had found, in her presence and her talk, the aesthetic amusement which a reflective man is apt to seek in desultory intercourse with pretty women.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: The pretty colour of the first, the affected drawing of the second, had entirely satisfied his aesthetic sensibilities.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Friendly, good-natured, and easy to talk to.
etymology: From Latin affabilis "easy to speak to," from ad- "to" + fari "to speak."

examples.text: Mr Ebbers' team, meanwhile, are looking to portray him as an affable boss, who by his own admission is more PE graduate than economist.
As the conductor went on his affable way, huge watch-chain jingling against his blue chest, Babbitt and Ted gravely considered colleges.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: He went up to Madame Stahl, and addressed her with extreme courtesy and affability in that excellent French that so few speak nowadays.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Behavior, speech, or manner that is artificial and designed to impress.
etymology: From Latin affectatio "a striving after," from affectare "to aim at, pretend to have."

examples.text: Its Literature and Art have what one might call the kink of the unseen about them, and this persists even through decadence and affectation.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: The others all followed, dispirited and shamefaced, and only much later were they able to regain their former affectation of indifference.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: She had even learnt to detect, in the very gentleness which had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness to disgust and weary.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: A natural liking for or sympathy with someone or something; a close similarity or resemblance.
etymology: From Latin affinitas "relationship by marriage," from affinis "bordering on, related," from ad- "to" + finis "border."

examples.text: "It is very hard to work with people out there that have got an affinity with an animal, so it's a kind of tread lightly area," he said.
It was not in Bertha's habits to be neighbourly, much less to make advances to any one outside the immediate circle of her affinities.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Was there some subtle affinity between the chemical atoms that shaped themselves into form and colour on the canvas and the soul that was within him?
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

definition: An action or remark that causes outrage or offense; (verb) to offend the modesty or values of.
etymology: From Old French afronter "to strike on the forehead, confront," from Latin ad frontem "to the face."

examples.text: And, almost as though it were a personal affront, he declared, on the spot, that he was bored, sat down on the sofa and immediately fell asleep.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Thus they descended to the precincts of her father's homestead, and Arabella went in, nodding good-bye to him with a supercilious, affronted air.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: And he cursed his past follies and extravagances, and bemoaned his vast outlying debts above all, which must remain for ever as obstacles to prevent his wife's advancement in the world.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: The utterance of a blessing, especially at the end of a religious service; a state of being blessed.
etymology: From Latin benedictio, from benedicere "to speak well of, bless," from bene "well" + dicere "to speak."

examples.text: Now it is understood that he has composed an original speech of congratulation and benediction, and this is one of the events of the day.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: Returning to the Spouter-Inn from the Chapel, I found Queequeg there quite alone; he having left the Chapel before the benediction some time.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Mankind needs a world-wide benediction of understanding.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: A person who gives money or other help to a person, cause, or institution.
etymology: From Latin benefactor, from bene facere "to do well, do good."

examples.text: So speculation continues about the new benefactor, with trails leading to the Middle East and America, but all met with an understandable veil of secrecy from Anfield.
She thought of these and of the man who had been her constant protector, her good genius, her sole benefactor, her tender and generous friend.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: We should become their real benefactors; we should perform the office of their Great Father, the endearing title which they emphatically give to the Chief Magistrate of our Union.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Doing or producing good; actively kind and charitable.
etymology: From Latin beneficus "generous, doing good," from bene "well" + facere "to do."

examples.text: With this beneficent wish, Mr. Snagsby coughs a cough of dismal resignation and submits himself to hear what the visitor has to communicate.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The honour of great Persons, is to be valued for their beneficence, and the aydes they give to men of inferiour rank, or not at all.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: Resting upon this sure and substantial foundation, the superstructure of beneficent local governments can be built up, and not otherwise.
examples.author: Rutherford B. Hayes

definition: Well meaning and kindly; serving a charitable rather than profit-making purpose.
etymology: From Latin bene "well" + volens "wishing," from velle "to wish."

examples.text: I know no man more likely than Mr. Knightley to do the sort of thing—to do any thing really good-natured, useful, considerate, or benevolent.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Is it not (we may ask these projectors in politics) the true interest of all nations to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit?
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: If national pride is ever justifiable or excusable it is when it springs, not from power or riches, grandeur or glory, but from conviction of national innocence, information, and benevolence.
examples.author: John Adams

definition: Gentle and kindly; harmless or favorable; of a disease, not malignant.
etymology: From Old French benigne, from Latin benignus "kindly," from bene "well" + a root meaning "born."

examples.text: Spyware comes in many forms and at its most benign exploits lazy browsing habits to install itself and subject users to unwanted adverts.
examples.source: BBC News, “Microsoft sets sights on spyware”

examples.text: Then he would shake his head benignly, and over the ever-clicking rosary point out how free that elephant-calf was from the sin of pride.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: Union is recommended as well by the free and benign principles of our Government, extending its blessings to every individual, as by the other eminent advantages attending it.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: To leave property to someone by a will; to hand down or pass on to later generations.
etymology: From Old English becwethan "to declare, leave by will," from be- + cwethan "to say" (compare archaic "quoth").

examples.text: Far from being a dead branch of the human tree, the Neanderthals may even have bequeathed some of the traits in the H. sapiens genome that we see today.
He had bequeathed to her all that he possessed, and that comprised an income much exceeding what she or her friends thought necessary for her.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: It degrades to the purposes of wily craft the plan of rule our fathers established and bequeathed to us as an object of our love and veneration.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Deprived of or lacking something; sad and lonely, especially after a death or loss.
etymology: Past participle of "bereave," from Old English bereafian "to deprive, rob."

examples.text: Scotland looked bereft of ideas but a half-break from Paterson sparked them back to life just before the hour.
And as the tigress bereft of her young will turn with equal anger on any within reach, so did Mrs. Proudie turn upon her female guest.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: This appalling sight almost bereft me of my senses, and finding that I could no longer be of service to any one in the house, my only desire was to fly.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: To ask someone urgently and fervently; to beg or implore.
etymology: From Middle English bisechen, from be- (intensive) + sechen "to seek."

examples.text: When she dropped her pose and smiled down she discovered Kennicott apoplectic with domestic pride—and gray Guy Pollock staring beseechingly.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The monk, overwhelmed with sorrow, went to the OEcumenical Patriarch at Constantinople and besought him to release him from his obedience.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In our quest of understanding, we beseech God's guidance.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To surround a place with armed forces to force surrender; to crowd around or overwhelm with requests or complaints.

examples.text: Plunked down in the middle of the violence, players must make it to a water well and try to survive for seven days in a camp besieged by militia.
He was out of spirits and slightly out of temper, and a haunting horror of doing the same thing every day at the same hour besieged his brain.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: They did so, and the besieging party grew noisy and more and more abusive as the fact became apparent (to them) that our men were afraid to come out.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To damage someone's reputation; literally, to soil or make dirty.
etymology: From be- + "smirch" "to soil, stain."

examples.text: At the present instant one of the most revered names in England is being besmirched by a blackmailer, and only I can stop a disastrous scandal.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: There were too many people, provincials with foolish faces, foreigners poring over guide-books; their hideousness besmirched the everlasting masterpieces, their restlessness troubled the god's immortal repose.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Kalganov looked as though he had been besmirched with dirt.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: A flattering or pleasing statement or action used to persuade someone gently to do something.
etymology: From "blandish," from Old French blandir, from Latin blandiri "to flatter," from blandus "smooth-talking."

examples.text: They trusted to the sign to inveigle foreigners into their lairs, and trusted to their own blandishments to keep them there till they bought something.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: The ordeal through which he had gone in resisting the blandishments of the lady of Rome had certainly done much towards the strengthening of his character.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Nations that are conscious of a steady improvement in their industry, education, health and standard of living are not apt to fall prey to the blandishments of communist imperialists.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Speaking irreverently about God or sacred things; disrespect toward something regarded as sacrosanct.
etymology: From Greek blasphemia "slander, profane speech," via Latin and Old French.

examples.text: Pullman's trilogy has been attacked by some Christian teachers and by the Catholic press as blasphemy.
examples.source: BBC News, “God cut from Dark Materials film”

examples.text: He had been accustomed to eat it himself, as it seemed blasphemous to throw it away, but Philip's keen appetite relieved him from the duty.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Its teachings are good and peaceful, and those who commit evil in the name of Allah blaspheme the name of Allah.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Done openly and unashamedly; completely obvious, especially of something bad.
etymology: Apparently coined by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene (1596) for the "blatant beast," a monster of slander.

examples.text: Like every track Robbie has released as a single, it's a blatant but poor facsimile of something that someone else has done better before.
examples.source: BBC News, “Scissor Sisters triumph at Brits”

examples.text: He says while blatant racism is not tolerated in mainstream films or television, in video games "it's below the radar".
Had he been a girl—my friend wrote—one could have said he was blooming—blooming modestly—like a violet, not like some of these blatant tropical flowers.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Something that spoils or damages; a plant disease; (verb) to spoil, harm, or destroy.

examples.text: New Zealand apple growers have questioned the ability of Australian quarantine workers to inspect their orchards for the plant disease fire blight.
If the likeness of that face don't turn to burning fire, at the thought of offering money to me for my child's blight and ruin, it's as bad.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And while the blight of communism has been increasingly exposed and isolated in the Americas, liberty has scored a gain.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: Showing casual, often improper indifference; carefree and cheerful.
etymology: From Old English blithe "joyous, kind, gentle."

examples.text: The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

examples.text: How blithely she sang that evening, and how they all laughed at her because she woke Amy in the night by playing the piano on her face in her sleep.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: On the present festive occasion he emerged from his room, when the blithe bells were going, the picture of misery, in a full suit of Sunday penitentials.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To talk loudly, aggressively, or boastfully with little effect; (noun) such loud, empty talk.

examples.text: It was mere swagger and challenge; but in this particular, as in many others, blustering assertion goes for proof, half over the world.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She knew that he loved her—a frank, blustering fellow without guile enough to conceal his feelings, and no desire to do so.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: But when I gave him every particular that had occurred, he tried to bluster and took down a life-preserver from the wall.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Noisy, energetic, and cheerful; rowdy.

examples.text: Delight is to him, whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: He saw that Philip was depressed by what he had gone through and with unaffected kindliness set himself boisterously to cheer him up.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Any body's and every body's notion of a pleasure excursion is that the parties to it will of a necessity be young and giddy and somewhat boisterous.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To support or strengthen; to prop up.
etymology: Old English bolster "long pillow, cushion." The verb sense "prop up," as with a pillow, dates from the 1500s.

examples.text: Miller's remarks reflected concern that the U.S. central bank might feel compelled to tighten credit as a means of bolstering the dollar.
examples.source: Reuters, “Budget Chief Miller Warns Fed On Interest Rates”

examples.text: For this is one of those disheartening instances where truth requires full as much bolstering as error.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: So, we must prepare for peace not only by reducing weapons but by bolstering prosperity, liberty, and democracy however and wherever we can.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: A thing that is helpful or beneficial; a blessing.
etymology: From Old Norse bon "prayer, request"; the sense shifted from a favor asked to a favor granted.

examples.text: Economists point out that whatever Europe says, in the short term a weaker dollar is a boon to President George W Bush's administration.
examples.source: BBC News, “Europe blames US over weak dollar”

examples.text: Whoever embarked on a policy of the sort, he said, and ventilated the matter thoroughly would confer a lasting boon on everybody concerned.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: If we have the brain power to invent these machines, we have the brain power to make certain that they are a boon and not a bane to humanity.
examples.author: Lyndon B. Johnson

definition: Rough and bad-mannered; coarse and insensitive.
etymology: From "boor," from Dutch boer "farmer, peasant."

examples.text: Don Quixote laughed at Sancho's boorish eulogies and thought that, saving his lady Dulcinea del Toboso, he had never seen a more beautiful woman.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: These, after exhausting other modes of amusement, now thronged about Hester Prynne with rude and boorish intrusiveness.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: We became particularly hot upon some boorish sneer of Drummle's, to the effect that we were too free with our money.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: A person who boasts loudly about achievements or possessions.

examples.text: I was quite conscious of the possibility that the whole was the extravagance of an old braggart and gossip.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: At first they laughed at him, called him a little liar, a braggart, but that only egged him on.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The sculptors of those days had stocks of such funereal emblems in hand; as you may see still on the walls of St. Paul's, which are covered with hundreds of these braggart heathen allegories.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: A bold manner or show of courage intended to impress or intimidate, often masking fear.
etymology: From Spanish bravada, from bravo "bold."

examples.text: "Though the battles have the blood-and-sinew bravado you expect from Oliver Stone, this three-hour buttnumbathon is hamstrung by a hectoring grandiosity," wrote one reviewer in Rolling Stone magazine.
examples.source: BBC News, “Box office blow for Alexander”

examples.text: Such a paradox they could not understand, and therefore sank into listless indifference, or shiftlessness, or reckless bravado.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: The extraordinary mixture of prompt decision, far-sighted cunning, and mountebank bravado in this speech, staggered me for a moment—and only for a moment.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Bold and without shame; literally, made of brass.
etymology: From Old English bræsen "made of brass."

examples.text: Prince Harry should see for himself "the results of the hated symbol he so foolishly and brazenly chose to wear", Rabbi Marvin Hier, founder of Jewish human rights group the Simon Wiesenthal Center said.
examples.source: BBC News, “Straw to attend Auschwitz service”

examples.text: At her third ascent the rick suddenly brightened with the brazen glare of shining majolica—every knot in every straw was visible.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: The deficient buttons on his plaid frock had evidently been supplied from one of Mr. Jellyby's coats, they were so extremely brazen and so much too large.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Concise and exact use of words; shortness of duration.
etymology: From Latin brevitas, from brevis "short."

examples.text: He answered, as it were, reluctantly, with extreme brevity, with a sort of disgust which grew more and more marked, though he answered rationally.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But what plays the mischief with this masterly code is the admirable brevity of it, which necessitates a vast volume of commentaries to expound it.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: These were all the speeches that were made, and I recommend them to parties who present policemen with gold watches, as models of brevity and point.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To raise a sensitive or difficult subject for discussion; to pierce a container to draw out liquid.
etymology: From Old French brochier "to pierce," from broche "spike, pointed tool."

examples.text: She had been told that this was the only safe way to carry money in Italy; it must only be broached within the walls of the English bank.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: I could see that he had something on his mind which he wanted to say, but felt some hesitancy about broaching the subject.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: He hasn't broached the question sooner because their return was uncertain—seemed in fact for the present impossible.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: Abrupt or offhand in speech or manner; curt.
etymology: From French brusque "lively, fierce," from Italian brusco "sour, tart."

examples.text: But she saw or she imagined that the women who had gurgled at her so welcomingly when she had first come to Gopher Prairie were nodding at her brusquely.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: And then I made a brusque movement, and one of the remaining posts of that vanished fence leaped up in the field of my glass.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Any mention of her 'works' always had a bad effect upon Jo, who either grew rigid and looked offended, or changed the subject with a brusque remark, as now.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: Relating to the pleasant aspects of the countryside or country life; pastoral.
etymology: From Greek boukolikos "pastoral," from boukolos "cowherd," from bous "ox."

examples.text: The bucolic character at Hayslope, you perceive, was not of that entirely genial, merry, broad-grinning sort, apparently observed in most districts visited by artists.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: In the question of the grazing lands his peevish asperity is notorious and in Mr Cuffe's hearing brought upon him from an indignant rancher a scathing retort couched in terms as straightforward as they were bucolic.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Nor was he interested in the dim, bucolic past.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: A ridiculous but amusing person; a clown or fool.
etymology: From Italian buffone "jester," from buffa "joke."

examples.text: Ivan and Miuesov would come from curiosity, perhaps of the coarsest kind, while his father might be contemplating some piece of buffoonery.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: And just as the buffoon and satyr are foreign to him in body and conscience, so Aristophanes and Petronius are untranslatable for him.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: She must not be touched by the buffoons, nor by the ignorant vulgar, incapable of comprehending or appreciating her hidden treasures.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: A defensive wall; a person or thing that acts as a defense or safeguard.
etymology: From Middle Dutch bolwerc, probably from bole "tree trunk, plank" + werc "work."

examples.text: Here I expect we shall be told that the militia of the country is its natural bulwark, and would be at all times equal to the national defense.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: The inherited stupidity of the race—sound English common sense he jovially termed it—was shown to be the proper bulwark for society.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

examples.text: But the bulwark of our defense is the national militia, which in the present state of our intelligence and population must render us invincible.
examples.author: Andrew Jackson

definition: To polish by rubbing; to enhance or improve a reputation or image.
etymology: From Old French burnir "to make brown, polish," from brun "brown."

examples.text: Toyota has led the market to date with the Prius, popularised by a number of celebrities keen to burnish their "green" credentials.
examples.source: BBC News, “US prepares for hybrid onslaught”

examples.text: The fields were burnished in sun and wind with the colour of kingfisher and parrot and humming-bird, the hues of a hundred flowering flowers.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: It was a rather curious one of Moorish workmanship, made of dull silver inlaid with arabesques of burnished steel, and studded with coarse turquoises.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

definition: To support or strengthen; (noun) a structure built against a wall for support, or any source of support.

examples.text: On the highest point stood the church—an ancient, weather-beaten building, with heavy buttresses at its sides, and a clumsy square tower in front.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: They skirted a shoulder painfully for hours, and, behold, it was but an outlying boss in an outlying buttress of the main pile!
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: I should say here that we have much reason to be proud of the progress our people are making in mutual understanding—the chief buttress of human and civil rights.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: A secret political clique or faction plotting for its own ends.
etymology: From French cabale, from medieval Latin cabala, ultimately from Hebrew qabbalah "tradition" (the source of "kabbalah").

examples.text: Every mere council of appointment, however constituted, will be a conclave, in which cabal and intrigue will have their full scope.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: It has ever been one of the objects of my life—which, unfortunately, has not had many objects—to be inoffensive, and to keep out of cabals and interferences.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But the Subalterns' and Captains' ladies (the Major is unmarried) cabal against her a good deal.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: A rhythmic rise and fall of the voice or sounds; a regular beat; in music, a closing sequence of chords.
etymology: From Latin cadere "to fall," via Italian cadenza and Old French.

examples.text: The child went singing away, following up the current of the brook, and striving to mingle a more lightsome cadence with its melancholy voice.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: Deronda paused in his pleading: his mother looked at him listeningly, as if the cadence of his voice were taking her ear, yet she shook her head slowly.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He made Kim learn whole chapters of the Koran by heart, till he could deliver them with the very roll and cadence of a mullah.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

definition: To persuade someone by flattery or gentle, persistent coaxing.
etymology: From French cajoler "to coax, flatter."

examples.text: At first, doubtless, he must flatter and cajole, perhaps yield in some things, but he did not doubt of ultimate triumph.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: But there is a patent defence at hand,—the defence of deception and flattery, of cajoling and lying.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: Such tender cajolery served to quiet the mother, as it had often done before after like collisions.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: An event causing great and often sudden damage or distress; a disaster.
etymology: From Latin calamitas "damage, disaster."

examples.text: It is the third year at Hogwarts and studies are interrupted, as they always are, by a calamity that only Harry, Ron and Hermione can put right.
examples.source: BBC News, “DVD review: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban”

examples.text: In wandering round the shattered walls and through the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the calamity was not of late occurrence.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: We must strive to break the calamitous cycle of frustrations and crises which, if unchecked, could spiral into nuclear disaster; the ultimate insanity.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Showing cruel disregard for others; emotionally hardened and insensitive.
etymology: From Latin callosus "hard-skinned," from callum "hardened skin."

examples.text: In the course of a month or two after the receipt of the books Jude had grown callous to the shabby trick played him by the dead languages.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Sometimes, though, he is not at all morbid, but simply cold and inhumanly callous; it's as though he were alternating between two characters.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: He remembered with what a callous selfishness his uncle had treated her, how obtuse he had been to her humble, devoted love.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: The making of false and damaging statements about someone to harm their reputation; slander.
etymology: From Latin calumnia "trickery, false accusation."

examples.text: It would be a calumny on Mrs. Proudie to suggest that she was sitting in her bedroom with her ear at the keyhole during this interview.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He had only just been protesting against Luzhin's calumny and declaring that he had seen the girl last night for the first time, and suddenly she had walked in.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: An attempt at divorce could lead to nothing but a public scandal, which would be a perfect godsend to his enemies for calumny and attacks on his high position in society.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Truthful and straightforward; frank; of a photograph, taken informally.
etymology: From Latin candidus "white, pure, sincere," from candere "to shine."

examples.text: A documentary which takes a candid look at the life of chart-topping singer George Michael will be shown at this year's Berlin Film Festival.
examples.source: BBC News, “Singer's film to show at festival”

examples.text: She blushed when Vronsky brought in Golenishtchev, and he was extremely charmed by this childish blush overspreading her candid and handsome face.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Since our hope is peace, we owe ourselves and the world a candid explanation of the military measures we are taking to make that peace secure.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: The quality of being open, honest, and sincere in expression; frankness.
etymology: From Latin candor "whiteness, purity, sincerity," from candere "to shine."

examples.text: It is my rule never to make unnecessary mysteries, and never to set people suspecting me for want of a little seasonable candour on my part.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: So, in a word, Briggs told all her history, and Becky gave a narrative of her own life, with her usual artlessness and candour.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Because our strengths are so great, we can afford to appraise our weaknesses with candor and to approach them with hope.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: Having or showing shrewdness and good judgment, especially in money or business.
etymology: A Scottish formation from "can" in the sense "know how."

examples.text: Charles Kennedy is far too canny to make any grand claims about how his party may fare at the general election.
Fuller was the driving force behind the Spice Girls phenomenon, using canny marketing and catchy pop songs to secure their place as the most lucrative girl group in history.
examples.source: BBC News, “Music mogul Fuller sells company”

examples.text: It is the sort of move you would expect from Walter, who is a canny manager.
examples.source: BBC News, “Time to get tough on friendlies?”

definition: Having a lot of space inside; roomy.
etymology: From Latin capax "able to hold much," from capere "to take, hold."

examples.text: In the capacious belly of the ox were a dozen soft little sucking-pigs, which, sewn up there, served to give it tenderness and flavour.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: They crawl all over him, popping in and out of his waistcoat, and sitting in couples, white as snow, on his capacious shoulders.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: I have no one near me, gentle yet courageous, possessed of a cultivated as well as of a capacious mind, whose tastes are like my own, to approve or amend my plans.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: Given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behavior.
etymology: From Italian capriccio "a sudden start," popularly linked with capra "goat," as if moving with a goat's unpredictable leaps.

examples.text: After sipping a dozen spoonfuls of tea, he suddenly released his head, pushed the spoon away capriciously, and sank back on the pillow.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: And all this was to have come without study or other inconvenience, purely by the favor of providence in the shape of an old gentleman's caprice.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But the next morning when he awoke he felt rather vexed with her, and decided that she was rather unreasonable, not to say capricious.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Tending to find fault or raise petty objections.
etymology: From Latin captiosus "sophistical, deceptive," from captio "a taking, deceiving."

examples.text: We are not boy and girl, to be captiously irritable, misled by every moment's inadvertence, and wantonly playing with our own happiness.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Georgiana, who had a spoiled temper, a very acrid spite, a captious and insolent carriage, was universally indulged.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: "A little too fond," said Mr. Featherstone, captiously.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: A depiction exaggerating certain features for comic or grotesque effect; (verb) to portray in this way.
etymology: From Italian caricatura, from caricare "to load, exaggerate."

examples.text: Joshua Reynolds: The Creation of Celebrity will feature prints, caricatures, and sculpture by the 18th Century artist, who painted some of the most famous personalities of his day.
examples.source: BBC News, “Public show for Reynolds portrait”

examples.text: Indeed, in the wild school of caricature then current, Mr Max Beerbohm had represented him as a proposition in the fourth book of Euclid.

examples.text: Tom partly uncovered a dismal caricature of a house with two gable ends to it and a corkscrew of smoke issuing from the chimney.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To drink plenty of alcohol and enjoy oneself with others in a noisy, lively way.
etymology: From German gar aus "all out," as in drinking a cup to the bottom.

examples.text: Archer turned from the fascinated contemplation of a small painting representing two Cardinals carousing, in an octagonal ebony frame set with medallions of onyx.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: He had been in Mokroe more than once before, he had caroused there for two days together already, he knew the old big house with all its passages and outbuildings.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: When they had brought her to the Hall the maiden was placed in an upper chamber, while Hugo and his friends sat down to a long carouse, as was their nightly custom.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: To reprimand someone severely.
etymology: From Latin castigare "to correct, punish," from castus "pure" (also the source of "chaste").

She was in a very paroxysm of self-castigation, and, concluding, she looked with defiant resolution at the elder.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: "I suppose," observes Volumnia, having taken a little time to recover her spirits after her late castigation, "I suppose Mr. Tulkinghorn has been worked to death."

definition: Unambiguously explicit and direct; absolute and without qualification.

examples.text: She categorically denied reports that her beliefs on issues such as contraception would make her refuse to serve as a health or international development minister.
examples.source: BBC News, “Kelly trails new discipline power”

examples.text: Apart from the value of such assertions as "there is a categorical imperative in us," one can always ask: What does such an assertion indicate about him who makes it?
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: Earlier I made mention of changing categorical grants to States and local governments into block grants.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Able to burn or corrode organic tissue by chemical action; sarcastic in a scathing and bitter way.
etymology: From Greek kaustikos "capable of burning," from kaiein "to burn" (also in "cauterize").

examples.text: "I'm not going to be the Mr Nasty of books," said Cowell, 54, in reference to his brother's caustic remarks on TV shows Pop Idol and The X-Factor.

examples.text: Mr Flintwinch, after scraping his chin, and looking about with caustic disparagement of the Pig-Market, nodded to Arthur, and followed.

examples.text: His—if I may say so—his caustic placidity, and, at the same time, his intelligent sympathy with Jim's aspirations, appealed to me.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: To make petty or unnecessary objections; (noun) a trivial objection.
etymology: From Latin cavillari "to jeer, quibble."

examples.text: The count appeared, dressed with the greatest simplicity, but the most fastidious dandy could have found nothing to cavil at in his toilet.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: They ought not to have wandered into inflammatory declamations and unmeaning cavils about the extent of the powers.

examples.text: I am too gratified to get such a mark of your friendship at any price to cavil at the tone.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To give up power, territory, or a right, typically unwillingly.
etymology: From Latin cedere "to yield, go away."

examples.text: However, in the face of sterling's apparently inexorable climb, the authorities today decided to cede to pressure and allow a half-point cut.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.K. Issues One Billion Stg Bond Tranche”

examples.text: Nothing is more certain than the indispensable necessity of government, and it is equally undeniable, that whenever and however it is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights in order to vest it with requisite powers.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: We cannot cede to other nations the technology that will power new jobs and new industries, we must claim its promise.
examples.author: Barack Obama

definition: Swiftness of movement or action.
etymology: From Latin celeritas, from celer "swift."

examples.text: As he thundered out this he made a rush at Bildad, but with a marvellous oblique, sliding celerity, Bildad for that time eluded him.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: But hardly had he tasted a morsel when the man with the wand touched the plate with it, and they took it away from before him with the utmost celerity.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: They slid down behind it with remarkable celerity, and from this position they began briskly to slice up the blue men.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: To express severe, often formal disapproval of; (noun) such strong official criticism.
etymology: From Latin censura "judgment, assessment," from censere "to assess."

examples.text: Cavaco Silva's minority Social Democratic Party, PSD, was toppled in a parliamentary censure vote by left-wing parties.
examples.source: Reuters, “Portuguese Economy Remains Buoyant Despite Crisis”

examples.text: Undoubtedly the manner of asserting an opinion, even though it be a true one, may be very objectionable, and may justly incur severe censure.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: The decisions of upright and enlightened tribunals fall equally on all whose crimes subject them, by a fair interpretation of the law, to its censure.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical; relating to the brain.
etymology: From Latin cerebrum "brain."

examples.text: The humpbacks also have structures that resemble 'islands' in the cerebral cortex, also seen in some other mammals.
For two nights I had hardly had a wink of sleep, and my brain was beginning to feel that numbness which marks cerebral exhaustion.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: Two weeks later his wife, Judy, suffered a cerebral aneurysm.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: Distress or embarrassment at having failed or been humiliated.
etymology: From French chagrin "sorrow, grief."

examples.text: The media then called anything that had a swinging beat, syncopated melody or soulful feeling "Jazz", much to the chagrin of the artists.
The cover was lifted from within, and the pigeons flew away with a clatter that brought the chagrined poulterer cursing and swearing to the door.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: In her own past behaviour, there was a constant source of vexation and regret; and in the unhappy defects of her family, a subject of yet heavier chagrin.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: A person falsely claiming special knowledge or skill; a fraud.
etymology: From Italian ciarlatano, from ciarlare "to babble, chatter."

examples.text: They implied that he was insolent, pretentious, and given to that reckless innovation for the sake of noise and show which was the essence of the charlatan.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He was a charlatan but a successful charlatan, and in that was always something for the comic spirit to rejoice in.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Yet he was neither a charlatan nor a child; but a hot, logical Latin who liked a certain thing and was it.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Cautiously or suspiciously reluctant to do something; sparing in giving.
etymology: From Old English cearig "sorrowful, anxious," related to "care."

examples.text: What were his prospects that he should be so chary of running risk, when important and urgent labour could not be carried on without such risk?
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: As he had no idea of deceiving her, and always desired to please her, he was thus made chary of launching into expense.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Now they stretched themselves out on their elbows and began to puff, charily, and with slender confidence.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To rebuke or reprimand severely; formerly, to punish physically.
etymology: Related to "chasten," from Latin castigare "to correct, punish."

examples.text: It is this: The punishment which may be the consequence of conviction upon impeachment, is not to terminate the chastisement of the offender.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Spain chastised the Moors five or six years ago, about a disputed piece of property opposite Gibraltar, and captured the city of Tetouan.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: I did not need to be guided to the well-known room, to which I had so often been summoned for chastisement or reprimand in former days.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: To scold or rebuke mildly.
etymology: From Old English cidan "to quarrel, complain."

examples.text: The greatest punishment we could invent for her was to keep her separate from him: yet she got chided more than any of us on his account.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: There was the first of them, awaiting her upon the very portal; a robust old white-haired man, chiding her for returning home so late.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: Natasha, flushed and eager, seeing her mother in prayer, suddenly checked her rush, half sat down, and unconsciously put out her tongue as if chiding herself.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: An unrealistic or impossible hope or fantasy; in myth, a fire-breathing monster combining lion, goat, and serpent.
etymology: From Greek khimaira "she-goat," the name of the mythical monster.

examples.text: With his head bent, and his big feet spread apart, he began explaining his reasons for thinking the abbe's plan chimerical.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: And there was Don Quixote observing all these strange proceedings attentively without uttering a word, and attributing the whole to chimeras of knight-errantry.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: Besides, were not those riches chimerical?—offspring of the brain of the poor Abbe Faria, had they not died with him?
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Bad-tempered or irritable; easily angered.
etymology: From Greek kholē "bile"; in medieval medicine an excess of yellow bile was thought to cause anger.

examples.text: On hearing this the regimental commander hung his head, silently shrugged his shoulders, and spread out his arms with a choleric gesture.

examples.text: The choleric face which Mr Meagles turned upon him smoothed when he saw who it was, and he put out his friendly hand.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Gordon was a man by nature ill-suited to be a schoolmaster: he was impatient and choleric.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Rude in a mean-spirited and surly way; ungracious.
etymology: From "churl," Old English ceorl "peasant, common man."

examples.text: The Kiwis shocked the rugby world with a 9-3 triumph in Wellington, sparking great celebrations across the country, but Bedell-Sivright churlishly suggested that the victors would have no chance when they visited the UK.

examples.text: The passion for God: there are churlish, honest-hearted, and importunate kinds of it, like that of Luther—the whole of Protestantism lacks the southern DELICATEZZA.

examples.text: All this struck Ivan instantly; he took it all in and noted it at once—most of all the look in Smerdyakov's eyes, positively malicious, churlish and haughty.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Longer than the most direct way; indirect and roundabout.
etymology: From medieval Latin circuitosus, from Latin circuitus "a going around."

examples.text: During the U.S. Bombing of alleged terrorist targets in Libya last April, France refused to allow British-based U.S. Planes to overfly its territory, forcing them to take a circuitous route.

examples.text: He was anxious less the time should be consumed before this circuitous course of talk could lead them back to the topic he most cared about.

examples.text: At ten o'clock he came away, choosing a circuitous route homeward to pass the gates of the college whose head had just sent him the note.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: The use of many words where fewer would do, especially to be vague or evasive.
etymology: From Latin circumlocutio, from circum "around" + loqui "to speak."

examples.text: But here wee must take notice, that by a Name is not alwayes understood, as in Grammar, one onely word; but sometimes by circumlocution many words together.

examples.text: "Sir," said Madame de Saint-Meran, without using any circumlocution, and as if fearing she had no time to lose, "you wrote to me concerning the marriage of this child?"

examples.text: "I want to get a situation, uncle, so that I may earn some money," said Tom, who never fell into circumlocution.

definition: To restrict something within limits; in geometry, to draw a figure around another.
etymology: From Latin circumscribere, from circum "around" + scribere "to write, draw."

examples.text: Here, with you, everything is circumscribed, here all is formulated and geometrical, while we have nothing but indeterminate equations!

examples.text: We shall discover that the former are altogether unlimited, and that the latter are circumscribed within very moderate bounds.

examples.text: Life was cheaper because it was circumscribed: that most expensive luxury, the kind of life that can be changed at any moment, was no longer his nor did he wish for it.

definition: Wary and unwilling to take risks; careful to consider all circumstances.
etymology: From Latin circumspectus, from circumspicere "to look around."

examples.text: For as the swift monster drags you deeper and deeper into the frantic shoal, you bid adieu to circumspect life and only exist in a delirious throb.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: At the sight of that we crawled as circumspectly as possible out of the twilight of the kitchen into the darkness of the scullery.

examples.text: But on the subject of Count Fosco (who interests me infinitely more than his wife), Laura is provokingly circumspect and silent.

definition: To find a way around an obstacle or rule, often cleverly or deceptively.
etymology: From Latin circumvenire, from circum "around" + venire "to come."

examples.text: It circumvents Content Scrambling System measures placed on DVDs and let people make perfect digital copies of copyrighted DVDs in minutes.
He cited the example of a California company which transports live U.S. Cattle to Japan by air for slaughter to circumvent the beef quota.

examples.text: He gave Philip a slight smile, in which was a trace of satisfied cunning at having circumvented his enemy once more.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Kept secret or done secretively, especially because illicit.
etymology: From Latin clandestinus, from clam "secretly."

examples.text: And Chelsea boss Jose Mourinho had claimed that he was in Milan talking to Adriano on the day he is alleged to have held a clandestine meeting with Arsenal defender Ashley Cole.
