examples.text: That opening of the door which I had heard after I had returned to my room might mean that he had gone out to keep some clandestine appointment.

definition: Mercy or lenience, especially toward an offender; mildness of weather.
etymology: From Latin clementia, from clemens "mild, merciful."

examples.text: Once he asked the pensioner, in that general clemency which asked him anything to keep him afloat, how old his younger grandchild was?
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Oh, Frankenstein, be not equitable to every other and trample upon me alone, to whom thy justice, and even thy clemency and affection, is most due.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: He encouraged Stefano to bring his family to him, saying that he thanked God for having given him the opportunity of showing his clemency and liberality.
examples.author: Niccolò Machiavelli (tr. W. K. Marriott)

definition: A covered walk in a monastery, or a monastic life of seclusion; (verb) to seclude from the world.
etymology: From Old French cloistre, from Latin claustrum "enclosure," from claudere "to shut."

examples.text: But she gave us her blessing, and the assurance of her lasting friendship, and spoke to us, generally, as became a Voice from the Cloister.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: A yard or two from the wall ran parallel to it a linked and tangled line of lime-trees, forming a kind of cloister along the side of the road.

examples.text: That this Ford car might stand in front of the Bon Ton Store, Hannibal invaded Rome and Erasmus wrote in Oxford cloisters.

etymology: From Latin coercere "to restrain," from co- "together" + arcere "to shut up, ward off."

examples.text: "We asked people had they experienced coercion, or felt coercion in terms of undertaking testing, and most respondents answered no they had not," she says.

examples.text: In Asia we shall continue to give help to nations struggling to maintain their freedom against the threat of Communist coercion or subversion.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
etymology: From Latin cogere "to compel," from co- "together" + agere "to drive."

examples.text: The third, and most cogent reason for restricting the interference of government, is the great evil of adding unnecessarily to its power.

examples.text: The more attentively I consider and investigate the reasons which appear to have given birth to this opinion, the more I become convinced that they are cogent and conclusive.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Caesar gave way before such cogent reasoning, and the cardinals were consequently invited to dinner.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: To think deeply about something; to meditate or reflect.
etymology: From Latin cogitare "to think," the verb in Descartes's "cogito, ergo sum."

examples.text: After some cogitation, accompanied with an intent look at his patron, Mr. Cruncher conceived the luminous idea of replying, "Agicultooral character."

examples.text: She stopt to blush and laugh at her own relapse, and then resumed a more serious, more dispiriting cogitation upon what had been, and might be, and must be.

examples.text: And he walked away up the dark avenue towards the house, his hands clasped behind him and his big head bent in cogitation.

definition: Having knowledge or awareness of something.
etymology: From Old French conoisance "knowledge," from Latin cognoscere "to get to know."

examples.text: The analyst, who asked not to be identified, said the rise in the stock today was likely the result of "U.S. investors that were not completely cognizant of the size or the importance of the (Reynolds') holdings in Australia."

examples.text: Osborne partially regained cognizance, but never could speak again, though he tried dreadfully once or twice, and in four days he died.

examples.text: Wage negotiations should also take cognizance of the right of the public generally to share in the benefits of improvements in technology.

definition: Used in ordinary or familiar conversation rather than formal or literary language.
etymology: From Latin colloquium "conversation," from con- "together" + loqui "to speak."

examples.text: No one had interfered in the dispute, which was beyond the French colloquial powers of Edward Dorrit, Esquire, and scarcely within the province of the ladies.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: His colloquialisms seemed to Carol no more lax than their habitual slang.

examples.text: He spoke to Philip in correct, rather archaic English, having learned it from a study of the English classics, not from conversation; and it was odd to hear him use words colloquially which Philip had only met in the plays of Shakespeare.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Secret or illegal cooperation in order to cheat or deceive others.
etymology: From Latin collusio, from colludere "to play together, act in collusion," from ludere "to play."

examples.text: Environmental groups like Greenpeace reject the findings as "whitewash", collusion "with the nuclear lobby" and "insulting for the victims".
Has he forgotten about shoot to kill, torture, internment without trial, collusion with loyalist death squads etc?

examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Corresponding in size, extent, or degree; proportionate.
etymology: From late Latin commensuratus, from com- "together" + mensurare "to measure."

examples.text: The company said transaction prices for contract accounts, which have a duration of six months or more, will also be increased to commensurate levels.
examples.source: Reuters, “Bethlehem Steel ≪Bs> Sets Steel Price Increases”

examples.text: The only conception that can explain the movement of the peoples is that of some force commensurate with the whole movement of the peoples.

examples.text: I also urge the Congress to approve a long overdue increase in the salaries of Members of the Congress and of the Federal judiciary to a level commensurate with their heavy responsibilities.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Showing smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements.
etymology: From Latin complacere "to please very much." In the 1600s it meant simply "pleasing"; the sense of smugness came later.

examples.text: "We are, however, operating in a global market and there is no room for complacency simply because we are currently profitable and successful."

examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: History and experience tells us that moral progress cannot come in comfortable and in complacent times, but out of trial and out of confusion.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: Willing to please others or to accept what they do without protest; obliging.
etymology: From French complaire "to please," from Latin complacere.

examples.text: Whether it was the heart which dictated this new system of complaisance and humility adopted by our Rebecca, is to be proved by her after-history.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: It was not, according to his showing, on account of any weak complaisance on the part of his family towards their Norman neighbours.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Anne had always felt that she would pretend what was proper on her arrival, but the complaisance of the others was unlooked for.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: To add to something in a way that enhances or completes it; (noun) a thing that completes, or a full number.
etymology: From Latin complementum "that which fills up," from complere "to fill up."

examples.text: Several security companies have developed methods which complement or replace passwords, which are easily compromised and easy to forget.
examples.source: BBC News, “Solutions to net security fears”

examples.text: In like manner, the Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London, put in at the Shetland Islands, to receive the full complement of their crew.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: We intend to have at all times the capacity to resist non-nuclear or limited attacks - as a complement to our nuclear capacity, not as a substitute.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: A feeling of guilt or moral scruple that prevents or follows wrongdoing.
etymology: From Latin compunctio "a pricking (of conscience)," from compungere "to prick severely."

examples.text: I had little doubt then, and I have less doubt now, that he would have knocked me down without the least compunction, if I had hesitated.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Will had bruised her pride too sorely for her to feel any compunction towards him and Dorothea: her own injury seemed much the greater.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Now he was smitten with compunction, yet irritated that so trifling an omission should be stored up against him after nearly two years of marriage.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To admit that something is true, often reluctantly; to surrender a right, point, or territory.
etymology: From Latin concedere "to yield, give way," from con- + cedere "to go, yield."

examples.text: He conceded his comments may have been offensive but were not racist, and said earlier this week he would not apologise even if Mr Blair asked.
examples.source: BBC News, “Blair moves to woo Jewish voters”

examples.text: I am willing to believe each of us has a guardian angel, if you fellows will concede to me that each of us has a familiar devil as well.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: That it was a wise, just, and providential act, fraught with good for all concerned, is not generally conceded throughout the country.
examples.author: Rutherford B. Hayes

definition: Excessive pride in oneself; a fanciful or ingenious idea or extended metaphor, especially in literature.
etymology: Formed from "conceive" on the model of deceive/deceit; it originally meant "a thing conceived, a notion."

examples.text: Lydgate's conceit was of the arrogant sort, never simpering, never impertinent, but massive in its claims and benevolently contemptuous.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: And now, when one wants to smooth the thing over, some conceit prevents your apologizing, and you wish to make the whole affair public.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: You are not really shocked: for, with your superior mind, you cannot be either so dull or so conceited as to misunderstand my meaning.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Jointly arranged or carried out; done with determined, coordinated effort.

examples.text: They anticipated a concerted effort to prop up the dollar and restrain the yen via a mixture of open market intervention and public comments.
examples.source: Reuters, “Yen Seen Rising After G-7 Communique”

examples.text: But the precautions which have been so happily concerted in the system under consideration, promise an effectual security against this mischief.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: It demands the concerted action of all those in responsible positions in the Government and the earnest cooperation of the Congress.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To stop someone from being angry or discontented; to placate or reconcile.
etymology: From Latin conciliare "to bring together, win over," from concilium "council."

examples.text: If you have never seen that sight, then suspend your decision about the propriety of devil-worship, and the expediency of conciliating the devil.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Yet his manners are so conciliating and gentle that the sailors are all interested in him, although they have had very little communication with him.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Repeated, liberal, and candid discussions in the Legislature have conciliated the sentiments and approximated the opinions of enlightened minds upon the question of constitutional power.
examples.author: John Quincy Adams

definition: Intended or likely to placate or pacify.
etymology: From Latin conciliare "to bring together, unite," from concilium "council."

examples.text: Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone sounded a conciliatory note in Japan's increasingly bitter row with the United States over trade in computer microchips.
examples.source: Reuters, “Nakasone Sounds Conciliatory Note In Chip Dispute”

examples.text: Elizabeth disdained the appearance of noticing this civil reflection, but its meaning did not escape, nor was it likely to conciliate her.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: When I became President only 5 months ago, I promised the last Congress a policy of communication, conciliation, compromise, and cooperation.

definition: To invent a story, excuse, or plan; to make a dish or drink by combining ingredients.
etymology: From Latin concoquere "to cook together," from con- + coquere "to cook."

examples.text: She was at the moment concocting the Irish stew destined to satisfy the noonday wants of fourteen young birds, let alone the parent couple.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: She asked her daughter to see and satisfy herself that there was no poison prepared in the little daily messes that were concocted for Georgy.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: She told no one, but concocted a 'thrilling tale', and boldly carried it herself to Mr. Dashwood, editor of the Weekly Volcano.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: Naturally accompanying or associated; (noun) a phenomenon that naturally accompanies another.
etymology: From Latin concomitari "to accompany," from con- + comes "companion."

examples.text: And will not weakness, disorder, an undue distribution of the burdens and calamities of war, an unnecessary and intolerable increase of expense, be its natural and inevitable concomitants?
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: What concomitant phenomenon took place in the vessel of liquid by the agency of fire?
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: People must think children are very silly, or else they can never have reflected upon the nature of belief in their own minds, if they imagine that children will believe the words that are said to them, by way of moral, when the countenance, manner, and every concomitant circumstance tell them a different tale.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

definition: Agreement or harmony between people or groups; a treaty.
etymology: From Latin concordia, from concors "of one mind," from con- "together" + cor "heart."

examples.text: All my confidence is bestowed on him, all his confidence is devoted to me; we are precisely suited in character—perfect concord is the result.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: They will be governed by mutual interest, and will cultivate a spirit of mutual amity and concord.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: It should be our constant and earnest endeavor mutually to cultivate a spirit of concord and harmony among the various parts of our Confederacy.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: To be of the same opinion; to agree; to happen at the same time.
etymology: From Latin concurrere "to run together," from con- + currere "to run."

examples.text: "Their disagreement is about whether the legislation should include a requirement for consultation or concurrence - a very narrow dispute, in Lord Woolf's words," she said.
examples.source: BBC News, “Top judge clashes with ministers”

examples.text: Mr Venus, having wafted his attention to this discourse over three successive saucers of tea, signified his concurrence in the views advanced.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: No law or resolution can now be passed without the concurrence, first, of a majority of the people, and then, of a majority of the States.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: To show feelings of superiority; to do something one regards as beneath one's dignity.
etymology: From Latin condescendere "to stoop," from con- + descendere "to descend."

examples.text: Dignified clergymen of sixty years of age could not condescend to discuss such a matter with a young man with such clothes and such a beard.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He told me, when I shook hands with him, that he was proud to be noticed by me, and that he really felt obliged to me for my condescension.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Yet it is mistaken, and condescending, to assume that whole cultures and great religions are incompatible with liberty and self-government.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: To accept or allow behavior considered morally wrong or offensive; to overlook.
etymology: From Latin condonare "to give up, remit," from con- + donare "to give."

examples.text: He must at any rate be clearer as to what—should he continue to do that for convenience—he was still condoning.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: "The Arrowpoints have condoned the marriage, and he is spending the Christmas with his bride at Quetcham."
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: In this process evil things formerly accepted will not be so easily condoned.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: Making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible; favorable to.
etymology: From "conduce," from Latin conducere "to bring together, lead."

examples.text: Variable stars, which grow hotter and cooler, probably would not be conducive to life, so they are thrown out, as are stars that are too young or too old.
As far as this would be conducive to the interests of commerce, so far it must tend to the extension of the revenue to be drawn from that source.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: And more and more of our citizens now get most of their information in very negative and aggressive ways that are hardly conducive to honest and open conversations.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: A person with whom one shares secrets or private matters, trusting them not to repeat them.
etymology: From French confident, from Italian confidente, from Latin confidere "to trust."

examples.text: Anil has accused Anand Jain, a confidant of his brother Mukesh, of playing a negative role in the Ambani family, and being responsible for the trouble between the brothers.
examples.source: BBC News, “India's Reliance family feud heats up”

examples.text: Gould, another close confidante, has known Baker for years.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Treasury Policies Said Unchanged By Departure”

examples.text: Pierre was one of those people who, in spite of an appearance of what is called weak character, do not seek a confidant in their troubles.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: An extensive, destructive fire; a large-scale violent conflict.
etymology: From Latin conflagratio, from conflagrare "to burn up," from con- + flagrare "to blaze."

examples.text: A red glow as of a conflagration spread above the horizon from the rising full moon, and that vast red ball swayed strangely in the gray haze.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: In the roaring and raging of the conflagration, a red-hot wind, driving straight from the infernal regions, seemed to be blowing the edifice away.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: On the ground the groups of villagers were still occupied in doing all they could to keep down the conflagration, which was not much.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To cause surprise or confusion by acting against expectations; to prove wrong; to mix up.
etymology: From Old French confondre, from Latin confundere "to pour together, mix up."

examples.text: Voters' "pent up passion" could confound predictions of a low turnout in the coming general election, Charles Kennedy has said.
And really, after a day or two of confusion worse confounded, it was delightful by degrees to invoke order from the chaos ourselves had made.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: This conviction leads us into the world to help the afflicted, and defend the peace, and confound the designs of evil men.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Pleasant because suited to one's tastes; friendly and agreeable in nature.
etymology: From Latin con- "together" + genialis "of birth, genial," from genius "spirit."

examples.text: Over the next few months, our panel of experts will be listening to your gripes about where you work, and suggesting ways to make your workspace more efficient, more congenial or simply prettier.
examples.source: BBC News, “Making your office work for you”

examples.text: Any further conversation between these congenial souls was prevented by the advent of Mr. Thorne, who came to lead the countess to the tent.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Stepan Arkadyevitch would have been the companion most congenial to him, but he was going out, he said, to a soiree, in reality to the ballet.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: An opinion or conclusion formed from incomplete information; (verb) to guess or speculate.
etymology: From Latin conjectura, from conicere "to throw together, infer."

examples.text: Sir Hugo's conjectures had worked so industriously with his knowledge, that he fancied himself well informed concerning the whole situation.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: It was enough that the servants knew her to be in the house with Trenor—there must be nothing to excite conjecture in her way of leaving it.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: These have been widened beyond conjecture; the members of our Confederacy are already doubled, and the numbers of our people are incredibly augmented.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: An expert judge in matters of taste, especially in the fine arts, food, or drink.
etymology: From obsolete French connoisseur "one who knows," from Latin cognoscere "to get to know."

examples.text: You would only have made a better or worse portrait with a background which every connoisseur would give a different reason for or against.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He tried to avoid meeting musical connoisseurs or talkative acquaintances, and stood looking at the floor straight before him, listening.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: "Excuse the admiration of a connoisseur," said he as he waved his hand towards the line of portraits which covered the opposite wall.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: To make or declare sacred; to dedicate formally to a purpose.
etymology: From Latin consecrare, from con- + sacrare "to dedicate," from sacer "sacred."

examples.text: And as concerning Imposition of Hands, whether it be needfull, for the authorizing of a King to Baptize, and Consecrate, we may consider thus.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: His hopes, however, were they innocent or sinful, were not fated to be realized, and Dr. Proudie was consecrated Bishop of Barchester.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: To that oath I now add this sacred commitment: I shall consecrate my office, my energies, and all the wisdom I can summon, to the cause of peace among nations.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: To deliver to someone's keeping; to relegate or banish to an unpleasant place or state.
etymology: From Latin consignare "to mark with a seal," from con- + signum "mark."

examples.text: Martin Mubanga claimed in the Observer that an MI6 officer played a key role in consigning him to the US camp in Cuba, following his arrest in Zambia.
Billington, of 7, The Crescent, who this morning went aboard and formally took possession of the goods consigned to him.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: He must now consign the patient to her care; and he proceeded to repeat to her Lydgate's directions as to the quantity of each dose.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: In agreement or harmony; consistent with; (noun) a speech sound that is not a vowel.
etymology: From Latin consonare "to sound together," from con- + sonare "to sound."

examples.text: A government founded on principles more consonant to the wishes of the larger States, is not likely to be obtained from the smaller States.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: And for the Power Ecclesiasticall of the same Soveraigns, I ground it on such Texts, as are both evident in themselves, and consonant to the Scope of the whole Scripture.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: Nothing could have been less consonant with Selden's mood than Van Alstyne's after-dinner aphorisms, but as long as the latter confined himself to generalities his listener's nerves were in control.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Standing out so as to be clearly visible; attracting notice or attention.
etymology: From Latin conspicuus, from conspicere "to look at attentively."

examples.text: Given the conspicuously low audience figures, that support may be more symbolic than significant.
examples.source: BBC News, “Bangkok film festival battles on”

examples.text: With the child in his arms his figure was now more conspicuous than before, and a group of Russians, both men and women, gathered about him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The violent and decayed central cities of our great metropolitan complexes are the most conspicuous area of failure in American life today.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: Feelings of anxiety or dismay, typically at something unexpected.
etymology: From Latin consternatio, from consternare "to terrify, dismay."

examples.text: "In Colombia's case, we watch with consternation that, while we try to effectively combat drug trafficking, countries which support us in this fight seek to cut our jugular vein," Cardenas said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Colombia Traders Say New Coffee Strategy Vital”

examples.text: Without making any reply, she hurried out of the room as fast as possible, and returned in a few moments, with a look of extreme consternation.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: And he imagined the consternation and the ejaculations of his mother and the young lady at the seminary as they drank his recitals.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: A component part of a whole; a voter in a district represented by an official; (adjective) forming part of a whole.

examples.text: As one of Kilroy-Silk's East Midlands constituents I hope those who voted for him are proud to have been taken in by such charming vacuity.
It is a sound and important principle that the representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Some of you have heard from constituents, I know, afraid that social security checks, for example, were going to be taken away from them.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: To compel toward a course of action; to severely restrict the scope or extent of.
etymology: From Old French constraindre, from Latin constringere "to bind tightly."

examples.text: Economic growth is likely to be constrained during the next few years by increased pressure on household budgets and rising taxes, Deloitte believes.
examples.source: BBC News, “'Golden economic period' to end”

examples.text: My readers will guess from what I have written that I myself do not like Mr. Slope, but I am constrained to admit that he is a man of parts.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Then I felt constrained to convene the Congress in extraordinary session to devise revenues to pay the ordinary expenses of the Government.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: To interpret a word, action, or statement in a particular way.
etymology: From Latin construere "to build, construct," later "to analyze grammatically."

examples.text: Parry's statements are clever in that any future Gerrard transfer cannot be construed as a lack of ambition by the club to not try and keep their best players.
I construed this remark into an indication of a wish that he should have my place, so I blushingly offered to resign it.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The Federal Constitution is a grant from the States to Congress of certain specific powers, and the question whether this grant should be liberally or strictly construed has more or less divided political parties from the beginning.
examples.author: James Buchanan

definition: Showing great skill and flair; complete or perfect; (verb, KON-suh-mayt) to complete or make perfect.
etymology: From Latin consummare "to bring to completion," from con- + summa "sum, total."

examples.text: The companies will consummate the transactions as soon as the required approvals are obtained, McLean said.
Fletcher was described as a "consummate professional" by his friend and fellow broadcaster Michael Pointon.
examples.source: BBC News, “Veteran comic Cyril Fletcher dies”

examples.text: I am going to behave with consummate discretion and win golden opinions, But I shall run up to town now and then, just for a peep into Gad Eden.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Showing contempt; scornful and disdainful.

examples.text: He was a distinguished bird of prey—swooping thin nose, turtle mouth, thick brows, port-wine cheeks, floss of white hair, contemptuous eyes.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The peasant was silently and slyly watching him, with insulting composure, and even a sort of contemptuous condescension, so Mitya fancied.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Weyrother met all objections with a firm and contemptuous smile, evidently prepared beforehand to meet all objections be they what they might.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Causing or likely to cause argument; controversial; (of a person) inclined to quarrel.
etymology: From Latin contentiosus, from contentio "strife," from contendere "to strive."

examples.text: The Oscars nominations list has left out some of the most controversial films of the past year in favour of safer, less contentious cinema.
examples.source: BBC News, “Oscars steer clear of controversy”

examples.text: His countenance had, perhaps for years, become so set in its contentious expression that it did not soften, even now when he was quiet.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: We could focus on some of the less contentious spending cuts that are still pending before the Congress.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Sharing a common border; touching; next or together in sequence.
etymology: From Latin contiguus "touching," from contingere "to touch."

examples.text: The State Gold Mining Corp of Ghana granted the venture an additional 14.5 square kilometers in Teberebie, Ghana, contiguous to 11.5 square kilometers granted earlier.
examples.source: Reuters, “Pioneer Group Unit Gets More Ghana Gold Land”

examples.text: He has already dug up all the garden two or three times to find the famous spring, and, being unsuccessful, he will soon purchase all the contiguous houses.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: It had been a Cistercian Convent in old days, when the Smithfield, which is contiguous to it, was a tournament ground.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Dependent on something uncertain; occurring by chance; (noun) a group forming part of a larger body.
etymology: From Latin contingere "to befall, happen to," from con- + tangere "to touch."

examples.text: The agreement also incudes the right to buy GM's Canadian Transit Bus and Parts business, contingent on a satisfactory labor agreement.
examples.source: Reuters, “Greyhound ≪G> Buys General Motors ≪Gm> Bus Unit”

examples.text: Special quick excursion trains and upholstered charabancs had been provided for the comfort of our country cousins of whom there were large contingents.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Even this amount is exclusive of large contingent liabilities, so numerous and extensive as to be almost beyond description.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To violate a law, treaty, or code of conduct; to conflict with a right or principle.
etymology: From late Latin contravenire, from contra "against" + venire "to come."

examples.text: But the charges of running an illegal bar and contravening health and safety, fire hazard and noise abatement laws were dropped.
examples.source: BBC News, “Franz Ferdinand's art school lesson”

examples.text: A government spokesman said in a statement that if Ankara believed Greece was contravening international law, it could bring the issue before the courts.
examples.source: Reuters, “Greece Repeats It Can Decide On Aegean Drilling”

examples.text: This is the more necessary where the frame of the government is so compounded that the laws of the whole are in danger of being contravened by the laws of the parts.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Feeling or expressing remorse at the recognition of having done wrong.
etymology: From Latin contritus "ground to pieces," from conterere "to grind, wear away."

examples.text: A contrite counsel for AWB, James Judd QC, told the commission the email was a crucial document and had it been produced months ago, the length of the Cole inquiry would have been shortened.
Papa said you would call,' continued he, after recovering a little from Catherine's embrace; while she stood by looking very contrite.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: On my last bed I lie utterly helpless and humble, and I pray forgiveness for my weakness and throw myself, with a contrite heart, at the feet of the Divine Mercy.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: The state of feeling remorseful and penitent; sincere regret for wrongdoing.
etymology: From Latin contritio "grinding," from conterere "to grind," used figuratively of a heart broken by sin.

examples.text: "Looking at the draft statement of contrition, it's an excellent letter of apology," he said.
It was necessary for her mistress to comfort her—which she did, I must say, with a good deal of contrition—before she could be got beyond this.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He owned with contrition that his irregularities and his extravagance had already wasted a large part of his mother's little fortune.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: To create or bring about by deliberate, often clever or artful use of skill; to manage despite difficulty.
etymology: From Old French controver "to find, invent."

examples.text: In his memoirs, he also argues the strategy contrasted with Neil Kinnock's "contrived photo opportunities" and attempts at an artful campaign.
examples.source: BBC News, “Analysis: No pain, no gain?”

examples.text: It had not been necessary, and the few occasions of its being possible for her to go to the Hall she had contrived to evade and escape from.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: It produces wild schemes of expenditure and begets a race of speculators and jobbers, whose ingenuity is exerted in contriving and promoting expedients to obtain public money.
examples.author: James Buchanan

definition: A confusing and difficult problem or question; a riddle whose answer involves a pun.

examples.text: The most troubling conundrum was accounting for the tremendous amount of speed Triton must have shed to leave itself vulnerable to Neptune's gravitational embrace.
You know that when I became enough of a man to find myself an embodied conundrum, I bored myself to the last degree by trying to find out what I meant.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Martin Cunningham forgot to give us his spellingbee conundrum this morning.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: To come or bring together for a meeting or activity; to assemble.
etymology: From Latin convenire "to come together," from con- + venire "to come."

examples.text: The meeting was originally convened on June four when shareholders approved the sale of Becor's Western Gear Corp subsidiary before adjourning.
That, being convened from different parts of the country, they brought with them and communicated to each other a variety of useful information.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: The United States will ask the UN Security Council to convene on February 5th to consider the facts of Iraq's ongoing defiance of the world.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Friendly, lively, and enjoyable; fond of feasting, drinking, and good company.
etymology: From Latin convivium "a feast," from con- "with" + vivere "to live."

examples.text: How could he forget that in his Island days, Queequeg, for one, must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, convivial indiscretions.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Throughout their whole journey by boat and train they were highly convivial, but they instinctively kept together.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: He walked to the fireplace and warmed himself, humming the fag end of a tune in a rich convivial bass voice.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Abundant in supply or quantity.
etymology: From Latin copiosus, from copia "abundance" (compare "cornucopia").

examples.text: Young Rawdon's aunt, we have said, was very fond of him, as was her little girl, who wept copiously when the time for her cousin's departure came.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Her copious rich brown hair was worn in Grecian bandeaux round her head, displaying as much as possible of her forehead and cheeks.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Even Hotspur, one would think, must have been patient in his slippers on a warm hearth, taking copious snuff, and sipping gratuitous brandy-and-water.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: A proposition or consequence that follows naturally from one already proven or established.
etymology: From Latin corollarium "money paid for a garland, gratuity," from corolla "small garland."

examples.text: What inchoate corollary statement was consequently suppressed by the host?
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Baxter had been open at least eight hours by this time, for it was nearly five o'clock; and if people are to quarrel often, it follows as a corollary that their quarrels cannot be protracted beyond certain limits.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: This faith, with its corollary that to grow and flourish people must be free shapes the interests and aspirations of every American.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Relating to the body; having a material, physical form rather than a spiritual one.
etymology: From Latin corporeus "of the body," from corpus "body."

examples.text: There was a corporeal humility in looking up at him; and a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg truce of a fortress.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: It was mournful, indeed, to witness the subjugation of that vigorous spirit to a corporeal infirmity.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: We all looked on in horrified amazement as we saw, when he stood back, the woman, with a corporeal body as real at that moment as our own, pass in through the interstice where scarce a knife-blade could have gone.

definition: Having a large, bulky body; fat.
etymology: From Latin corpulentus, from corpus "body."

examples.text: Bishop Onderdonk lived at the head of six white steps,—corpulent, red-faced, and the author of several thrilling tracts on Apostolic Succession.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: He was a man of somewhat less than average height, inclined to corpulence, with his hair, worn long, arranged over the scalp so as to conceal his baldness.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The accident of time might have helped him as well—his immense corpulence might have come with his later years.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding.
etymology: From Latin corroborare "to strengthen," from com- + robur "strength, oak" (also in "robust").

examples.text: This was corroborated by his landlord, who had received by messenger the key of the house together with the rent due, in English money.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: I mention it now, only as a corroboration (though I hope it may be needless) of my being free from the sordid design attributed to me.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: To doubt any longer was impossible; there was the evidence of the senses, and ten thousand persons who came to corroborate the testimony.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Tending to destroy or wear away gradually, whether by chemical action or by a harmful influence.
etymology: From Latin corrodere "to gnaw to pieces," from com- (intensive) + rodere "to gnaw."

examples.text: That claim was repeated in Robert Peston's book, a book which amply demonstrates this corrosive Downing Street soap opera is nowhere near its final act.
Earlier this year, researchers presented research into the corrosive potential of acidic drinks at the American Association for Dental Research annual meeting in Florida.
After completion of laconic epistolary compositions she abandoned the implement of calligraphy in the encaustic pigment, exposed to the corrosive action of copperas, green vitriol and nutgall.

definition: Familiar with and at ease in many countries and cultures; including people or elements from many parts of the world; a worldly person.
etymology: From Greek kosmopolitēs "citizen of the world," from kosmos "world" + politēs "citizen."

examples.text: With 53% of UK households now with access to the net, the government, suggests Mr Davies, could act as an intermediary or "middleman" to set up public online places of debate and exchange to encourage more "cosmopolitan politics" and public trust in policy.
examples.source: BBC News, “Online commons to spark debate”

examples.text: They sat at a teak and marble table eating Eggs Fooyung, and listened to a brassy automatic piano, and were altogether cosmopolitan.

examples.text: Their central idea, their grand aim, is to subjugate you, keep you down, make you feel insignificant and humble in the blaze of their cosmopolitan glory!

definition: A person's face or facial expression; to tolerate, approve, or permit.
etymology: From Old French contenance "bearing, behavior," from Latin continentia "restraint," from continere "to hold together."

examples.text: Despite official denials, some traders still feel the U.S. would countenance a lower dollar to help trim the nation's trade deficit.

examples.text: She raised her eyes to my face, on being thus addressed, and her fingers plied their work, and she looked at me with an unmoved countenance.

examples.text: Over the years the world has come to understand clearly that it is our firm policy not to countenance aggression.

definition: Contemptibly lacking in courage; cowardly.

examples.text: It was craven of him perhaps, but he would, for the high amenity of the occasion, have liked Waymarsh not to be so sure of his wit.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: I saw on that ivory face the expression of sombre pride, of ruthless power, of craven terror—of an intense and hopeless despair.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Here also over these craven hearts his shadow lies and on the scoffer's heart and lips and on mine.

definition: Belief in or acceptance of something as true; the likelihood of something being true.
etymology: From Medieval Latin credentia, from Latin credere "to believe."

examples.text: "I strongly doubt that there is going to be any hostile takeover," Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc's Houston-based analyst John Olson said, putting little credence in the rumors.

definition: Having or showing too great a readiness to believe things.
etymology: From Latin credulus "trusting," from credere "to believe" (also in "credit" and "creed").

examples.text: For she is credulous and good-hearted, and she believes everything from the goodness of her heart and... and... and she is like that... yes...

examples.text: He who had been a boy very credulous of life was no longer greatly interested in the possible and improbable adventures of each new day.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: He threw out biting remarks on Lydgate's tricks, worthy only of a quack, to get himself a factitious reputation with credulous people.

definition: Sad and disappointed, especially after a setback.
etymology: From crest + fallen, picturing an animal whose crest has drooped.

examples.text: A crestfallen France coach, Bernard Laporte, simply observed: "There was a French half and there was a Welsh half".

examples.text: Behind him Razumihin strode in gawky and awkward, shamefaced and red as a peony, with an utterly crestfallen and ferocious expression.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It is rumored that Prince Vasili played a very despicable part in this affair and that he returned to Petersburg quite crestfallen.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Deserving blame.
etymology: From Latin culpabilis, from culpa "fault, blame," as in the phrase mea culpa.

examples.text: The conduct of those uninteresting people who managed the business of the world had been culpable just in the points most injurious to her in particular.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: If the resources which ought to have been devoted to them, had been diverted from them for the most prudent investment, the moral culpability would have been the same.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: For the first time in history the legal culpability of war makers is being determined.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Large or heavy and therefore hard to carry or use; slow and complicated.
etymology: From Middle English cumber "to hinder" + -some.

examples.text: Business leaders had opposed the plan as they said it would be too costly and cumbersome.
examples.source: BBC News, “Ban on forced retirement under 65”

examples.text: One was found to have too small a print for a child's eyes, and the other to be too cumbersome for her to carry about.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Again, I wish my successor, working with a substantial majority of his own party, the best of success in reforming the costly and cumbersome machinery of the Federal Government.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: Greed for money or possessions.
etymology: From Latin cupiditas "desire," from cupidus "desirous," from cupere "to desire" (compare Cupid).

examples.text: So intolerable indeed is it regarded by some, that no cupidity could persuade them to moor alongside of it.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: I never saw such an expression of cupidity as the flickering lamp revealed in those two countenances.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: In the meantime, as the nation's wards, they should be promptly defended against the cupidity of designing men and shielded from every influence or temptation that retards their advancement.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Hasty and therefore not thorough or detailed.
etymology: From Late Latin cursorius "of a runner," from Latin currere "to run."

examples.text: Miuesov took a cursory glance at all these "conventional" surroundings and bent an intent look upon the elder.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But the cursory glance my father had taken of my volume by no means assured me that he was acquainted with its contents, and I continued to read with the greatest avidity.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: From the cursory view here taken, it must clearly appear to have been an arduous part.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Rudely brief in speech or manner.
etymology: From Latin curtus "shortened, cut short."

examples.text: Then, for three years which passed like one curt paragraph, she ceased to find anything interesting save the Bjornstams and her baby.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: He spoke curtly, feeling the ache of despair as to his being able to carry out any purpose that Rosamond had set her mind against.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He was growing used now to the long waiting at the back of a shop on the chance that he would be taken on, and the curt dismissal.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Showing fearlessness and determination.
etymology: From daunt (Old French danter, from Latin domitare "to tame") + -less.

examples.text: Until this dauntless worldling came in and broke the spell, and lifted the latch, we too have forborne to enter into that sad chamber.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: "And law is law, Mr. Farmer, and shall have its course, to your cost," cried the attorney, exasperated by the dauntless spirit of this village Hampden.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: This circumstance, added to his well-known integrity and dauntless courage, made me very desirous to engage him.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: A scarcity or lack of something.
etymology: Middle English derthe, from dear in the old sense "costly" + the noun suffix -th. When food was dear, it was scarce.

examples.text: The dearth of strong moral character, of unbending righteousness, he felt, was their great shortcoming, and here he would begin.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: And oh, this dearth of the human physiognomy! and, worse than all, the terrible intimation of Kenneth that I need not expect to be out of doors till spring!
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: The contralto will not care to catechise the bass; the tenor will foresee no embarrassing dearth of remark in evenings spent with the lovely soprano.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: To reduce in quality, value, or character; to degrade.
etymology: From de- "down" + base "low," on the model of abase.

examples.text: Instead of working wickedness by night and growing more debased in the assimilating of it by day, she shall take her place with the other Angels.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: The victim, from my cradle, of pecuniary liabilities to which I have been unable to respond, I have ever been the sport and toy of debasing circumstances.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: We see the bad with the good, the debased and decadent with the sound and vital.
examples.author: Woodrow Wilson

definition: Excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures such as drinking and sex.
etymology: From French débaucher "to lead astray from one's work."

examples.text: The habits of the military class are the absence of freedom, that is, discipline, idleness, ignorance, cruelty, debauchery, and drunkenness.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: This ball was held in a big dance hall, and was one of the occasions when the city's powers of debauchery gave themselves up to madness.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: And afterwards, how he had all at once broken out: he had associated with the most horrible people, and rushed into the most senseless debauchery.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To make very weak and infirm; to hinder or impair.
etymology: From Latin debilitare, from debilis "weak."

examples.text: The debilitating bacterial infection is believed to be brought on by dry and dusty weather, and costs the industry millions of dollars a year.
A proposal to require imported tropical oils to be labeled as saturated fats suffered a narrow and possibly debilitating defeat in the U.S. Senate.
examples.source: Reuters, “Us Tropical Oil Labeling Plan Suffers Defeat”

examples.text: Lady Dedlock asks on sitting down to dinner, still deadly pale (and quite an illustration of the debilitated cousin's text), whether he is gone out?
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Moral or cultural decline marked by excessive indulgence in pleasure or luxury.
etymology: From Medieval Latin decadentia, from decadere "to fall away," from de- "down" + cadere "to fall."

examples.text: A bull-ring, however, without a bull would only be a memento of the decadence of the times, and she felt herself constrained to abandon the idea.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: 'I must confess that my satisfaction with my first theories of an automatic civilization and a decadent humanity did not long endure.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: It is only in the days of their decadence that a strong light beats into heaven.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: In keeping with good taste and propriety; polite and restrained.
etymology: From Latin decorus "seemly, fitting," from decor "beauty, grace."

examples.text: Jo couldn't even lose her heart in a decorous manner, but sternly tried to quench her feelings, and failing to do so, led a somewhat agitated life.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: Well, and that's enough, I think, by way of a decorous oraison funebre for the most tender wife of a most tender husband.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: He fell often and joyously into his old irreverence about the lords of Gopher Prairie, but always—with a certain difficulty—he added something decorous and appreciative.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Behavior in keeping with good taste and propriety.
etymology: From Latin decorum "that which is seemly," neuter of decorus.

examples.text: He stood a little behind the governor and held himself with military decorum through the service, meditating on a great variety of subjects.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The words of our morning service, how beautiful, how apposite, how intelligible they were, when read with simple and distinct decorum!
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Whether by shock, disgust, joy of combat, or physical activity, all the party were freed from their years of social decorum.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To publicly denounce or criticize as bad or wrong.
etymology: From French décrier, from dé- "down" + crier "to cry."

examples.text: They have decried all free government as inconsistent with the order of society, and have indulged themselves in malicious exultation over its friends and partisans.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Although our productions have afforded more extensive and unaffected pleasure than those of any other literary corporation in the world, no species of composition has been so much decried.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: I could not bear to hear my old nurse so decried, and made the subject of such a wish.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To arrive at a conclusion by reasoning from evidence or general principles.
etymology: From Latin deducere "to lead down," from de- "down" + ducere "to lead."

examples.text: But others said it kept several options open and it was not possible to deduce too much from it.
examples.source: Reuters, “Analysts Say U.K. Budget Points To Base Rate Cuts”

examples.text: As a planet passes in front of the Sun, scientists can use spectroscopy to deduce information about its atmosphere by comparing the difference in the electromagnetic spectrum given off by the Sun and the planet.
She who had so feared he would take her condition too lightly was now vexed with him for deducing from it the necessity of taking some step.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: The act of damaging someone's good reputation through false statements.
etymology: From Latin diffamare "to spread news of, disgrace," from dis- + fama "report, reputation."

examples.text: Marion Jones has filed a lawsuit for defamation against Balco boss Victor Conte following his allegations that he gave her performance-enhancing drugs.
He says concerns about blogging are related to issues like disclosure of confidential information or defamation of bosses, clients or colleagues, which originally focused on email.
He did not take in the paper containing the defamatory article, and had passed the morning in writing letters and in trying a horse.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Humble submission and respect.
etymology: From French déférence, from déférer "to yield," from Latin deferre "to carry down, refer."

examples.text: He bowed with icy deference when my terms of eulogy were all exhausted, and silently opened the door for me to go out into the passage again.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: Governor and commander are interchangeable terms with Phil, expressive of the same respect and deference and applicable to nobody but Mr. George.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: If, on the other hand, we hang back in deference to local economic pressures, we will find ourselves cut off from our major allies.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: To make impure or unclean; to desecrate something sacred.
etymology: From Old French defouler "to trample down," influenced by the obsolete English befile "to make foul."

examples.text: I really don't recollect now what decent little port on the shores of the Baltic was defiled by being the nest of that precious bird.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Miuesov was on the point of shouting, but he suddenly checked himself, and said with contempt, "You defile everything you touch."
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: He urged me (stating that he felt it his mission in life to urge me) to defile the marriage bed, to commit adultery at the earliest possible opportunity.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Quick and skillful; neatly clever.
etymology: A Middle English variant of daft, which originally meant "mild, meek."

examples.text: But Vinci's game fell to pieces after that and Martinez swept her aside with some crisp cross-court returns and deft volleys.
examples.source: BBC News, “Martinez sees off Vinci challenge”

examples.text: At first I used to be a little alarmed at the approach of bedtime in the one lone bedroom, but embarrassment was very deftly avoided.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: He liked to see her deft movements, and she watched him too now and then with that maternal spirit of hers which was so amusing and yet so charming.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: To decline or deteriorate physically, mentally, or morally; (adjective, dih-JEN-ur-it) having lost normal or desirable qualities.
etymology: From Latin degenerare "to fall from one's ancestral quality," from de- "away from" + genus "race, kind."

examples.text: The trade minister said yesterday should Seoul revalue the won suddenly Korea would run "a tremendous trade deficit and could degenerate into a country, like many other developing countries, which is reneging on its international obligations."

examples.text: He knew and acknowledged to himself that it was useless in these degenerate days publicly to contend with "The Jupiter" on such a subject.

examples.text: It is only when the people become ignorant and corrupt, when they degenerate into a populace, that they are incapable of exercising the sovereignty.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: To do something one considers beneath one's dignity; to condescend.
etymology: From Old French deignier, from Latin dignari "to deem worthy," from dignus "worthy."

examples.text: I am unclean to His eyes, and shall be until He may deign to let me stand forth in His sight as one of those who have not incurred His wrath.

examples.text: For so many years I've been silent with the whole world and not deigned to speak, and all of a sudden I reel off a rigmarole like that.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: "How is it you have deigned to look me up in this den?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, and not content with shaking hands, he kissed his friend.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Causing harm or damage.
etymology: From Greek dēlētērios "noxious," from dēleisthai "to hurt, damage."

examples.text: The MPAA said in a statement that it would continue to provide easy access to similar tools in the coming months to combat "the deleterious effects of peer-to-peer software, including such common problems as viruses, Trojan horses and identity theft".
examples.source: BBC News, “Movie body targets children's PCs”

examples.text: Or might it suffice him that every wholesome growth should be converted into something deleterious and malignant at his touch?
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: He was a mournful dyspeptic, intent on finding out the deleterious ingredients of every dish and diverted from this care only by the sound of his wife's voice.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To describe or portray precisely; to indicate the exact boundary of.
etymology: From Latin delineare "to sketch out," from de- + linea "line."

examples.text: Petro-Canada, Canada's state-owned oil company, said it will drill two delineation wells this summer at the Terra Nova oil field offshore Newfoundland.
examples.source: Reuters, “Petro-Canada To Drill Two Terra Nova Test Wells”

examples.text: The convention, in delineating the boundary between the federal and State jurisdictions, must have experienced the full effect of them all.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Because the vast spread of national and human interests is involved within it, I shall not in this Message attempt its detailed delineation.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To impose a false belief on; to deceive.
etymology: From Latin deludere "to mock, deceive," from de- + ludere "to play."

examples.text: Our beloved Sonia scraped into the women's 5K final as a fastest loser and for a couple of days, the country attempted to delude itself into believing that she might be in the medal shake-up.
examples.source: BBC News, “2004: An Irish Athletics Year”

examples.text: Misshapen from my birth-hour, how could I delude myself with the idea that intellectual gifts might veil physical deformity in a young girl's fantasy?

examples.text: Yet we must not delude ourselves that safety necessarily increases as expenditures for military research or forces in being go up.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: A severe flood or heavy downpour; an overwhelming quantity of something; to inundate.
etymology: From Old French deluge, from Latin diluvium, from diluere "to wash away."

examples.text: Many extortionists are targeting net-based betting firms and threatening to cripple their websites with deluges of data unless a ransom is paid.
examples.source: BBC News, “Rings of steel combat net attacks”

examples.text: Planet Earth had its sixth hottest year on record and a deluge of severe record-breaking weather, according to a new report.
The window went up, a maid-servant's discordant voice profaned the holy calm, and a deluge of water drenched the prone martyr's remains!
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: A political leader who seeks support by appealing to popular prejudices and emotions rather than reason.
etymology: From Greek dēmagōgos "leader of the people," from dēmos "people" + agōgos "leading."

examples.text: Some of this opposition is, of course, mere envy; the disappointment of displaced demagogues and the spite of narrow minds.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: Do you know that the orange lodges agitated for repeal of the union twenty years before O'Connell did or before the prelates of your communion denounced him as a demagogue?

examples.text: If this continues to be the ruling passion of our souls, the weaker feeling of the mistaken enthusiast will be corrected, the Utopian dreams of the scheming politician dissipated, and the complicated intrigues of the demagogue rendered harmless.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: To cause a severe loss in the dignity of or respect for someone or something.

examples.text: Mr Rodgers, of the Fullness of Joy Church, said he was concerned about the rapper's lyrics that include references to drugs, sex and violence, and songs that the minister said were demeaning to women.
examples.source: BBC News, “Church urges Nelly show boycott”

examples.text: Pfuel only snorted contemptuously and turned away, to show that he would never demean himself by replying to such nonsense as he was now hearing.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: In the areas of Federal responsibility, we have made historic progress in eliminating from among our people demeaning practices based on race or color.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Outward behavior or bearing.
etymology: From Middle English demenen "to conduct oneself," from Old French demener "to lead, guide."

examples.text: But Gordon Brown is never going to put on a show and even as he was out to cast himself as the man who will win Labour an historic third term, his demeanour remained quiet, confident and reassuring.
Seeing from his violent demeanour that he was English, they gave him a ticket for the furthest station on the way thither that the train reached.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: The first variation which manifested itself in Mr F.'s Aunt's demeanour when she had finished her piece of toast, was a loud and prolonged sniff.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To raise doubts or objections, or show reluctance; (noun) an objection or hesitation.
etymology: From Old French demorer "to delay, linger," from Latin demorari, from de- + morari "to delay."

examples.text: At the mention of gentlemen whom Society called capitalists, Mr Dorrit had coughed, as if some internal demur were breaking out of him.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There was nothing really to demur to in her leaning on Jude's arm; but she withdrew her hand, and Jude thought that Phillotson had looked surprised.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: I told her I should ask you to see her, and though she demurred at first—I know why, old fellow—she finally consented.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Reserved, modest, and shy, often in an affected way.

examples.text: The ceremony was muted with the glitz turned down and many female stars opting for demure dark dresses.
examples.source: BBC News, “How the Academy Awards flourished”

examples.text: The young man, who was dining alone with his mother and sister, glanced up in surprise and saw Mrs. Archer's gaze demurely bent on her plate.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: She showed him her ball book with demure satisfaction when he strolled instead of rushed up to claim her for the next, a glorious polka redowa.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: To publicly declare to be wrong or evil; to inform against.
etymology: From Old French denoncier, from Latin denuntiare "to announce, threaten," from de- + nuntiare "to announce."

examples.text: Victoria, a lobbyist for disabled rights, denounced her father's actions and heaped insult on injury when she joined the calls for him to resign.
examples.source: BBC News, “Former NI minister Scott dies”

examples.text: The country needs all the foreign exchange it can get, and shipowners have been quick to denounce seamen for the harm the strike is doing to exports.
examples.source: Reuters, “Striking Brazil Seamen Threaten Mass Resignation”

examples.text: At the end of it I sat, tempering nuts with a cigarette, regretting Ogilvy's rashness, and denouncing the shortsighted timidity of the Martians.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: To feel or express strong disapproval of; to regret deeply.
etymology: From Latin deplorare "to lament," from de- (intensive) + plorare "to weep, wail."

examples.text: In a separate statement on Japan, the EC ministers said they "deplore the continued aggravation of the imbalance in trade (and) expect Japan to open up its market more."
examples.source: Reuters, “Ec Warns U.S. And Japan On Trade Tensions”

examples.text: She thanked him in the most ardent terms for his intended services towards her parent, and at the same time she gently deplored her own fate.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Surely, they did not do this to advance the politics of petty bickering and extreme partisanship they plainly deplore.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: Moral corruption; wickedness.
etymology: From Latin depravare "to distort, corrupt," from de- + pravus "crooked, wicked."

examples.text: If I may not be permitted to allude to the natural depravity of the human heart, at least I may—I must—be permitted, so far to refer to misplaced confidence.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There too, opposite to him, was Lynch whose countenance bore already the stigmata of early depravity and premature wisdom.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: All that infamy had obviously only touched her mechanically, not one drop of real depravity had penetrated to her heart; he saw that.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To express disapproval of; to play down or belittle.
etymology: From Latin deprecari "to pray against, ward off," from de- "away" + precari "to pray."

examples.text: That the whole or any large part of the education of the people should be in State hands, I go as far as any one in deprecating.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: "I beg your excellency's pardon," interposed the steward in a deprecating manner, "for venturing to observe that it is already two o'clock."
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Meantime, however, our friend perceived, he was announcing a step of some magnanimity on Mrs. Pocock's part, so that he could deprecate a sharp question.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: To diminish in value over time; to disparage or belittle.
etymology: From Late Latin depretiare "to lower the price of," from de- + pretium "price."

examples.text: The Zambian currency further depreciated yesterday at the second auction since the introduction of a two-tier foreign exchange system last month.
examples.source: Reuters, “Zambian Currency Falls At Foreign Exchange Auction”

examples.text: In a sulky triumph, Drummle showed his morose depreciation of the rest of us, in a more and more offensive degree, until he became downright intolerable.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Larger deficits seemed certain—deficits which would have depreciated the value of the dollar and pushed the cost of living still higher.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: In very poor condition from disuse and neglect; shamefully negligent of duty; (noun) a homeless or abandoned person.
etymology: From Latin derelictus, past participle of derelinquere "to abandon completely."

examples.text: "Over the past couple of decades we've bought some land that was derelict, mainly on the Western Tiers," he said.
I shall send, in time for your next issue, further details of the derelict ship which found her way so miraculously into harbour in the storm.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: It was evidently the derelict remains of some vast structure, to what end built I could not determine.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: To express contempt for; to ridicule.
etymology: From Latin deridere "to laugh at," from de- "down" + ridere "to laugh."

examples.text: Mr Blair derided Tory claims they could cut £35bn in "wasteful spending" saying the party had got its sums wrong.
examples.source: BBC News, “Howard and Blair tax pledge clash”

examples.text: Old-fashioned New York dined at seven, and the habit of after-dinner calls, though derided in Archer's set, still generally prevailed.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: As for Derick, he seemed quite confident that this would be the case, and occasionally with a deriding gesture shook his lamp-feeder at the other boats.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Contemptuous ridicule or mockery.
etymology: From Latin derisio, from deridere "to laugh at."

examples.text: "Labor proposed a summit on climate change and water some two years ago and that suggestion was met with derision by the Government," he said.
Mr Fledgeby could only express the feelings to which this incredible statement gave rise in his breast, by a prodigiously long derisive sniff.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She looked at his two sisters, and saw them making signs of derision at each other, and at Darcy, who continued, however, imperturbably grave.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: Imitative of another's work and lacking originality; (noun) something derived from another source.
etymology: From Latin derivativus, from derivare "to draw off (a stream)," from de- + rivus "stream."

examples.text: Energy drinks typically consist of carbohydrates, B vitamins, caffeine and taurine, a derivative of an amino acid found in animal tissue.
Sucralose is a chlorinated derivative of ordinary sugar.
examples.source: Reuters, “Agency To Review Johnson And Johnson Sweetener”

examples.text: But in regard to the interfering acts of a superior and subordinate authority, of an original and derivative power, the nature and reason of the thing indicate the converse of that rule as proper to be followed.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: To treat a sacred place or thing with violent disrespect; to violate.
etymology: Formed from de- "undo" + the Latin root of consecrate, sacrare "to make sacred."

examples.text: She thought she was prospering finely, but unconsciously she was beginning to desecrate some of the womanliest attributes of a woman's character.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: To be sure there was no adequate ground, indeed no ground at all, for presuming that such a desecration could even be contemplated.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: The low thunder, muttering in all quarters of the sky at once, seemed to threaten vengeance for this attempted desecration, and to mutter, 'Let them rest!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Bleakly empty and without people; feeling utterly wretched and alone.
etymology: From Latin desolatus, past participle of desolare "to abandon," from de- + solus "alone."

examples.text: The researchers camp out in the desolate region in the summers, working between sandstorms.
But the more he felt this glittering desolation in the moonlit land, the more his own chivalric folly glowed in the night like a great fire.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: A decade ago, in the death and desolation of European battlefields, I saw the courage and resolution, I felt the inspiration, of American youth.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: In low spirits from loss of hope or courage.
etymology: From Latin despondere "to give up, lose heart," from de- "away" + spondere "to promise."

examples.text: Wilson has twice tried to resurrect Factory - which lasted for 14 years before folding - but conceded these efforts had been "despondent and dismal experiences".
examples.source: BBC News, “Mogul Wilson backing UK rap band”

examples.text: "Generally, the industry feel a little bit despondent with the Japanese market because we've worked for years and years and it's cost a lot of money as you say, a lot of heartache,"he said.

examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Extremely poor and lacking the means to provide for oneself; (with "of") completely lacking something.
etymology: From Latin destitutus "forsaken," past participle of destituere "to abandon."

examples.text: The glamour of youth enveloped his parti-coloured rags, his destitution, his loneliness, the essential desolation of his futile wanderings.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: I only said a word to her in passing yesterday of the possibility of her obtaining a year's salary as a destitute widow of a government clerk.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In a modern industrial society, banishment of destitution and cushioning the shock of personal disaster on the individual are proper concerns of all levels of government, including the federal government.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another.
etymology: From Latin desultorius "of a circus rider who leaps from horse to horse," from desilire "to leap down."

examples.text: Philip saw several fellows with a desultory, timid look dawdling around, and surmised that, like himself, they were there for the first time.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Suddenly her expression changed from desultory enjoyment to active conjecture, and she turned to Selden with a question.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Then they spoke of other things—the desultory talk of those who have been fighting to reach one another, and whose reward is to rest quietly in each other's arms.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: To diminish the worth or value of something (usually with "from").
etymology: From Latin detrahere "to draw away, disparage," from de- "away" + trahere "to draw."

examples.text: It is a testament to San Andreas' magnificence that it has a number of prominent flaws, but plus-points are so numerous that the niggles don't detract.
examples.source: BBC News, “GTA sequel is criminally good”

examples.text: She was growing a little stout, but it did not seem to detract an iota from the grace of every step, pose, gesture.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: In proportion, therefore, as the General Government encroaches upon the rights of the States, in the same proportion does it impair its own power and detract from its ability to fulfill the purposes of its creation.
examples.author: Andrew Jackson

definition: Tending to cause harm.
etymology: From Latin detrimentum "loss, damage," from deterere "to wear away."

examples.text: Chris Byrne from the Riverland Wine Grape Growers Association says the type of development is detrimental to the whole industry.
I wondered how many other clerks there were upstairs, and whether they all claimed to have the same detrimental mastery of their fellow-creatures.
examples.author: Charles Dickens
