examples.text: In negotiating these agreements, we intend to seek settlements which will not encumber world trade through war debts of a character that proved to be so detrimental to the stability of the world economy after the last war.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Using underhanded tactics to achieve goals; not straightforward or direct.
etymology: From Latin devius "out of the way," from de- "away from" + via "way."

examples.text: By many devious ways, reeking with offence of many kinds, they come to the little tunnel of a court, and to the gas-lamp (lighted now), and to the iron gate.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It was the devious-cruising Rachel, that in her retracing search after her missing children, only found another orphan.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: The mourners moved away slowly without aim, by devious paths, staying at whiles to read a name on a tomb.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Entirely lacking or free from (followed by "of").
etymology: From Old French devoidier "to empty out," from de- + voider "to empty."

examples.text: The majority of media criticism centred on the way in which France produced a performance devoid of running rugby in their opening two games.
Although what Metrov was saying was by now utterly devoid of interest for him, he yet experienced a certain satisfaction in listening to him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The world will be doomed to deadly conflict, devoid of hope for real peace.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands; mental adroitness.
etymology: From Latin dexteritas "readiness," from dexter "on the right, skillful."

examples.text: Walker and a team of researchers from eight institutions in the US and Israel built a strong, dexterous robotic arm that uses tubes pumped with compressed air to mimic the muscles that control tongues, trunks and tentacles.
Young John locked his door for him as they went out, slided the key into his pocket with great dexterity, and led the way to his own residence.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Again and again to such gamesome talk, the dexterous dart is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held in skilful leash.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Intended to teach, particularly in having moral instruction as an ulterior motive; sometimes, overly preachy.
etymology: From Greek didaktikos "apt at teaching," from didaskein "to teach."

examples.text: On many nights those passing by his little back garden might hear his high, didactic voice laying down the law to men and particularly to women.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: She sent this didactic gem to several markets, but it found no purchaser, and she was inclined to agree with Mr. Dashwood that morals didn't sell.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: "And the more there is of 'em, the more they must love one another," Mrs. Moss went on, looking at her children with a didactic purpose.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence.
etymology: From Latin diffidere "to mistrust," from dis- "not" + fidere "to trust." To lack trust in oneself.

examples.text: At the class-dinner he had seen poor Overbrook, in a shiny blue serge business-suit, being diffident in a corner with three other failures.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Every time their eyes met, I saw more and more what a tremendous power that weak, diffident school-girl could wield if she chose to do it.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: The same diffidence induces me to hope for instruction and aid from the coordinate branches of the Government, and for the indulgence and support of my fellow citizens generally.
examples.author: Andrew Jackson

definition: Spread out over a large area; wordy and unfocused; (verb, dih-FYOOZ) to spread or scatter widely.
etymology: From Latin diffusus, past participle of diffundere "to pour out," from dis- "apart" + fundere "to pour."

examples.text: "Attacks are getting more diffuse and more sophisticated," said Malcolm Seagrave, security expert at Energis.
Gossip is a sort of smoke that comes from the dirty tobacco-pipes of those who diffuse it: it proves nothing but the bad taste of the smoker.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: The facilities for popular education have been vastly enlarged and more generally diffused.
examples.author: Benjamin Harrison

definition: To leave the main subject temporarily in speech or writing.
etymology: From Latin digredi "to step away," from dis- "aside" + gradi "to step."

examples.text: To return to what I have digressed from, let me add that perhaps they think I report them to you, deliver little messages, and the like.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I think that the digression of my thoughts must have done me good, for when I got back to bed I found a lethargy creeping over me.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: Here, I hope you will permit me to digress long enough to express something that is much on my mind.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To make or become wider or larger; to speak or write at length.
etymology: From Latin dilatare "to spread out," from dis- "apart" + latus "wide."

examples.text: Depression, anxiety, hostility and anger are already known to impair nitric oxide pathways that help blood vessels to dilate.
The faintest possible smile of derision played round her mouth, and her nostrils were slightly dilated, as if in sure anticipation of her triumph.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He glanced over the back of the bench, dilating his nostrils, and thought as little of exchanging civilities with me as with my companion the cat.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Slow to act; intended to cause delay.
etymology: From Latin dilatorius, from dilator "delayer," from differre "to delay, defer."

examples.text: He had had full warning of Mr. Flack's intentions, and might have bought the plot before building commenced: but he was apathetic and dilatory.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: It was notorious that any fool could pass the examinations of the Bar Council, and he pursued his studies in a dilatory fashion.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: He always moved with the alertness of a mind which could neither be undecided nor dilatory, but now he seemed more sudden than usual in his disappearance.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: A person who cultivates an area of interest, such as the arts, without real commitment or knowledge.
etymology: From Italian dilettante "lover (of an art)," from dilettare "to delight." Originally a compliment; by the 1800s it implied superficiality.

examples.text: Surely we have wit enough to found a Negro college so manned and equipped as to steer successfully between the dilettante and the fool.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: The cottage was far from that standard at present, for Lisbeth's rheumatism had forced her to give up her old habits of dilettante scouring and polishing.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He had dawdled over his cigar because he was at heart a dilettante, and thinking over a pleasure to come often gave him a subtler satisfaction than its realisation.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Extremely small; (noun) a word or form of a name expressing smallness or affection.
etymology: From Latin diminutivus, from deminuere "to lessen."

examples.text: Diminutive wing Shane Williams fielded a kick ahead and danced past the onrushing Andrea Masi and Aaron Persico into the Italian half.
The truncated conical crater summit of the diminutive volcano emitted a vertical and serpentine fume redolent of aromatic oriental incense.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: For some thirty years Bogucharovo had been managed by the village Elder, Dron, whom the old prince called by the diminutive "Dronushka."
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: To free someone from a mistaken idea or belief.
etymology: From dis- "reverse" + abuse in its old sense "to deceive."

examples.text: There is little about it to disabuse one's mind of the error if he should take it into his head that he was in the heart of Arabia.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: And now look again, and see what will naturally follow if the prisoners are released and disabused of their error.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: He did not exactly know what there was to be explained, or why Dr. Grantly's mind should not be disabused of the mistake into which he had fallen, but nevertheless he promised.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: To perceive, recognize, or distinguish, especially with difficulty.
etymology: From Latin discernere "to separate, distinguish," from dis- "apart" + cernere "to sift."

examples.text: Shadow home secretary David Davis said the research appeared to acknowledge that CSOs were having no discernible effect on crime figures.
examples.source: BBC News, “Row over 'police' power for CSOs”

examples.text: Bending forward, he could just discern the marks made by the little feet on the virgin snow, and he followed their track to the furze bushes.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Give us, we pray, the power to discern clearly right from wrong, and allow all our words and actions to be governed thereby, and by the laws of this land.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Having or showing good judgment and insight.
etymology: From discern, from Latin discernere "to separate, distinguish."

examples.text: "The Japanese consumer is extremely discerning when it comes to quality and freshness of any meat," he said.
If I could have been habitually imposed upon, instead of habitually discerning the truth, I might have lived as smoothly as most fools do.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Those discerning citizens are well aware that the mechanic and manufacturing arts furnish the materials of mercantile enterprise and industry.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: To make uneasy or embarrassed; to disconcert.
etymology: From Old French desconfire "to defeat," from des- + confire "to make, prepare."

examples.text: I could make nothing of this, except that it was meant that I should make nothing of it, and I went home again in complete discomfiture.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He narrated the circumstance a dozen times to Horrocks in the course of the evening, and greatly to the discomfiture of Miss Horrocks.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: With this final sentence, Bartle Massey gave a sharper rap than ever with his knobbed stick, and the discomfited lads got up to go with a sulky look.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: To disturb the composure of; to unsettle.
etymology: From obsolete French disconcerter, from des- + concerter "to bring into agreement."

examples.text: "Whatever happens the market is going to be disconcerted and on the back foot until the April IMF meetings," said John Reade, an analyst at UBS.
examples.source: BBC News, “Gold falls on IMF sale concerns”

examples.text: When Dora was very childish, and I would have infinitely preferred to humour her, I tried to be grave—and disconcerted her, and myself too.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: His face was no longer disconcerted, but rather resolute, and, perhaps only through the reflections of the snow, a trifle paler than usual.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Too unhappy to be comforted.
etymology: From Medieval Latin disconsolatus, from dis- + consolatus "consoled."

examples.text: He was a little disconsolate that no one had come to meet him, and felt very shy when the porter left him at the front door of a big white house.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: This rather increased the Robinson Crusoe feeling in Mr. Turnbull, and he looked about almost disconsolately for some sign of life.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: In the first interview she accorded to Mr Meagles, she slided herself into the position of disconsolately but gracefully yielding to irresistible pressure.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Disagreement between people; lack of harmony between musical notes.
etymology: From Latin discordia, from discors "disagreeing," from dis- "apart" + cor "heart."

examples.text: Because of this discord and the market's momentum for a lower dollar, analysts said intervention looks doomed to fail.
And any difference which arises among them will be regarded by them as discord only—a quarrel among friends, which is not to be called a war?
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: The last, perhaps the greatest, of the prominent sources of discord and disaster supposed to lurk in our political condition was the institution of domestic slavery.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: Disagreeing or incongruous; harsh and jarring in sound.
etymology: From Old French discordant, from Latin discordare "to disagree."

examples.text: There is no longer the measured quiet sound of throbbing activity, like the sound of boiling water, but diverse discordant sounds of disorder.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Its discordant clashes sweep upward in one harmonious tone that blends with the music of other worlds—to complete God's orchestra.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: We need harmony; we have had a chorus of discordant voices.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: To harm the good reputation of; to cause an idea or evidence to seem false; (noun) loss of reputation.

examples.text: Plaid Cymru's Elfyn Llwyd has suggested the security services could have been involved, with the intention of discrediting the nationalist vote.
examples.source: BBC News, “Plaid MP's cottage arson claim”

examples.text: Nor is there anything which tends more to discredit and frustrate the better means of influencing conduct, than a resort to the worse.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: We're not asking them to replace discarded and often discredited government programs dollar for dollar, service for service.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Careful and prudent in speech or action, especially to keep confidences or avoid embarrassment; unobtrusive.
etymology: From Medieval Latin discretus "discerning," from Latin discernere "to separate, distinguish"; "discrete" is the same word with a different spelling.

examples.text: Small groups of marines armed with submachineguns stand on the quays near the strike-bound ships, but the military presence here is generally discreet.
examples.source: Reuters, “Brazil'S Sarney Meets Strikes With Show Of Force”

examples.text: Slung on a cord, the player would not look too geeky dangling discreetly from the neck.
examples.source: BBC News, “Gadgets galore on show at fair”

examples.text: Vronsky intentionally avoided that select crowd of the upper world, which was moving and talking with discreet freedom before the pavilions.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: A lack of compatibility or similarity between facts or claims that should agree.
etymology: From Latin discrepare "to sound differently," from dis- "apart" + crepare "to rattle, creak."

examples.text: But there is a big discrepancy between livestock yardings and the number of both cattle and sheep being slaughtered at abattoirs.
Note - World imports/exports may not balance due to differing marketing years, grains in transit and reporting discrepancies.
examples.source: Reuters, “World Supply/Demand Estimates Issued By Usda”

examples.text: Of course our trip through France was not really tedious because all its scenes and experiences were new and strange; but as Dan says, it had its "discrepancies."
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: The quality of behaving so as to avoid offense or revealing private information; the freedom to decide what should be done.
etymology: From Late Latin discretio "discernment," from discernere "to separate, distinguish."

examples.text: They added that if member countries were unable to fulfil their quotas their extra tonnage would be reallocated to other members at the ATPC's discretion.
examples.source: Reuters, “Atpc Members Find Ways To Curb Tin Exports”

examples.text: An Elizabeth in brain and a Mary Stuart in spirit, she often performed actions of the greatest temerity with a manner of extreme discretion.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: I venture this as a suggestion only, for the course to be taken by Congress, upon the call of the Executive, is wholly within its discretion.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: The feeling that someone or something is unworthy of respect; to regard or reject with scorn.
etymology: From Old French desdeignier, from Latin dedignari "to reject as unworthy," from dignus "worthy."

examples.text: The pact was a major turning point in U.S. Policy, ending a period of disdain for economic cooperation and intervention in currency markets.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Treasury Policies Said Unchanged By Departure”

examples.text: Disdaining the heroic outfit, excitable in her methods, garrulous, episodical, shrill, she misled her lover much as she had misled her aunt.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: The most recent proof of their disdain of international obligations, solemnly undertaken, is their announced intention to abandon their responsibilities respecting Berlin.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Having lost determination or confidence; dispirited.

examples.text: At home he said many people were turning to the Liberal Democrats as they became disheartened with the politics of the other two main parties.
examples.source: BBC News, “Choose hope over fear - Kennedy”

examples.text: When he had 'worked round,' as he called it, to Paris in his pilgrimage, and had wholly failed in it so far, he was not disheartened.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: If there are those among us who would make our way more difficult, we must not be disheartened, but the more earnestly dedicate ourselves to the task upon which we have rightly entered.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Not influenced by personal advantage; impartial (often used loosely to mean "uninterested").

examples.text: Genuine, disinterested tax collection might well work wonders in Russia; the problem with recent examples has been the erratic and unpredictable way laws are enforced.
examples.source: BBC News, “Could Yukos be a blessing in disguise?”

examples.text: Bishops, even though they be poor, can provide for clerical children, and Mr. Slope began to regret that he had not been more disinterested.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He was the most disinterested of men,—did everything for Society, and got as little for himself out of all his gain and care, as a man might.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Lacking a coherent sequence or connection; disconnected.

examples.text: The shaking figure, unnerved and disjointed from head to foot, put out its two hands a little way, as making overtures of peace and reconciliation.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: On the thirteenth day I drank some more water, and dozed and thought disjointedly of eating and of vague impossible plans of escape.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: She hastily slipped on her clothes, stumped down the disjointed staircase with its hundred creaks, ran to Coggan's, the nearest house, and raised an alarm.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To regard or represent as being of little worth; to belittle.
etymology: From Old French desparagier "to marry someone of unequal rank," from des- "apart" + parage "equality of rank," from Latin par "equal."

examples.text: They paid high for poor accommodation, and disparaged a place while they pretended to like it: which was exactly the Marshalsea custom.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It is not meet that I should make too disparaging comparisons between humdrum travel on a railway and that royal summer flight across a continent in a stagecoach.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: The dangerous antimilitary sentiment discouraged defense spending and unfairly disparaged the men and women who serve in our Armed Forces.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: A great difference, especially one that is unfair.
etymology: From Late Latin disparitas, from Latin dispar "unequal."

examples.text: However, "differentiated policy treatment is required" to take account of large disparities in the situation around the EC, he said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Consensus Builds For World Agricultural Reform”

examples.text: He says he may set up an inquiry to investigate the disparity between classification systems used to grade old-growth logging in Indonesia, PNG and Australia.
I might have seen there was too great a disparity between the ages of the parties to make it likely that they were man and wife.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Not influenced by strong emotion; rational and impartial.

examples.text: Second should be a dispassionate re-evaluation of the huge increase in defence spending over the past three years, much of it unrelated to Afghanistan, Iraq, or terrorism.
examples.source: BBC News, “The 'ticking budget' facing the US”

examples.text: But Mrs. Gascoigne was less dispassionate on her husband's account, and felt Grandcourt's haughtiness as something a little blameable in Gwendolen.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: And although there is at times much difficulty in distinguishing the false from the true spirit, a calm and dispassionate investigation will detect the counterfeit, as well by the character of its operations as the results that are produced.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: To make a doubt, feeling, or belief disappear; to drive away or scatter.
etymology: From Latin dispellere, from dis- "apart" + pellere "to drive."

examples.text: The development, published online today in the journal Nature, could dispel ethical objections to medical research using such cells.
The prospect before her now, was threatening to a degree that could not be entirely dispelled—that might not be even partially brightened.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: We have seen time gradually dispel every unfavorable foreboding and our Constitution surmount every adverse circumstance dreaded at the outset as beyond control.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: The state of being held in low esteem; a poor reputation.

examples.text: Reports of his new party plans have prompted a formal complaint to UKIP's disciplinary committee for bringing the party into "disrepute".
There are fears the case could bring Chinese inventions into disrepute.
Fraser, the tutor, died however, and the school which had begun well sank from disrepute into infamy.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: To conceal one's true motives, feelings, or beliefs; to disguise or feign.
etymology: An alteration of Old French dessembler, influenced by "resemble"; from Latin dissimulare "to disguise."

examples.text: But in this, our last interview of friendship, I approached her with a sense of guilt that almost took from me the power of dissembling.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: He told me his secret in a thousand ways because he could not dissemble, but he does not dream that he has told it.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Noting her dissembled distress Jude kissed her, and said it was time to go and see if the lodgings were ready.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To spread information, ideas, or knowledge widely.
etymology: From Latin disseminare "to scatter seed," from dis- "abroad" + semen "seed."

examples.text: The complaint said an "unidentified individual... has recently misappropriated and disseminated confidential information".
examples.source: BBC News, “Apple sues to stop product leaks”

examples.text: If the aim was the dissemination of ideas, the printing press could have accomplished that much better than warfare.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The existence of such a government as ours for any length of time is a full proof of a general dissemination of knowledge and virtue throughout the whole body of the people.
examples.author: John Adams

definition: The holding or expression of opinions at odds with those commonly or officially held; to disagree.
etymology: From Latin dissentire "to differ in feeling," from dis- "apart" + sentire "to feel."

examples.text: Ed Faber, who took over as chairman and chief executive officer, revamped the company's royalty plan, which help quell much of the franchisee dissent.
The bill, however, was read and re-read, and in some undistinguished manner passed through its eleven stages without appeal or dissent.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Communist Nicaragua is the odd man out—suppressing the Church, the press, and democratic dissent and promoting subversion in the region.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: To disperse or vanish; to squander money or energy wastefully.
etymology: From Latin dissipare "to scatter."

examples.text: Volcker said attempts to drive the dollar much lower would undermine the hard won gains against inflation and would risk dissipating the flow of foreign capital.
examples.source: Reuters, “Inflation Still A Concern, Volcker Says”

examples.text: He felt that all his forces, hitherto dissipated, wasted, were centered on one thing, and bent with fearful energy on one blissful goal.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: We've made other countries rich while the wealth, strength, and confidence of our country has dissipated over the horizon.
examples.author: Donald Trump

definition: Lax in morals; given to immoral pleasures.
etymology: From Latin dissolutus "loose, lax," past participle of dissolvere "to loosen."

examples.text: Alexander Vronsky, in spite of the dissolute life, and in especial the drunken habits, for which he was notorious, was quite one of the court circle.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: And then again the more dissolute Italian youths of Milan frequented the Stanhope villa and surrounded her couch, not greatly to her father's satisfaction.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: She was a sensible woman and so she could not help looking upon me as a dissolute profligate incapable of real love.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To persuade someone not to take a course of action.
etymology: From Latin dissuadere, from dis- "against" + suadere "to advise, urge."

examples.text: The survey found that BT and Tiscali have been actively dissuading customers from leaving by offering them a lower price when they phone up to cancel their subscription.
examples.source: BBC News, “Britons fed up with net service”

examples.text: The Commission may also take other steps to dissuade producers from their chosen course, such as removing the time limit on storage contracts, which presently means that intervention stocks have to be removed by the end of September, Czarnikow says.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ec May Offer Intervention Sugar To Local Market”

examples.text: You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be dissuaded from it.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: To swell or cause to swell by pressure from inside.
etymology: From Latin distendere "to stretch out," from dis- "apart" + tendere "to stretch."

examples.text: In approaching the door, his toe kicked something which felt and sounded soft, leathery, and distended, like a boxing-glove.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: His shoulders reappeared, jammed in the small opening; his head hung out, distended and tossing like a captive balloon, perspiring, furious, spluttering.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: It has a sort of howdah on its back, and its distended tusked mouth into which the billows are rolling, might be taken for the Traitors' Gate leading from the Thames by water into the Tower.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: To extract the essential meaning or most important aspects of; to purify a liquid by vaporizing and condensing it.
etymology: From Latin distillare, from de- "down" + stillare "to drip."

examples.text: The nanowires are washed in distilled water and, when still the consistency of wet pulp, cast into 3D shapes such as tubes, bowls and cups.
It was also distilled to a volatile salts for fainting ladies, the same way that the horns of the male deer are manufactured into hartshorn.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: I have shared many moments of pride with you, pride in the ability of the Congress of the United States to act, to meet any crisis, to distill from our differences strong programs of national action.
examples.author: Lyndon B. Johnson

definition: Deeply upset and agitated.

examples.text: He could distinctly see the distraught yet angry expression on the faces of these two men, who evidently did not realize what they were doing.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The Father of the Marshalsea always lifted up his eyebrows at this point, and became amiably distraught and smilingly absent in mind.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Catherine was near distraught: still, she persisted that she must go home, and tried entreaty in her turn, persuading him to subdue his selfish agony.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: To deprive or dispossess someone of power, rights, or possessions; to rid oneself of something, such as an investment.
etymology: From Medieval Latin divestire, from dis- "away" + vestire "to clothe."

examples.text: Gould said the move is part of its previously announced plan to divest assets unrelated to its computer and electronics businesses.
examples.source: Reuters, “Gould≪Gld> Completes Sale Of French Battery Unit”

examples.text: "In government there is a likelihood I would have to divest most or all of those holdings."
With this apostrophe Mr Fledgeby appropriately proceeded to divest himself of his Turkish garments, and invest himself with Christian attire.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To make known private or sensitive information.
etymology: From Latin divulgare "to publish widely," from dis- + vulgare "to make common," from vulgus "the common people."

examples.text: In making his ruling, Judge Kleinberg said that laws covering the divulging of trade secrets outweighed considerations of public interest.
examples.source: BBC News, “Apple makes blogs reveal sources”

examples.text: Lord Steyne, laughing, promised he never would divulge their conversation, and when he and Miss Briggs parted he laughed still more.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Were there no means still remaining to him to achieve the rejuvenation which these reminiscences divulged to a younger companion rendered the more desirable?
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Ready to accept control or instruction; submissive.
etymology: From Latin docilis "teachable," from docere "to teach."

examples.text: Gaffer was not there, but a pretty strong muster of Miss Abbey's pupils were, who exhibited, when occasion required, the greatest docility.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I am thy creature, and I will be even mild and docile to my natural lord and king if thou wilt also perform thy part, the which thou owest me.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Whether Noirtier understood the young man's indecision, or whether he had not full confidence in his docility, he looked uneasily at him.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: A principle or set of principles laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true.
etymology: From Greek dogma "opinion, decree," from dokein "to seem good, think."

examples.text: She had a strange religion of transmigration of souls all her own, in which she had firm faith, troubling herself little about the dogmas of the Church.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: For there are scoffers who maintain that it has fallen, that all dogma lies on the ground—nay more, that it is at its last gasp.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: On this day, we come to proclaim an end to the petty grievances and false promises, the recriminations and worn-out dogmas that for far too long have strangled our politics.
examples.author: Barack Obama

definition: Inclined to lay down principles as undeniably true, without consideration of evidence or the opinions of others.
etymology: From Greek dogma "opinion, decree," from dokein "to seem good, think."

examples.text: "After eight years of persistent change, dogmatic enforcement of regulation, and overbearing government initiatives - we need action, not a vision," said Mr Burns.
examples.source: BBC News, “Plan to give elderly care control”

examples.text: Two thousand years ago such dogmatism, readily welcome, would have scouted the idea of blond races ever leading civilization.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: There is no subject of economic discussion so intricate and so likely to evoke differing views and dogmatic statements as this one.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: A state of stagnation, inactivity, or low spirits; a calm region of the ocean near the equator.

examples.text: "As long as his buying tactics remain the same the market is likely to stay in the doldrums, and I see no indication he is about to alter his methods," he added.
examples.source: Reuters, “Dutch Cocoa Processors Unhappy With Icco Buffer”

examples.text: "However, the figures do suggest only a modest weakening, and we stand by our view that the property market will remain in the doldrums for some time, though a collapse is still unlikely."
examples.source: BBC News, “No seasonal lift for house market”

examples.text: However, as a matter of fact though, the preposterous surmise about him being in some description of a doldrums or other or mesmerised which was entirely due to a misconception of the shallowest character, was not the case at all.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Feeling or expressing great sorrow or distress.
etymology: From Late Latin dolorosus, from Latin dolor "pain, grief."

examples.text: The Burgundy from the public house at the corner warmed her heart, and she forgot that she ought to preserve a dolorous countenance.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: She sat in a rocker amid a debris of candy-boxes and cheap magazines, and she sounded dolorous when she did not sound derisive.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: "But," said she in dolorous voice, all but overcome by her cares, "it was specially signified that there were to be sports."
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Asserting one's will over others in an arrogant way.
etymology: From Dutch domineren, from French dominer, from Latin dominari "to rule."

examples.text: The revival, directed by David Leveaux, will also star Jessica Lange as the domineering mother, Amanda Wingfield.
examples.source: BBC News, “Slater to star in Broadway play”

examples.text: Franz was less enthusiastic; but the count exercised over him also the ascendency a strong mind always acquires over a mind less domineering.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: So long as these two rules are observed, the government can fully meet its obligation without creating a dependent population or a domineering bureaucracy.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Deceitfulness; double-dealing.
etymology: From Late Latin duplicitas "doubleness," from duplex "twofold."

examples.text: If I were not afraid of judging harshly, I should be almost tempted to say that there is a strong appearance of duplicity in all this.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: I was a precocious actress in her eyes; she sincerely looked on me as a compound of virulent passions, mean spirit, and dangerous duplicity.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Yet Communist tactics against the free nations have shifted in emphasis from reliance on violence and the threat of violence to reliance on division, enticement and duplicity.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: The movement of the tide out to sea; to gradually lessen or decline.
etymology: From Old English ebba "low tide."

examples.text: At his lowest ebb Lomu was so ill he could barely walk, but he says he is now getting stronger every day and his long-term target is to play for New Zealand again.
examples.source: BBC News, “Lomu relishing return to action”

examples.text: It would have been difficult to sink to a lower ebb of disorder, but to Raskolnikov in his present state of mind this was positively agreeable.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: History has an ebb and flow of justice, but history also has a visible direction, set by liberty and the Author of Liberty.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: A large, imposing building; a complex system of beliefs or ideas.
etymology: From Latin aedificium "building," from aedes "dwelling" + facere "to make."

examples.text: The Palais de Justice communicated with the prison,—a sombre edifice, that from its grated windows looks on the clock-tower of the Accoules.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The house of Lazarus is a three-story edifice, of stone masonry, but the accumulated rubbish of ages has buried all of it but the upper story.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: That edifice of character is built in families, supported by communities with standards, and sustained in our national life by the truths of Sinai, the Sermon on the Mount, the words of the Koran, and the varied faiths of our people.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: To instruct or improve someone morally or intellectually.
etymology: From Latin aedificare "to build," later used figuratively for building up faith.

examples.text: And this was more terrific to her husband (as perhaps she knew) than any flow of eloquence with which she could have edified the company.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He began to describe in detail the beauties of the picture, but at this table at Gravier's they who spoke at length spoke for their own edification.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: There were occasional gatherings of long-coated theatrical natives who discussed metaphysics in English and Bengali, to Mr Lurgan's great edification.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

definition: To erase a mark from a surface; to make oneself appear insignificant.
etymology: From French effacer, from es- "out" + face "face."

examples.text: You may think what you like, but I desire now to do all I can to efface that impression and to show that I am a man of heart and conscience.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But he presently went into his father's room, and the sight there touched him in a way that effaced the slighter impressions of the previous hour.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: I began one, 'How can I ever hope, my dear Agnes, to efface from your remembrance the disgusting impression'—there I didn't like it, and then I tore it up.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Vivacious and enthusiastic; giving off bubbles.
etymology: From Latin effervescere "to boil up," from ex- "out" + fervere "to boil."

examples.text: The French primary bond market is showing signs of renewed effervescence after several weeks of lethargy and the trend is expected to continue if hopes of imminent interest rate cuts are fulfilled, market operators said.
examples.source: Reuters, “French Primary Bond Market Shows New Sparkle”

examples.text: There was a fellow I used to meet at Rome who was in an effervescence of surprise at contact with the simplest information.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Franz and Emil are jolly little lads, quite after my own heart, for the mixture of German and American spirit in them produces a constant state of effervescence.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: The ability to produce a desired or intended result.
etymology: From Latin efficacia, from efficere "to accomplish."

examples.text: Australia's free trade deal with the US may mean nanotherapies may be rushed through tests for safety, efficacy and quality, one critic says.

While the technique of routing mail via mail servers of net service firms might cause problems for those that use blacklists and block lists it did not mean that other techniques for stopping spam lost their efficacy too.
examples.source: BBC News, “Warnings about junk mail deluge”

examples.text: The second answer is, that the existence of such a power in the Constitution will have a strong influence in giving efficacy to requisitions.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Insolent or impertinent behavior; shameless boldness.
etymology: From French effronterie, from Late Latin effrons "shameless," from ex- "out" + frons "forehead." Barefaced, putting one's forehead forward.

examples.text: He was not in truth much surprised at Mr. Slope's effrontery, but he was obliged to act as though he had been to save his daughter's feelings.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He stood close to her, and the effrontery in his eyes repelled the old, vanishing self in her, yet drew all her awakening sensuousness.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: I wonder—yes I wonder how he has the effrontery to look me in the face, to dare to claim acquaintance with me.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Expressing gratitude, pleasure, or approval in an unrestrained or heartfelt manner.
etymology: From Latin effusus "poured out," past participle of effundere.

examples.text: She thanked him with just so much effusiveness as was seemly in presence of the grief he might be supposed to feel, and left him.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: He was silent and rather awkward, but sometimes, when he was alone with any one, he became talkative and effusive, and would laugh at anything or nothing.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: There was an entire absence of effusive benevolence in his manner; there was something almost cold in the gravity of his look and voice.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Outstandingly bad; shocking.
etymology: From Latin egregius "standing out from the flock, distinguished," from ex- "out" + grex "flock"; the negative sense developed in the 16th century.

examples.text: It would be "blatantly inconsistent" with obligations of the EC under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, GATT, the resolution said, and "constitute another egregious attempt" to impose EC agricultural costs on trading partners.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Senate Hits Ec Oils Tax, Vows Retaliation”

examples.text: And he is so condescending to the son he so egregiously deludes that you might suppose him the most virtuous of parents.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Tonight I ask you to pass legislation to prohibit the most egregious abuses of medical research: human cloning in all its forms, creating or implanting embryos for experiments, creating human-animal hybrids, and buying, selling, or patenting human embryos.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: To draw out a response, answer, or fact from someone.
etymology: From Latin elicere "to draw out," from ex- "out" + lacere "to entice."

examples.text: Evocative impact is the ability of a work of art to elicit an emotional reaction, while closure is the sense that a painting is finished and complete.
It would have rankled in me more than it did, if I had not regarded myself as eliciting it by being so set apart for her and assigned to her.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: At nine o'clock the names were called, Sue's being pronounced three times sonorously by Miss Traceley without eliciting an answer.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing; clearly expressive.
etymology: From Latin eloqui "to speak out," from e- "out" + loqui "to speak" (compare "loquacious").

examples.text: What can I add to Mr. Forsyth's eloquently put arguments... except applause!
Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent an extremely long and characteristically eloquent letter in which he begged her to lend him three roubles.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Their newly found economic strength is eloquent testimony to the striking success of the policies of economic cooperation which we and they have pursued.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To make something clear; to explain.
etymology: From Late Latin elucidare "to make light," from ex- + lucidus "bright."

examples.text: "It elucidates how it is possible that you can so quickly and effortlessly, in just a few hundred milliseconds, recognise faces."
These examples are sufficient to elucidate the maxims which have been mentioned, and to designate the manner in which they should be used.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: How did he elucidate the mystery of an invisible attractive person, his wife Marion (Molly) Bloom, denoted by a visible splendid sign, a lamp?
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Difficult to find, catch, or achieve; hard to define or remember.
etymology: From Latin elus-, the past participle stem of eludere "to escape by trickery."

examples.text: Her international team got the cooperation of the government in Cameroon and they hired skilled trackers to locate the elusive chimps.
With the elusiveness of her curious double nature, however, Sue did not stand still for any further greeting, though it wanted some time to the burial.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: It requires the most elusive of all things in a democracy: unity.
examples.author: Joe Biden

definition: Abnormally thin or weak, especially from illness or lack of food.
etymology: From Latin emaciare "to make thin," from e- "out" + macies "thinness."

examples.text: In spite of his exaggerated stoop, and the emaciation that was so striking from his height, his movements were as rapid and abrupt as ever.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: She was a rather tall, slim and graceful woman, terribly emaciated, with magnificent dark brown hair and with a hectic flush in her cheeks.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Yet this emaciation seemed to be his natural habit, and due to no disease, for his eye was bright, his step brisk, and his bearing assured.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: To involve someone deeply in a conflict, argument, or difficult situation.
etymology: From French embrouiller "to tangle, confuse," from brouiller "to mix up."

examples.text: Two of the most controversial traveller sites - Cottenham in Cambridgeshire and Minety in Wiltshire - remain embroiled in an ongoing legal battle.
Wendy's is currently embroiled in litigation brought by Pepsi, which holds a contract with the company, analysts said.
It behoved him, therefore, to upset this state of affairs and embroil the powers, so as to make himself securely master of part of their states.
examples.author: Niccolò Machiavelli (tr. W. K. Marriott)

definition: To match or surpass a person or achievement, typically by imitation.
etymology: From Latin aemulari "to rival," from aemulus "rivaling."

examples.text: The game has also tried to emulate franchises such as Jak and Daxter and Ratchet and Clank on PS2 and so there are a number of combat elements.
I will endeavour, in my relations with Mrs. Merridew, to emulate the moderation which Betteredge displays in his relations with me.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: And we know that the best way to enhance freedom in other lands is to demonstrate here that our democratic system is worthy of emulation.
examples.author: Jimmy Carter

definition: A speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly.
etymology: From Greek enkōmion "eulogy," originally a song in honor of a victor, from kōmos "revel."

examples.text: We were growing accustomed to encomiums on wonders that too often proved no wonders at all.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: These encomiums bring them to Mount Pleasant and to Grandfather Smallweed's house.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: When she had finished the wine and these encomiums, he charged her to load her basket (she was never without her basket) with every eatable thing upon the table, and to take especial care to leave no scrap behind.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To cause someone to feel drained of energy or vitality; to weaken. (It does not mean "energize.")
etymology: From Latin enervare "to weaken," literally "to remove the sinews," from e- "out" + nervus "sinew."

examples.text: Enervated, prostrate, and breathless, he became unconscious of outward objects; he seemed to be entering that vague delirium preceding death.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: If he possesses an unusual share of native energy, or the enervating magic of place do not operate too long upon him, his forfeited powers may be redeemable.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: An artful cabal in that council would be able to distract and to enervate the whole system of administration.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: A person or thing that is mysterious, puzzling, or difficult to understand.
etymology: From Greek ainigma "riddle," from ainissesthai "to speak in riddles."

examples.text: One of them came from the enigmatic Robben when he jinked his way through two Arsenal defenders only to see his poked shot saved by Almunia.
Scientists say they've solved a decade-old puzzle about the enigmatic 'strange quark', one of the fundamental building blocks of matter.
Daniel felt the presence of a new guest who seemed to come with an enigmatic veiled face, and to carry dimly-conjectured, dreaded revelations.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: The state or feeling of being actively hostile to someone or something.
etymology: From Old French enemistie, from Latin inimicus "enemy," from in- "not" + amicus "friend."

examples.text: This had happened before the affair of Fred Vincy's illness had given to Mr. Wrench's enmity towards Lydgate more definite personal ground.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Fly to a brother's aid whoever he may be, exhort him who goeth astray, raise him that falleth, never bear malice or enmity toward thy brother.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: But the enmities it will incur, the isolation into which it will descend, and the internal moral and physical softness that will be engendered, will, in the long term, bring it to disaster.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: A feeling of listlessness and dissatisfaction arising from boredom or lack of interest.
etymology: From French ennui "boredom, annoyance," from Old French enui, related to the source of English "annoy."

examples.text: Hitherto we have heard him speaking in a superficial interrupted drawl suggestive chiefly of languor and ennui.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: It was not a condition of life which fitted her, and she could see in it but an appalling and hopeless ennui.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: As we have said, he perfectly understood the old man's vocabulary, and if he did not use it more often, it was only indifference and ennui which prevented him from so doing.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: The great or extreme scale or wickedness of something bad; a grave crime or sin; also, great size.
etymology: From Latin enormitas, from enormis "irregular, immense," from e- "out of" + norma "rule, pattern."

examples.text: "I was totally shocked at the enormity and suddenness of the disaster and in tears on seeing the orphaned children wandering aimlessly in search of their parents," he said.
examples.source: BBC News, “Charity single for quake relief”

examples.text: I wish my people to be impressed with the enormity of the crime, the determination to punish it, and the hopelessness of escape.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Our support of reform must combine patience for the enormity of the task and vigilance for our fundamental interest and values.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: To ask someone earnestly or anxiously to do something.
etymology: From Old French entraitier "to treat," from traitier "to treat," from Latin tractare "to handle."

examples.text: Many timid remonstrances had she uttered to George in behalf of her brother, but the former in his trenchant way cut these entreaties short.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: As it happened that Elizabeth had much rather not, she endeavoured in her answer to put an end to every entreaty and expectation of the kind.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: To see her hand upon his arm in mute entreaty half-repressed, and her timid little shrinking figure turning away, was to see a sad, sad sight.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To say or pronounce clearly; to set forth or express an idea or theory precisely.
etymology: From Latin enuntiare "to announce, declare," from e- "out" + nuntiare "to announce."

examples.text: Her cheeks were red with anger, and when she answered her voice had the hard commonness which she concealed generally by a genteel enunciation.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: It is often flung out as a sort of prop to support a decaying conviction which, whilst strong, required no enunciation to prove it so.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Having exhibited himself in the new light of enunciating this tremendous threat, Mr Pancks, with a countenance of grave import, snorted several times and steamed away.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Lasting for a very short time.
etymology: From Greek ephēmeros "lasting only a day," from epi- "on" + hēmera "day."

examples.text: Georges says unlike other turtles, Chelodina longicollis has evolved the ability to take long overland hikes because it prefers ephemeral waters, such as temporary swamps and pools.
In fact, if there could be any hope, it would be very ephemeral, because there would be no claim for assistance in that case, far from it....
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: They talked on slight and ephemeral subjects, and when his tea was brought up he told the amazed little servant that a cup was to be set for Sue.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: A person who takes particular pleasure in fine food and drink.
etymology: From Epicurus, the Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure, rightly understood, is the highest good.

examples.text: "I like to do things like this," she said in the delicate voice of an epicure in emotions, which left no doubt that she spoke the truth.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Because at some more flexible period he had advanced from oranges to grape-fruit he considered himself an epicure.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Recollection of the best ordained banquets will scarcely cheer sick epicures.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: A pithy, witty saying expressing an idea cleverly; a short satirical poem.
etymology: From Greek epigramma "inscription," from epi- "upon" + graphein "to write."

examples.text: Stephen had fallen by mistake into his habit of playful appeal to Maggie, and she could not repress the answering flush and epigram.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But all the time he was uncomfortable and angry, he could not have said why—whether because he could not get his epigram just right, or from some other reason.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Pray, gentlemen, find my hat amongst you; it was a remarkably good one, a present from a nobleman for an epigram I made.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

definition: Calm and even-tempered; (of climate or conditions) not varying greatly.
etymology: From Latin aequabilis "uniform, equal," from aequare "to make equal," from aequus "even."

examples.text: The old chap goes on equably trusting Providence and the established order of the universe, but alive to its small dangers and its small mercies.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: She preserved an equable cheerfulness in the midst of her sympathy, which was not the least astonishing part of the change that had come over her.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He was equable and not cringing with his superiors, was free and ingratiating in his behavior with his equals, and was contemptuously indulgent with his inferiors.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus "even" + animus "mind."

examples.text: And therefore he will be least likely to lament, and will bear with the greatest equanimity any misfortune of this sort which may befall him.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: An exhausted composure, a worn-out placidity, an equanimity of fatigue not to be ruffled by interest or satisfaction, are the trophies of her victory.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But suddenly something happened which was very annoying and unpleasant for every one in the house, and completely upset Fyodor Pavlovitch's equanimity at once.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Fair and impartial; treating everyone justly.
etymology: From French équitable, from équité "equity," from Latin aequitas "fairness," from aequus "even."

examples.text: But proponents of an expanded 0/92 argue that the bill currently is not equitable for all grains producers, so it should be extended to other crops.
examples.source: Reuters, “House 0/92 Farm Proposal Seen Sparking Debate”

examples.text: Purchases bought by bulk in partnership had to be equitably divided, outstanding debts canceled, accounts compared, and trunks, boxes and packages labeled.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: We shall also continue negotiations looking to the full and equitable development of facilities for transportation and communications among nations.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: To use ambiguous language so as to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself.
etymology: From Late Latin aequivocare "to call by the same name," from aequus "equal" + vocare "to call."

examples.text: He made a curious grimace—one of his strange and equivocal demonstrations—threw down his cue and followed me from the room.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Jos had always had rather a mean opinion of the Captain, and now began to think his courage was somewhat equivocal.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: The three who had risen fell away from Gogol, and that equivocal person himself resumed his seat.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Wrong; incorrect.
etymology: From Latin erroneus "wandering," from errare "to wander, err."

examples.text: The idea that the "new terrorism" demands new powers is erroneous.
The labours of men of genius, however erroneously directed, scarcely ever fail in ultimately turning to the solid advantage of mankind.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Necessity, especially in politics, often occasions false hopes, false reasonings, and a system of measures correspondingly erroneous.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Having or showing great knowledge or learning.
etymology: From Latin eruditus "instructed," from erudire "to polish," literally "to bring out of roughness," from e- "out" + rudis "rough, untrained" (compare "rude").

examples.text: Did erudite Stubb, mounted upon your capstan, deliver lectures on the anatomy of the Cetacea; and by help of the windlass, hold up a specimen rib for exhibition?
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Lydgate said to himself that the clergyman whose abilities were so painful to Mr. Bulstrode, appeared to have found an agreeable resort in this certainly not erudite household.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Stroking his chin, drawling in the ecstasy of being erudite, Kennicott inquired, "Say, doctor, what success have you had with thyroid for treatment of pains in the legs before child-birth?"
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Deep, extensive learning gained by study.
etymology: From Latin eruditio, from erudire "to instruct," literally "to bring out of roughness," from e- "out" + rudis "rough."

examples.text: He had never been fond of Mr. Casaubon, and if it had not been for the sense of obligation, would have laughed at him as a Bat of erudition.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: In fact, his disappointment at the nature of those tongues had, after a while, been the means of still further glorifying the erudition of Christminster.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: But I delivered this written communication (slate and all) with my own hand, and Joe received it as a miracle of erudition.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To deliberately avoid using or doing something; to abstain from.
etymology: From Old French eschiver "to shun," of Germanic origin (related to German scheuen "to shy away").

examples.text: "While you must keep up the pressure on us to eschew protectionist policies, you must act too," Shultz said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Shultz Predicts Rapid Narrowing Of U.S. Trade Gap”

examples.text: He has already eschewed green coats, red neckcloths, and other worldly ornaments, and is preparing himself for a change in his condition.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Well may he eschew the calm of domestic life; it is not his element: there his faculties stagnate—they cannot develop or appear to advantage.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: To adopt or support a cause, belief, or way of life; archaically, to marry.
etymology: From Old French espouser "to marry," from Latin sponsare "to betroth," from spondere "to pledge."

examples.text: Who would not, when there was the pretext of casting disgrace upon him, confound his whole life and the truths he had espoused, in one heap of obloquy?
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: It was only to be found by continuous excursions into either realm, and though proportion is the final secret, to espouse it at the outset is to insure sterility.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: Fellow citizens, we have reached the close of a political contest marked by the excitement which usually attends the contests between great political parties whose members espouse and advocate with earnest faith their respective creeds.
examples.author: Rutherford B. Hayes

definition: No longer close or affectionate toward someone; alienated, especially from family or a spouse.
etymology: From Old French estranger, from Latin extraneare "to treat as a stranger," from extraneus "foreign."

examples.text: Margaret, though unable to understand her sister, was assured against estrangement, and returned to London with a more peaceful mind.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: She held out her hand to him, and with a mixed feeling of estrangement and tenderness pressed her lips to his forehead as he stooped to kiss her hand.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: It has alienated and estranged the people of the sister States from each other, and has even seriously endangered the very existence of the Union.
examples.author: James Buchanan

definition: Extremely delicate and light, seeming too perfect for this world; heavenly.
etymology: From Greek aitherios "of the upper air," from aithēr "upper air, sky."

examples.text: And as I have often said, you are absolutely the most ethereal, least sensual woman I ever knew to exist without inhuman sexlessness.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: It kept him down on a level with the lowest; him, the man of ethereal attributes, whose voice the angels might else have listened to and answered!
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: The Professor lifted his heavy lids, and gazed at Syme with large, wide-open, blue eyes of an almost ethereal honesty.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Soon passing out of sight, memory, or existence; quickly fading.
etymology: From Latin evanescere "to vanish," from e- "out" + vanescere "to vanish," from vanus "empty."

examples.text: He had thought he loved her to distraction; he had regarded his passion as adoration; and behold it was only a poor little evanescent partiality.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: So that to this hunter's wondrous skill, the proverbial evanescence of a thing writ in water, a wake, is to all desired purposes well nigh as reliable as the steadfast land.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: A party success that is achieved by unfair methods or by practices that partake of revolution is hurtful and evanescent even from a party standpoint.
examples.author: Benjamin Harrison

definition: To reveal the presence of a quality or feeling; to show clearly.
etymology: From Latin evincere "to overcome, prove," from e- "out" + vincere "to conquer."

examples.text: There seemed but little in the words, but the tone conveyed more of deep helpless sadness than the insane old man had ever before evinced.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: A cloud settled on his brow, evincing decided anxiety and uneasiness, instead of the expression of offended pride which had lately reigned there.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: It will evince a relaxation and want of tone in the Administration which will be felt by the whole community.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
etymology: From Latin exacerbare "to irritate," from ex- "thoroughly" + acerbus "harsh, bitter."

examples.text: Worries about the size of insurance liabilities dragged European shares down, although the impact was exacerbated by light post-Christmas trading.
examples.source: BBC News, “Asian quake hits European shares”

examples.text: Iran had warned the United States earlier in the day against exacerbating the Gulf crisis, saying military action would endanger American interests.
examples.source: Reuters, “Diplomats Call U.S. Attack On Oil Rig Restrained”

examples.text: The licensing changes have sparked concern among some MPs, councils and some senior police officers who fear they could exacerbate drinking problems.
examples.source: BBC News, “Police urge pub closure power”

definition: Making great demands on one's skill, attention, or other resources; severe in requirements.
etymology: From exact "to demand," from Latin exigere "to drive out, demand," from ex- "out" + agere "to drive."

examples.text: The schoolmaster, always severe, grew severer and more exacting than ever, for he wanted the school to make a good showing on "Examination" day.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: Madame Fosco in her maiden days was one of the most impertinent women I ever met with—capricious, exacting, and vain to the last degree of absurdity.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: Even if insuperable obstacles and opposition prevent the consummation of our task, we shall hardly be excused; and if failure can be traced to our fault or neglect we may be sure the people will hold us to a swift and exacting accountability.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: To praise highly; to raise to a higher rank or power.
etymology: From Latin exaltare "to raise," from ex- "out, up" + altus "high."

examples.text: A lad whose face had borne an expression of exalted courage, the majesty of he who dares give his life, was, at an instant, smitten abject.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

examples.text: She was placed at the grand exclusive table with his Royal Highness the exalted personage before mentioned, and the rest of the great guests.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Since freedom impelled, and independence inspired, and nationality exalted, a world supergovernment is contrary to everything we cherish and can have no sanction by our Republic.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: To irritate or frustrate someone intensely.
etymology: From Latin exasperare "to make rough, irritate," from ex- (intensive) + asper "rough."

examples.text: As is his habit nowadays, the prime minister was less rough with Mr Kennedy than he had been with Mr Howard - he prefers a more exasperated tone suggesting he believes the Lib Dems have, once again, just missed the point.
To be thrust out of the discussion in this way would have been enough to complete Mrs. Poyser's exasperation, even without the final threat.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Political subjects which but a few years ago excited and exasperated the public mind have passed away and are now nearly forgotten.
examples.author: James Buchanan

definition: To show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.
etymology: From Medieval Latin exculpare, from ex- "out of" + culpa "blame."

examples.text: She was helped home by poor Susan and treacherous Mrs. Betty, who, now the mischief was done, thought only of exculpating herself to her master.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: Two months passed away in hopeless expectation on my part, while I must do the magistrate the justice to say that he used every means to obtain information of the person I declared could exculpate me if he would.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The bishop thought it necessary to exculpate himself.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Extremely bad or unpleasant; deserving to be detested.
etymology: From Latin exsecrabilis "accursed," from exsecrari "to curse," from ex- "out" + sacrare "to consecrate."

examples.text: Your Minister may perhaps be good as a Minister, but as a general he is not merely bad but execrable, yet to him is entrusted the fate of our whole country....
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Philip's knowledge of the language was small, but he knew enough to tell that Cronshaw, although he had lived in Paris for several years, spoke French execrably.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: I play upon that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is nearly driven out of his body.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Serving as a desirable model; representing the best of its kind; (of punishment) serving as a warning.
etymology: From Latin exemplaris, from exemplum "example."

examples.text: "The prime minister has given instructions for exemplary penalties to be meted out against the accused and their accomplices if found guilty," he told the BBC's Network Africa programme.
These she put down upon the table without a word, glaring at me the while with exemplary firmness, and then retired, locking the door after her.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The horror of Pitt Crawley may be imagined, as these reports of his father's dotage reached the most exemplary and correct of gentlemen.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Including or considering all elements or aspects; fully comprehensive.
etymology: From exhaust, from Latin exhaurire "to draw off, drain," from ex- "out" + haurire "to draw (water)."

examples.text: But using a new palaeobiology database, they gave what they say are the most exhaustive details ever assembled of its effect.
At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch broke off to discuss exhaustively the suspected connection of Smerdyakov with the murder.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It is in such contemplations, my fellow countrymen, which are not exhaustive but only representative, that I find ample warrant for satisfaction and encouragement.
examples.author: Calvin Coolidge

definition: To strongly encourage or urge someone to do something.
etymology: From Latin exhortari "to encourage," from ex- (intensive) + hortari "to urge."

examples.text: It's no good just exhorting people to stop buying arms, or to stop arguing when all their incentives encourage them to carry on.
No doubt, ran the report, the situation was of the strangest and gravest description, but the public was exhorted to avoid and discourage panic.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: Stripped of the lure of profit by which to induce our people to follow their false leadership, they have resorted to exhortations, pleading tearfully for restored confidence.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: An urgent need or demand; a pressing state of affairs requiring immediate action.
etymology: From Latin exigentia, from exigere "to demand," from ex- "out" + agere "to drive."

examples.text: Who can pretend that commercial imposts are, or would be, alone equal to the present and future exigencies of the Union?
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Mina took a growing interest in everything and I was rejoiced to see that the exigency of affairs was helping her to forget for a time the terrible experience of the night.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: It was clearly, however, in the contemplation of the framers of the Constitution that such an exigency might arise, and provision was wisely made for it.
examples.author: Benjamin Harrison

definition: To officially absolve someone from blame or wrongdoing; to release from an obligation.
etymology: From Latin exonerare "to unburden," from ex- "from" + onus, oner- "burden."

examples.text: Meanwhile, BHP Billiton says an internal review into its involvement in the oil-for-food scandal has exonerated the company.
In a statement recorded for television, Mr Blair said the families deserved "to be completely and publicly exonerated".
In both of these trials the Commissioner of the Freedmen's Bureau was officially exonerated from any wilful misdoing, and his work commended.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: (Of a price or amount) unreasonably high; far exceeding what is fair or customary.
etymology: From Late Latin exorbitare "to go off the track," from ex- "out of" + orbita "wheel track."

examples.text: "It will just price itself out of the market and what happens is, when it gets to exorbitant levels, the Sydney market soaks up basically all the crab," he said.
There was food aboard, albeit at exorbitant prices, and the three of them contrived to eat a meal on one of the seats forward.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: Returning veterans often cannot find a satisfactory place for their families to live, and many who buy have to pay exorbitant prices.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Convenient and practical, though possibly improper or immoral; a means to an end, especially one that is convenient but questionable.
etymology: From Latin expedire "to free the feet, make ready," from ex- "out" + pes, ped- "foot."

examples.text: And it is the best expedient which can be devised in any government, to secure a steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: It might soon become an immediate practical question with him how far he could call it a wise expediency to conceal the fact of close kindred.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: The determination of labor policy must be governed not by the vagaries of political expediency but by the firmest principles and convictions.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To atone for guilt or sin; to make amends.
etymology: From Latin expiare "to make amends," from ex- (intensive) + piare "to appease," from pius "devout."

examples.text: I am expiating a moment of selfishness, and so I always say to La Carconte, when she complains, 'Hold your tongue, woman; it is the will of God.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: I keep it and rear it rather on the Roman Catholic principle of expiating numerous sins, great or small, by one good work.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: To be sensible of having (as we all have, every one of us, all the children of Adam!) offences to expiate and peace to make, does not justify the desire to forget.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To present and explain a theory or idea in detail.
etymology: From Old French espondre, from Latin exponere "to put forth, explain," from ex- "out" + ponere "to put."

examples.text: Alexey Alexandrovitch began expounding his views on the sole question that interested him besides the service—the education of his son.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Some make fun of it, some overpraise, and nearly all insist that I had a deep theory to expound, when I only wrote it for the pleasure and the money.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: A coordinate department of the judiciary has expounded the Constitution and the laws, settling in harmonious coincidence with the legislative will numerous weighty questions of construction which the imperfection of human language had rendered unavoidable.
examples.author: John Quincy Adams

definition: To erase or remove completely, especially something unwanted or unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin expungere "to prick out, mark for deletion," from ex- "out" + pungere "to prick."

examples.text: Poor control over the editing and amending process can mean that information that should be expunged survives final edits.
examples.source: BBC News, “Warning over Windows Word files”
