examples.text: Grandcourt, on his side, thought his uncle a superfluity and a bore, and felt that the list of things in general would be improved whenever Sir Hugo came to be expunged.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Without debate, we expunged Billfinger as Billfinger, and called him Ferguson.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Still in existence; surviving.
etymology: From Latin exstare "to stand out, exist," from ex- "out" + stare "to stand."

examples.text: "We don't know what the animal ate because it has a beak, and extant animals with beaks can eat almost anything," says Nesbitt.
For me was reserved the high honor of discovering among the rubbish of the ruined Coliseum the only playbill of that establishment now extant.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: Now, by all odds, the most ancient extant portrait anyways purporting to be the whale's, is to be found in the famous cavern-pagoda of Elephanta, in India.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Serving to make an offense or fault seem less serious; mitigating.
etymology: From Latin extenuare "to make thin, lessen," from ex- "out" + tenuis "thin."

examples.text: He confessed that much to me in extenuation of the shady part he had played in Sherif Ali's plot to do away with the infidel.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: On these three considerations alone is based the conception of irresponsibility for crimes and the extenuating circumstances admitted by all legislative codes.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: I have acted on this principle, pardoning those who appear to have been led astray by ignorance of the criminality of the acts they had committed, and suffering the law to take effect on those only in whose favor no extenuating circumstances could be urged.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: To praise enthusiastically.
etymology: From Latin extollere "to raise up," from ex- "out, up" + tollere "to raise."

examples.text: I extolled her beauty, her gaiety, her wit, so warmly, that my praises excited in him a desire to see a damsel adorned by such attractions.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: As he had continued to look steadily at me, I took it as a reminder that he objected to being extolled for his consideration.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It is the humor of many heads to extol the days of their forefathers, and declaim against the wickedness of times present.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Irrelevant or unrelated to the subject at hand; coming from outside.
etymology: From Latin extraneus "external, foreign," from extra "outside."

examples.text: But if such movements were due to extraneous factors, Lawson said the other pact countries would come to its aid through concerted intervention on the foreign exchanges.
examples.source: Reuters, “Paris Meet Agreed Not To Publish Bands - Lawson”

examples.text: The next three days demonstrated to her own complete satisfaction Miss Bart's ability to manage her affairs without extraneous aid.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: We need no national banks or other extraneous institutions planted around the Government to control or strengthen it in opposition to the will of its authors.
examples.author: James K. Polk

definition: To free someone or something from a constraint or difficulty.
etymology: From Latin extricare "to disentangle," from ex- "out" + tricae "perplexities, hindrances."

examples.text: The strikes in Brazil come as the government is trying to extricate itself from a serious debt crisis brought on by a deterioration in its trade balance.
examples.source: Reuters, “Brazilian Troops To Leave Oil Refineries”

examples.text: Instantly I began to extricate myself and crawl back again, with what speed and silence I could manage, to the more open portion of the wood.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

examples.text: Let us extricate our country from the dangers which surround it and learn wisdom from the lessons they inculcate.
examples.author: Andrew Jackson

definition: Full of energy, excitement, and cheerfulness; (of growth) lavish and abundant.
etymology: From Latin exuberare "to be abundant," from ex- (intensive) + uberare "to be fruitful," from uber "fertile."

examples.text: The Argentine had stoked up the temperature ahead of the match by saying Hewitt's exuberant on-court celebrations were "not very good for the sport".
Not a pleasant symptom to remark, be it what it might, at dear Lady Verinder's age, and with dear Lady Verinder's autumnal exuberance of figure.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: I wonder what his exuberant imagination would have made of Walpole islet—that most hopelessly forsaken crumb of dry land on the face of the waters.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: To show or feel elation or jubilation, especially as the result of a success.
etymology: From Latin exsultare "to leap up," from ex- "out" + saltare "to leap."

examples.text: Miss Dartle, leaning back upon the seat, with a light of exultation in her face, seemed almost to caress the sounds this fellow had uttered.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: A feeling of exultation overtook her, as if some power of significant import had been given her to control the working of her body and her soul.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: Standing at this point of time, looking back to that generation which has gone by and forward to that which is advancing, we may at once indulge in grateful exultation and in cheering hope.
examples.author: John Quincy Adams

definition: Treating serious issues with deliberately inappropriate humor; flippant.
etymology: From French facétieux, from Latin facetia "jest," from facetus "witty."

examples.text: Philip thought this answer would cause the boy a certain awkwardness, but Venning was not to be turned from his facetiousness for so little.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The baronet's small chronic complaint of facetiousness was at this moment almost as annoying to Gwendolen as it often was to Deronda.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: A chance meeting, a service rendered, a happy phrase, a knack of facetious mimicry, and a man's career might be made in a trice.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Ignoring the true complexities of an issue; superficial; also, achieved with apparently effortless ease.
etymology: From Latin facilis "easy to do," from facere "to do."

examples.text: Its very situation—withdrawn a little behind the facile splendours of St. Pancras—implied a comment on the materialism of life.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: Facile natures, whose emotions have little permanence, can hardly understand how much inward resistance he overcame before he rose from his seat and turned towards Arthur.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He invented a facile excuse, and having taken the vacant seat next to her, looked round to see who was there.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

definition: Based on a mistaken belief or unsound reasoning.
etymology: From Latin fallaciosus "deceptive," from fallacia "deceit," from fallere "to deceive."

examples.text: We have turned our attention to that experiment, on the suggestion of my family, and we find it fallacious.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Such were the consequences of the fallacious principle on which this interesting establishment was founded.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Hence the complete picture they give of life is of necessity fallacious; they can only represent what is unusual.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Capable of making mistakes or being wrong.
etymology: From Medieval Latin fallibilis, from Latin fallere "to deceive."

examples.text: The film has caused some controversy in showing Hitler as a fallible but human man, rather than a semi-mythical, historical monster.
examples.source: BBC News, “Oscars steer clear of controversy”

examples.text: As long as the reason of man continues fallible, and he is at liberty to exercise it, different opinions will be formed.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: It is the American story—a story of flawed and fallible people, united across the generations by grand and enduring ideals.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: To lose strength or momentum; to hesitate or waver in action or purpose; to speak hesitantly.

examples.text: The economy faces lackluster growth and the risk of recession this year if the recent improvement in U.S. exports should falter, economists say.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Economy Slowdown Raises Recession Fears”

examples.text: My Lady reclines in her chair composedly, though with a trifle less of graceful ease than usual perhaps, and never falters in her steady gaze.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: We've not come all this way — through tragedy, and trial and war — only to falter and leave our work unfinished.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Filled with excessive and single-minded zeal, especially for an extreme cause.
etymology: From Latin fanaticus "inspired by a god, frenzied," from fanum "temple."

examples.text: But even at that great distance they could see something so fanatical, so unquestionable in his figure, that they knew it was the Secretary himself.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: I call a man fanatical when his enthusiasm is narrow and hoodwinked, so that he has no sense of proportions, and becomes unjust and unsympathetic to men who are out of his own track.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: I fervently hope that the question is at rest, and that no sectional or ambitious or fanatical excitement may again threaten the durability of our institutions or obscure the light of our prosperity.
examples.author: Franklin Pierce

definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; very concerned about matters of cleanliness or taste.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus "disdainful, squeamish," from fastidium "loathing."

examples.text: Aye, I said, I knew all along that a fastidious gentleman like you would not be contented with the thoughts of other people about these matters.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: She fluttered toward the tailor shop, dashed into its slovenly heat with the comic fastidiousness of a humming bird dipping into a dry tiger-lily.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: It was evident, from her figure and the perfumes she had about her, that she was young and fastidious in her tastes, but that was all.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Silly and pointless; complacently foolish.
etymology: From Latin fatuus "foolish."

examples.text: He would rather seem stupid any day than fatuous, and he drew back as well, with a smothered inward shudder, from the consideration of what women—of highly-developed type in particular—might think of each other.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: "Don't you like the poor lonely bachelor?" he yammered in a fatuous way.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Then he turned his own rather fatuous face to the company.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Displaying exaggerated flattery or affection to win favor; obsequious.
etymology: From Old English fagnian "to rejoice, make glad," originally of a dog showing delight.

examples.text: Bab could descend, without shame, whenever it suited her purposes, from the height of insolent pride to the lowest meanness of fawning familiarity.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: The dog yelped running to them, reared up and pawed them, dropping on all fours, again reared up at them with mute bearish fawning.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: He received me in his usual fawning way, and pretended not to have heard of my arrival from Mr. Micawber; a pretence I took the liberty of disbelieving.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To pretend to be affected by a feeling, state, or injury.
etymology: From Old French feindre, from Latin fingere "to form, contrive" (also the source of "fiction").

examples.text: Souness dropped Bellamy for Sunday's game against Arsenal, claiming the Welshman had feigned injury after being asked to play out of position.
But, he feigned not to notice the two strangers, and fell into discourse with the triumvirate of customers who were drinking at the counter.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: No, no, Isabella, you sha'n't run off,' she continued, arresting, with feigned playfulness, the confounded girl, who had risen indignantly.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Well chosen or suited to the circumstances; apt; pleasing and fortunate.
etymology: From felicity, from Latin felicitas "happiness," from felix "happy, lucky."

examples.text: The felicitous word "demise," which had seasonably occurred to him, had raised his spirits even above their usual evening pitch.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Some muttered allusions, which followed, to dogs and the smell of roast-meat, struck me as singularly felicitous.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The felicitous idea occurred to me a morning or two later when I woke, that the best step I could take towards making myself uncommon was to get out of Biddy everything she knew.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Having or displaying a passionate intensity.
etymology: From Latin fervere "to boil, glow."

examples.text: How lovingly and fervently did it commend the pretty creature I had won, with all her artless graces best displayed, to my most gentle care!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Before him rose a grotesque mass of rocks, that resembled nothing so much as a vast fire petrified at the moment of its most fervent combustion.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Beyond that I only look to the gracious protection of the Divine Being whose strengthening support I humbly solicit, and whom I fervently pray to look down upon us all.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: Intensely enthusiastic or passionate, sometimes to an excessive degree.
etymology: From Latin fervidus "glowing, burning," from fervere "to boil."

examples.text: It was now the sweetest hour of the twenty-four:—"Day its fervid fires had wasted," and dew fell cool on panting plain and scorched summit.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Fond of company; sociable. (Of animals) living in flocks or herds.
etymology: From Latin gregarius, from grex "flock, herd" (also in "congregate" and "egregious").

examples.text: The normally gregarious Evans cut a peculiarly unshowbusiness-like figure as he sipped coffee and smoked cigarettes, wrapped in a big coat and scarf in front of his Aladdin's cave.
examples.source: BBC News, “Chris Evans back on the market”

examples.text: Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place for his habitual gregarious resort.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: The contrary instincts and inclinations now attain to moral honour, the gregarious instinct gradually draws its conclusions.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

definition: (Of something bad) very severe or serious; causing great pain or suffering.
etymology: From Old French grevos, from grever "to burden," from Latin gravis "heavy."

examples.text: Researchers from the Institute of Psychiatry at King's College London monitored the emotional responses of six men who had committed repeat offences such as attempted murder, rape with strangulation and grievous bodily harm.
I hope, from the bottom of my heart, he won't keep her waiting much longer, for it is quite grievous to see her look so ill and forlorn.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: In need of some brightening from without, was Mr Alfred Lammle, for he had the air of being dull enough within, and looked grievously discontented.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To act obsequiously to obtain forgiveness or favor; to lie or crawl face down in submission.

examples.text: Mr Johnson told Today: "It's perfectly true that I got into the grovelling game myself and when I apologised there were some things that I felt I ought to say sorry for... there were also other things I didn't think I should apologise for," he said.
The colour went from their six faces like enchantment; some leaped to their feet, some clawed hold of others; Morgan grovelled on the ground.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

examples.text: Meanwhile the really new people are very often unobserved by them, or even despised as reactionaries of grovelling tendencies.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Sly or cunning intelligence.
etymology: From Old French guile "deceit," probably of Germanic origin, related to "wile."

examples.text: Untrained human nature was not frank and innocent; it was full of the twists and defences of an instinctive guile.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: While Tom was eating his supper, and stealing sugar as opportunity offered, Aunt Polly asked him questions that were full of guile, and very deep—for she wanted to trap him into damaging revealments.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: From the time he received this news to the end of the campaign all Kutuzov's activity was directed toward restraining his troops, by authority, by guile, and by entreaty, from useless attacks, maneuvers, or encounters with the perishing enemy.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Innocent and without deception; artless.

examples.text: This guileless confectioner was not by any means sober, and had a black eye in the green stage of recovery, which was painted over.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The priest recommended him to do so, but insisted that the honour of entertaining the lama belonged to the temple—at which the lama smiled guilelessly.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: It was like a wonderful poem to him, and he took it all in guilelessly—even to the conspicuous signs demanding immaculate cleanliness of the employees.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

definition: (Of a phrase or idea) overused and consequently lacking significance or freshness.
etymology: From hackney, a horse hired out for ordinary riding, hence something made common by overuse.

examples.text: I have seen a gipsy vagabond; she has practised in hackneyed fashion the science of palmistry and told me what such people usually tell.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: As he bowed over her he smiled, and quoted the hackneyed and beautiful lines from The Rape of the Lock about Belinda's diamonds, "which Jews might kiss and infidels adore."
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Philip had a queer feeling in his heart, it seemed very full, it seemed to melt (the hackneyed phrases expressed precisely the curious sensation), he felt happy and anxious and expectant.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Denoting a period in the past that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
etymology: From Greek alkyōn "kingfisher," a bird that, according to legend, calmed the seas to nest at the winter solstice.

examples.text: "Yes," he said again, "stronger, more evil, and more profound; also more beautiful"—and thereby the tempter-god smiled with his halcyon smile, as though he had just paid some charming compliment.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: That is what a man wants in a wife, the halcyon.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The kitchen, the butler's pantry, the servants' hall, the entrance hall, were equally alive; and the saloons were only left void and still when the blue sky and halcyon sunshine of the genial spring weather called their occupants out into the grounds.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Unfortunate; unlucky.
etymology: From hap "luck, chance," from Old Norse happ, + -less.

examples.text: Roland de Marigny took over the kicking duties for Italy from the hapless Orquera, and he landed a penalty either side of the break to edge Italy into a 9-8 lead.
I told her that I believed she had given me a faithful account of herself, and that we had both been hapless instruments in designing hands.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I heard of the discovery of the American hemisphere and wept with Safie over the hapless fate of its original inhabitants.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: A lengthy and aggressive speech; to lecture someone at length in an aggressive manner.
etymology: From Old French arenge, from Medieval Latin harenga, probably from a Germanic word for an assembly or a crowd.

examples.text: The International Rugby Board may have to step in to stop frustrated coaches and players from publicly haranguing referees when things go belly-up.
When Lebeziatnikov finished his long-winded harangue with the logical deduction at the end, he was quite tired, and the perspiration streamed from his face.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But the venom of the chaplain's harangue had worked into his blood, and sapped the life of his sweet contentment.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: A person or thing that signals or foreshadows the approach of another.
etymology: From Old French herbergere "one who provides lodging," originally a person sent ahead to arrange accommodation.

examples.text: Another respondent, Ed Lyell, an expert on the internet and education, says today's 'ecoterrorists' are the harbingers of this likely trend.
And lo, wonder of metempsychosis, it is she, the everlasting bride, harbinger of the daystar, the bride, ever virgin.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: The attempt of those of one State to control the domestic institutions of another can only result in feelings of distrust and jealousy, the certain harbingers of disunion, violence, and civil war, and the ultimate destruction of our free institutions.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Arrogantly superior and disdainful.
etymology: From obsolete haught "high, lofty," from Old French haut, from Latin altus "high."

examples.text: Kitty, with a haughty air, without making peace with her friend, took the necklace in a little box from the table and went to her mother.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: With a haughty action, and without looking towards him, Mrs Lammle held out her left hand, and into it Mr Boffin put the little packet.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And while he was talking to her husband, her big brown eyes moved from one speaker to the other with the same haughty and questioning expression.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Showing a reckless lack of care or attention.

examples.text: The youth, after rushing about and throwing interrogations at the heedless bands of retreating infantry, finally clutched a man by the arm.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

examples.text: What the laborer wanted was to work as pleasantly as possible, with rests, and above all, carelessly and heedlessly, without thinking.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: A heedless pride in our present strength and position would blind us to the facts of the past, to the pitfalls of the future.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: (Of a person or wrongful act) utterly odious or wicked.
etymology: From Old French haineus, from hair "to hate."

examples.text: The story goes that two prisoners are jointly charged with a heinous crime, and are locked up in separate cells.
Nor are the most conscientious compilations of Natural History for the benefit of the young and tender, free from the same heinousness of mistake.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Of course I guess there is something—some awful little scrape—which you know all about—but if I am sure that it is terribly heinous, I fancy one could manage to forgive it.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Not conforming with accepted or orthodox standards or beliefs.
etymology: From Greek heterodoxos, from heteros "other" + doxa "opinion."

examples.text: Where any people has made a temporary approach to such a character, it has been because the dread of heterodox speculation was for a time suspended.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: Both indurated by early domestic training and an inherited tenacity of heterodox resistance professed their disbelief in many orthodox religious, national, social and ethical doctrines.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: I declined answering Mrs. Dean's question, which struck me as something heterodox.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Diverse in character or content; composed of unlike parts.
etymology: From Greek heterogenēs, from heteros "other" + genos "kind."

examples.text: He says the method can also be applied to other heterogeneous and divisible items, like dividing land or deciding how much rent each flatmate pays.
Our bodies are half made up of glands and tubes and organs, occupied in turning heterogeneous food into blood.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: It was a small group still, with heterogeneous figures suspended in large unpeopled spaces; but Lily did not take long to learn that its regulation was no longer in Mr. Stancy's hands.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: A thing that provides resistance, delay, or obstruction to something or someone.

examples.text: "So far our copper has been reaching its destinations without hindrance," he told the Times.
His small stature was no hindrance to him—here he could see over the heads of the ladies who were seated near the outermost part of the bench.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: The challenge for us in government is to be worthy of them — to make government a help, not a hindrance to our people in the challenging but promising days ahead.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Special honor or respect shown publicly; a work that pays tribute to another.
etymology: From Old French homage, from homme "man," originally a vassal's formal acknowledgment of allegiance to a lord.

examples.text: I shall never more know the sweet homage given to beauty, youth, and grace—for never to any one else shall I seem to possess these charms.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Open the door, beautiful Mrs Flintwinch, and in the meantime let me to pass upstairs, to present my compliments—homage of Blandois—to my lady!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: In tendering this homage to the Great Author of every public and private good, I assure myself that it expresses your sentiments not less than my own, nor those of my fellow citizens at large less than either.
examples.author: George Washington

definition: Of the same kind; alike; consisting of parts all of the same kind.
etymology: From Greek homogenēs, from homos "same" + genos "kind."

examples.text: "Having a market at our disposal which is as homogeneous and accessible as that of Europe is an incredible piece of luck," he told Le Figaro in an interview.
examples.source: Reuters, “French Employers Chief Sees Hope For Growth”

examples.text: Thus, when you look at the painting, the surface appears homogeneous.
Ultimately he was reduced well-nigh to a homogeneous sop, and the dyes of his clothes trickled down and stood in a pool at the foot of the ladder.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Lacking excitement or variety; boringly monotonous.

examples.text: Miss Price told him a long, involved story, which made out that Mrs. Otter, a humdrum and respectable little person, had scabrous intrigues.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Becky was very respectable and orderly at first, but the life of humdrum virtue grew utterly tedious to her before long.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: It was rumoured that he was tired of the humdrum life among the people in our parts, and longing to go back and wander off on the tramp again in the wild places of the East.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: A mode of behavior or way of thought peculiar to an individual; a distinctive characteristic.
etymology: From Greek idiosynkrasia, from idios "one's own" + synkrasis "mixture, temperament."

examples.text: But such was his idiosyncrasy that these very facts had produced within him, in early life, a state of mind that was not natural to him.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: It was written to me (as it told me in so many words), perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And when ordinary fellows like you and me attempt to cope with their idiosyncrasies the result is bungling.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

definition: Extreme admiration, love, or reverence for something or someone; the worship of idols.
etymology: From Greek eidōlolatreia, from eidōlon "idol" + latreia "worship."

examples.text: It is odd that a thing which I have been taught to regard with disfavour and as idolatrous should in a time of loneliness and trouble be of help.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: He mixed up these Roman halfpence with the honour of the Carstairs family in the same stiff, idolatrous way as his father before him.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: But a certain awe mingled itself with her idolatrous love of Adam, and when he said, "Leave me alone," she was always silenced.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Dishonorable, base, or shameful in character or purpose; of humble or low birth.
etymology: From Latin ignobilis "unknown, low-born," from in- "not" + gnobilis, an old form of nobilis "noble, well-known."

examples.text: But it is not ignoble to feel that the fuller life which a sad experience has brought us is worth our own personal share of pain.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But eighteen glasses of gin consumed among boxers in an ignoble pot-house—it was an odious crime and not to be pardoned readily.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Deep would have been the blot upon his escutcheon if his chocolate had been ignobly waited on by only three men; he must have died of two.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Deserving or causing public disgrace or shame; humiliating.
etymology: From Latin ignominia "disgrace," from in- "not" + nomen "name, reputation."

examples.text: Meantime tea was to be brought in by the cook, and the two naughty children were to have theirs in an ignominious manner in the kitchen.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: The punishment seemed to me in a high degree ignominious, especially for so great a girl—she looked thirteen or upwards.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Yes, the modern world has retained all those parts of police work which are really oppressive and ignominious, the harrying of the poor, the spying upon the unfortunate.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Based on illusion; not real, though seeming to be.
etymology: From Latin illusorius "mocking," from illudere "to mock," from in- "against" + ludere "to play."

examples.text: The suit also charges the offer is illusory and designed to manipulate the market in Caesars World stock to enable Sosnoff to sell the Caesars World stock he already owns for a substantial profit.
examples.source: Reuters, “Caesars World ≪Caw> Files Suit Against Sosnoff”

examples.text: She had only time to feel that all this was hazy and perhaps illusory; but one thing was clear and determined—her answer.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: You had said you knew so well "that kind of thing," its illusory satisfaction, its unavoidable deception.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: To drink, especially alcohol; to absorb or assimilate ideas or knowledge.
etymology: From Latin imbibere "to drink in," from in- "in" + bibere "to drink."

examples.text: But you would have to quaff more than 17 pints to imbibe a medically effective dose of xanthohumol, the apparently cancer-fighting antioxidant found in hops, says researcher Emily Ho.
She had been free, as she knew freedom, partly to show him that, unlike other little persons she knew, she had imbibed that ideal.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: Much that the white boy imbibes from his earliest social atmosphere forms the puzzling problems of the black boy's mature years.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: To inspire or permeate with a feeling, quality, or idea; to saturate with color or moisture.
etymology: From Latin imbuere "to wet, soak, stain."

examples.text: A certain leanness falls upon houses not sufficiently imbued with life (as if they were nourished upon it), which was very noticeable here.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Let every man be fully imbued with the thought that we must defeat these hirelings of England, inspired by such hatred of our nation!
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Here, one would suppose, might have been sorrow enough to imbue the sunniest disposition through and through with a sable tinge.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

definition: Perfectly clean, neat, or tidy; free from flaws or mistakes.
etymology: From Latin immaculatus "unstained," from in- "not" + maculatus "spotted," from macula "spot."

examples.text: The winning try was conceived in O'Sullivan's mind, perfectly executed by the team and finished immaculately by Girvan Dempsey.
examples.source: BBC News, “A year to remember for Irish”

examples.text: Berg arrived in an immaculate brand-new uniform, with his hair pomaded and brushed forward over his temples as the Emperor Alexander wore his hair.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: In it were an obviously prosperous man and a black-haired, fine-skinned girl whose pumps rested on an immaculate horsehide bag.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Unchanging over time or unable to be changed.
etymology: From Latin immutabilis, from in- "not" + mutabilis "changeable," from mutare "to change."

examples.text: The blue lake and snow-clad mountains—they never change; and I think our placid home and our contented hearts are regulated by the same immutable laws.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: She believed that details could excitingly be altered, but that things-in-general were comely and kind and immutable.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The state of the Union is a measurement of the many elements of which it is composed—a political union of diverse States, an economic union of varying interests, an intellectual union of common convictions, and a moral union of immutable ideals.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: Not feeling or showing emotion.

examples.text: He was evidently distressed, and breathed painfully, but could not restrain the wild laughter that convulsed his usually impassive features.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: She remained impassive on the same spot, silent and motionless, until the striking of the church clock roused her, and she turned away.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Laura is perfectly impassive, perfectly careless about the question of all others in which a woman's personal interests are most closely bound up.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: In accordance with the highest standards; faultless.
etymology: From Latin impeccabilis "not liable to sin," from in- "not" + peccare "to sin."

examples.text: With impeccable and precisely-calculated timing, Tory defector Robert Jackson and his new Labour bosses have attempted to overshadow Michael Howard's latest announcement on taxation and spending.
examples.source: BBC News, “Defection timed to hit tax pledge”

examples.text: "But it is important to note that the physicians and other health care professionals who sit on expert medical advisory panels have impeccable integrity and base their decisions on independent judgments and research," he says.
Archer's New York tolerated hypocrisy in private relations; but in business matters it exacted a limpid and impeccable honesty.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: A hindrance or obstruction in doing something; a defect in speech, such as a stammer.
etymology: From Latin impedimentum, from impedire "to shackle the feet," from in- "in" + pes, ped- "foot."

examples.text: The Federal Government has endorsed a two-year action plan to remove impediments to the growth of Australia's uranium industry.
Legislation giving state rail authorities a monopoly over grain shipments was one notable impediment, it said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Awb Calls For Tighter Wheat Quality Controls”

examples.text: It could be no impediment to reforms of the State constitution by a majority of the people in a legal and peaceable mode.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: About to happen; imminent, often of something unwelcome.
etymology: From Latin impendere "to hang over," from in- "upon" + pendere "to hang."

examples.text: Yukos has said a US bankruptcy court will decide whether to block Russia's impending auction of its main production arm on Thursday.
examples.source: BBC News, “US to rule on Yukos refuge call”

examples.text: He had grown accustomed when going into action to think about anything but what would seem most likely to interest him—the impending danger.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Four years ago we stood on the brink of war without the people knowing it and without any preparation or effort at preparation for the impending peril.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Assuming power or authority without justification; arrogant and domineering.
etymology: From Latin imperiosus "commanding," from imperium "command, empire."

examples.text: When once that imperious old lady had recovered from her natural awe of a lama he thought it probable that she would be worth listening to.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: The interval had been short, but he had greatly complained of its length, and had been imperious with Mr Rugg touching the delay.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I understand what it must mean for a man who has been unfortunate, but who is proud, imperious and above all, impatient, to have to bear such treatment!
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Not showing proper respect; rude; not pertinent or relevant.
etymology: From Latin impertinens "not belonging," from in- "not" + pertinere "to relate to."

examples.text: When Carol was touched by the desire for heroism in Raymie and tried tactfully to express it, Vida made her feel like an impertinent child.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The same fascination that caused him to think it an act which had a deliberate motive prevented him from regarding it as an impertinence.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: The results of such elections are not local, and the insistence of electors residing in other districts that they shall be pure and free does not savor at all of impertinence.
examples.author: Benjamin Harrison

definition: Unable to be upset or excited; calm and composed.
etymology: From Latin imperturbabilis, from in- "not" + perturbare "to disturb greatly."

examples.text: His imperturbable and mature calmness was that of an expert in possession of the facts, and to whom one's perplexities are mere child's-play.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: At the same time Mercedes reappeared, paler than before, but with that imperturbable expression of countenance which she sometimes wore.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Larger and ever more imperturbable was the mountain in the star-filtered darkness, and the lake a limitless pavement of black marble.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Unable to be affected by something; not allowing fluid to pass through.
etymology: From Latin impervius "impassable," from in- "not" + per "through" + via "way."

examples.text: Roads make up about one-fifth of the urban land area, he says, and about half the impervious surfaces.
The division was charged with thinking up and carrying out action to make US networks more impervious to attack and disruption by the viruses, worms and hack attacks that have become commonplace.
examples.source: BBC News, “US cyber security chief resigns”

examples.text: But Rosedale's natural imperviousness to hints made it easy for him to brush such resistance aside.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Acting or done quickly and without thought or care.
etymology: From Latin impetus "attack, force," from impetere "to rush upon."

examples.text: She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to go to him, when light, impetuous, and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: With those words uttered impetuously, Will rose, put out his hand to Rosamond, still with the air of a somnambulist, and went away.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Then impetuously he told her that Mildred had left him and that his unhappiness had been so great that he almost killed himself.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: The force or energy with which something moves; a stimulus that makes something happen.
etymology: From Latin impetus "assault, force," from impetere "to attack," from in- "toward" + petere "to seek."

examples.text: Money market analysts cited the debt renegotiation as the main impetus behind increases today in both the commercial and financial rand.
examples.source: Reuters, “South Africa Problems Remain Despite Debt Pact”

examples.text: The impetus was the growing number of people with handsets that could access the net, and the growth of 3G technologies.
examples.source: BBC News, “Video phones act as dating tools”

examples.text: Rex turned pale and was silent, but could not take his eyes off her, and the impetus was not yet exhausted that made hers dart death at him.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Showing a lack of respect for God or religion; lacking proper respect.
etymology: From Latin impius, from in- "not" + pius "dutiful, pious."

examples.text: Don't fancy it, impious scoundrel, for that beyond a doubt thou art, since thou hast set thy tongue going against the peerless Dulcinea.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: We should stamp every possible world with the flatness of our own inanity—which is necessarily impious, without faith or fellowship.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: We have heard of the impious doctrine in the Old World, that the people were made for kings, not kings for the people.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Unable to be appeased or placated; relentless.
etymology: From Latin implacabilis, from in- "not" + placare "to appease" (compare "placate").

examples.text: Her iron-grey hair hung in heavy bands on either side of her face—her dark eyes looked straight forward, with a hard, defiant, implacable stare.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: With these words, and a laugh, and laying a bitter stress on the word "ladyship," Mrs. Chadband folds her arms and looks implacably at Mr. Bucket.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Not a word more would he say, but sat in his implacable sullenness as indifferent to me as though I had not been in the room at all.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: To show someone to be involved in a crime or wrongdoing; to imply as a consequence.
etymology: From Latin implicare "to entangle, involve," from in- "in" + plicare "to fold."

examples.text: Giving evidence in the criminal trial of Mr Ebbers, ex-finance chief Scott Sullivan implicated his colleague in the accounting scandal at the firm.
And they are very clever maps... and there is three or four Prime Ministers of these parts implicated by the correspondence.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: Especially are we determined not to become implicated in the political controversies of the Old World.
examples.author: Calvin Coolidge

definition: Implied though not plainly expressed; absolute and unquestioning, as in implicit trust.
etymology: From Latin implicitus "entangled," a variant past participle of implicare "to fold in."

examples.text: The diplomats said they knew of no deal for Moscow to provide a naval escort for its own vessels, but "the idea of protection is implicit," one said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Soviet Tankers Set To Carry Kuwaiti Oil”

examples.text: There was a sort of implicit confidence in him that he was really such a good fellow at bottom, Providence would not treat him harshly.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: We have learned by experience a fruitful lesson — that an implicit and undeviating adherence to the principles on which we set out can carry us prosperously onward through all the conflicts of circumstances and vicissitudes inseparable from the lapse of years.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: To beg someone earnestly or desperately to do something.
etymology: From Latin implorare "to invoke with tears," from in- "toward" + plorare "to weep, cry out."

examples.text: Now we don't do it at Cubbie, and I implore the southern states to seriously look at their storage systems.
There were juvenile letters and petitions from Rebecca, too, in the collection, imploring aid for her father or declaring her own gratitude.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: I accept my part with single-mindedness of purpose and humility of spirit, and implore the favor and guidance of God in His Heaven.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: Unable to be captured or broken into; unable to be challenged or overcome.
etymology: From Old French imprenable, from in- "not" + prenable "able to be taken," from prendre "to take."

examples.text: That influence, in its last analysis, was simply the power of money: Bertha Dorset's social credit was based on an impregnable bank-account.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Furthermore: concerning these last mentioned Leviathans, they have two firm fortresses, which, in all human probability, will for ever remain impregnable.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Out of such universal service will come a new unity of spirit and purpose, a new confidence and consecration, which would make our defense impregnable, our triumph assured.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: Done without being planned or rehearsed; spontaneous.
etymology: From Latin in promptu "in readiness," from promptus "readiness."

examples.text: Five of the eight men held an impromptu news conference outside Charing Cross Police Station on Monday evening, after the charges were formerly put to them.
A new union was the result of this outburst, but the impromptu strike went to pieces in three days, owing to the rush of new labor.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: The charades came off according to her plans; and also some other little scenes not contemplated by her in which her acting was more impromptu.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Not having or showing foresight; spendthrift or thoughtless about future needs.
etymology: From Latin in- "not" + providens "foreseeing," from providere "to see ahead."

examples.text: The security of all would thus be subjected to the parsimony, improvidence, or inability of a part.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: She kept them secret from her father, whose improvidence was the cause of much of her misery.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: They are careless because they have not found that it pays to be careful; they are improvident because the improvident ones of their acquaintance get on about as well as the provident.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: Not showing due respect for another person; impertinent and shameless.
etymology: From Latin impudens "shameless," from in- "not" + pudens "ashamed," from pudere "to be ashamed."

examples.text: Standing in the doorway, he scanned the company, and laughing his prolonged, impudent, malicious chuckle, looked them all boldly in the face.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: This renewed timidity on his part was so different from the impudence with which he had walked into the sea, that I felt vaguely comforted.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: I mentioned what they had said about her, and she laughed, and told me they were impudent fellows who talked nonsense—but I knew it pleased her.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Exemption from punishment or freedom from the harmful consequences of an action.
etymology: From Latin impunitas, from impunis "unpunished," from in- "not" + poena "penalty."

examples.text: The measure said the attack was a firm indication of U.S. resolve that Iran "cannot take military action against the United States with impunity."
examples.source: Reuters, “Senate Backs U.S. Retaliation In Gulf”

examples.text: What right had I to decide, in my poor mortal ignorance of the future, that this man, too, must escape with impunity because he escaped ME?
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: Lasting peace can never be secured if we permit our dangerous opponents to plot future wars with impunity at any mountain retreat - however distant.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Not resulting from or achieved through deliberate planning; unintentional.
etymology: From Latin in- "not" + advertere "to turn toward," hence "not paying attention."

examples.text: Those clicking on the links will inadvertently download the Bofra virus which will then start searching for new addresses to send itself to.
examples.source: BBC News, “Toxic web links help virus spread”

examples.text: Surgeons may be able to use radio-tag technology to detect sponges they've inadvertently left inside their patient, a small US study suggests.
Inadvertently her backview revealed the fact that she is not wearing those rather intimate garments of which you are a particular devotee.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Silly; lacking sense or meaning.
etymology: From Latin inanis "empty, vain."

examples.text: And how inane was the life he led, lounging about bars and drinking in music halls, wandering from one light amour to another!
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Do we not wile away moments of inanity or fatigued waiting by repeating some trivial movement or sound, until the repetition has bred a want, which is incipient habit?
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: They stood in inane suspense till Bresnahan led them out, rumbling, "How about planning a fishing-trip, Will?"
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Unable to express one's ideas or feelings clearly or fluently; not expressed in words.

examples.text: Yet, after prolonged exertions, he could only succeed in getting the drunken man to utter absurd grunts, and violent, but inarticulate oaths.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: He came sliding down the rubbish and crept beside me in the darkness, inarticulate, gesticulating, and for a moment I shared his panic.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: It is probable that the agitated citizen has within his circle at least one inarticulate rebel with aspirations as wayward as Carol's.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Emitting light as a result of being heated; full of strong emotion, passionate or brilliant.
etymology: From Latin incandescere "to begin to glow," from in- "in" + candescere, from candere "to be white, shine."

examples.text: The fire burned brightly, and the soft radiance of the incandescent lights in the lilies of silver caught the bubbles that flashed and passed in our glasses.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: Incandescent rainbows shone above it, blue, red, and golden lights played about it; but the stream itself was white, ineffable.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: Other eyewitnesses depose that they observed an incandescent object of enormous proportions hurtling through the atmosphere at a terrifying velocity in a trajectory directed southwest by west.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: To make very angry; enrage.
etymology: From Latin incendere "to set on fire," the same source as the noun "incense" for fragrant smoke.

examples.text: But the England players are incensed - arguing that the pass was forward and the try should not stand.
She continued deliberately to toss the books severally upon the floor, till Jude, incensed beyond bearing, caught her by the arms to make her leave off.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Of late his mother, incensed with him on account of his love affair and his leaving Moscow, had given up sending him the money.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Continuing without pause or interruption, often annoyingly so.
etymology: From Latin incessans, from in- "not" + cessare "to cease."

examples.text: The visitors' pressure by now was incessant and Rooney had another shot blocked while Ronaldo slammed well over the bar again from a good position.
examples.source: BBC News, “Man Utd through after Exeter test”

examples.text: The case was therefore prepared owing to the incessant labor of Villefort, who wished it to be the first on the list in the coming assizes.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: All these facts emphasize the importance of striving incessantly for a just peace.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: In an initial stage; beginning to happen or develop.
etymology: From Latin incipere "to begin," from in- "into" + capere "to take."

examples.text: Lately both nations have said they will take steps to defuse incipient trade tensions.
examples.source: Reuters, “Economic Spotlight - U.S. Deficit With Nics”

examples.text: His eye became a degree less opaque: it was as though an incipient film had been removed from it, and she felt the pride of a skilful operator.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: His incipient friendship with her aunt had been nipped by the failure of his suit, and all that Oak learnt of Bathsheba's movements was done indirectly.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Intelligently analytical and clear-thinking; sharp and direct.
etymology: From Medieval Latin incisivus, from Latin incidere "to cut into."

examples.text: She had a quick, incisive way of speaking that seemed to go with her features, as the tone and timbre of a violin go with its form.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: "You must be prepared for anything," said the doctor in emphatic and incisive tones, and dropping his eyes, he was about to step out to the coach.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Our visitor glanced with some apparent surprise at the languid, lounging figure of the man who had been no doubt depicted to him as the most incisive reasoner and most energetic agent in Europe.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: To encourage or stir up violent or unlawful behavior; to urge or provoke someone to act.
etymology: From Latin incitare "to set in rapid motion," from in- "on" + citare "to rouse."

examples.text: The industry would halt any attempt by an artist to perform or release a song inciting violence against any group or gender, he said.
The dog, incited by its master, sprang over the wicket-gate and pursued the unfortunate baronet, who fled screaming down the yew alley.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: And today the North Korean regime is using its nuclear program to incite fear and seek concessions.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Of weather, unpleasantly cold or wet; harsh or unmerciful.
etymology: From Latin inclemens, from in- "not" + clemens "mild, merciful."

examples.text: The listening face, insensible to the inclement night, still drooped at the door, and the hands begged me—prayed me—not to cast it forth.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She had come abroad with the Welly Brys at the moment when fashion flees the inclemency of the New York spring.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: When I was thirteen years of age we all went on a party of pleasure to the baths near Thonon; the inclemency of the weather obliged us to remain a day confined to the inn.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: Expressed in a confused or unclear way; lacking logical connection or consistency.

examples.text: Four sides of incoherent and interjectional beginnings of sentences, that had no end, except blots, were inadequate to afford her any relief.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: During the mass Snegiryov became somewhat calmer, though at times he had outbursts of the same unconscious and, as it were, incoherent anxiety.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Year after year, Americans are burdened by an archaic, incoherent federal tax code.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or other aspects of something.
etymology: From Latin incongruus, from in- "not" + congruus "agreeing."

examples.text: "There seems to be some incongruity between technology and our biological wrapping."
Obstacles, incongruities, all melted into the sense of completion with which his soul was flooded by this outward satisfaction of his longing.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: The negative upon the acts of the legislative by the executive authority, and that in the hands of one individual, would seem to be an incongruity in our system.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Not able to be corrected, improved, or reformed.
etymology: From Latin incorrigibilis, from in- "not" + corrigere "to correct."

examples.text: Now, Bildad, I am sorry to say, had the reputation of being an incorrigible old hunks, and in his sea-going days, a bitter, hard task-master.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: "And one which will go far to efface the recollection of his father's conduct," added the incorrigible marquise.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The incorrigible pilgrims have come in with their pockets full of specimens broken from the ruins.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Unwilling or unable to believe something; showing disbelief.
etymology: From Latin incredulus, from in- "not" + credulus "believing," from credere "to believe."

examples.text: Stepan Arkadyevitch took the letter, looked with incredulous surprise at the lusterless eyes fixed so immovably on him, and began to read.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: When the strange idea flashed across her that his words had reference to himself, she was incredulous, and ashamed of entertaining it.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Had anyone told her a week ago that he would have put his arm round her waist at this party of Miss Thorne's, she would have been utterly incredulous.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: To instill an idea, attitude, or habit by persistent instruction or repetition.
etymology: From Latin inculcare "to tread in, press in," from in- "into" + calcare "to tread," from calx "heel."

examples.text: He was the first-born of Newland and May Archer, yet it had never been possible to inculcate in him even the rudiments of reserve.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Stubb's exordium to his crew is given here at large, because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in inculcating the religion of rowing.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: This is in entire accord with the genius of our institutions, and but emphasizes the advantages of inculcating even a greater love for law and order in the future.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Persisting tirelessly; incapable of being fatigued.
etymology: From Latin indefatigabilis, from in- "not" + defatigare "to wear out."

examples.text: And so having easily won the daughter's good-will, the indefatigable little woman bent herself to conciliate the august Lady Southdown.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: I heard him as I came upstairs, and the theatre is engaged of course by those indefatigable rehearsers, Agatha and Frederick.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: These two were so indefatigable in taking Don Quixote out to dance that they tired him down, not only in body but in spirit.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: Not able to be forgotten or removed; making marks that cannot be erased.
etymology: From Latin indelebilis, from in- "not" + delebilis "able to be destroyed," from delere "to destroy, blot out."

examples.text: The other common type of ink in elections is indelible visible ink - but as the elections in Afghanistan showed, improper use of this type of ink can cause additional problems.
examples.source: BBC News, “Ink helps drive democracy in Asia”

examples.text: Popular liberty might then have escaped the indelible reproach of decreeing to the same citizens the hemlock on one day and statues on the next.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: The incidents of the next few days are indelibly graven upon my recollection, and I can tell them without reference to the notes made at the time.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Poor; needy; a needy person.
etymology: From Latin indigens, present participle of indigere "to lack, need."

examples.text: Brute force budget cuts or spending caps would ill-serve the nation's elderly and indigent.
examples.source: BBC News, “The 'ticking budget' facing the US”

examples.text: She had not spirits to notice her in more than a few repulsive looks, but she felt her as a spy, and an intruder, and an indigent niece, and everything most odious.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: If any single scheme could produce the effect of arresting at once that mutation of condition by which thousands of our most indigent fellow-citizens by their industry and enterprise are raised to the possession of wealth, that is the one.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Feeling or showing anger at what is perceived as unfair treatment.
etymology: From Latin indignari "to regard as unworthy," from in- "not" + dignus "worthy."

examples.text: It was a massive-money deal that not only raised eyebrows but stirred active indignation in many quarters, with fans concerned that it is set to enable EA to monopolise the sports gaming landscape to an unhealthy degree.
examples.source: BBC News, “Sporting rivals go to extra time”

examples.text: Trailing at the end of the line Carol was indignant at the prodding curiosity of the others, their manner of staring at the poor as at a Zoo.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: She paused, and saw with no slight indignation that he was listening with an air which proved him wholly unmoved by any feeling of remorse.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: Done at random or without careful judgment; not distinguishing between things.

examples.text: Tasmania's chief vet says Australia's status as being free of mad cow disease (BSE) could be threatened by the indiscriminate use of animal-based pasture fertilisers.
He fell to musing by what process it could come to pass, that he could be humbled before all of them, indiscriminately—humbled by conviction.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Gerty Farish, seated next to Selden, was lost in that indiscriminate and uncritical enjoyment so irritating to Miss Bart's finer perceptions.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Wanting to avoid activity or exertion; lazy.
etymology: From Late Latin indolens "not feeling pain," from in- "not" + dolere "to suffer." Painless became "taking no trouble."

examples.text: Eliza generally took no more notice of her sister's indolence and complaints than if no such murmuring, lounging object had been before her.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: He was one of those, who, liking work, knew how to do it, and despite his indolence would sometimes spend a whole night at his writing table.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: When the first transports of rage which had produced his activity in seeking her were over, he naturally returned to all his former indolence.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: Impossible to subdue or defeat.
etymology: From Late Latin indomitabilis, from in- "not" + domitare "to tame."

examples.text: Her resolution not to enter on the question with him, and his knowledge of her indomitable character, enhanced his sense of helplessness.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It was an act of cold-blooded ferocity, and it consoled him on his deathbed like a memory of an indomitable defiance.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The indomitable spirit that is contributing to this victory for world peace and justice is the same spirit that gives us the power and the potential to meet our toughest challenges at home.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: Impossible to doubt; unquestionable.
etymology: From Latin indubitabilis, from in- "not" + dubitare "to doubt."

examples.text: "Of course," he said to himself, as though a logical, continuous, and clear chain of reasoning had brought him to an indubitable conclusion.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But however indubitable that conclusion and the officer's conviction based upon it, Pierre felt it necessary to disillusion him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: It would seem that both the mature young lady and the mature young gentleman must indubitably be Veneering's oldest friends.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.
etymology: From Latin ineffabilis, from in- "not" + effabilis "utterable," from effari "to speak out."

examples.text: It is an ineffably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm, after a prolonged squeezing, and subsequent decanting.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: "You don't expect anybody to believe this, about the lady and the sovereign, do you?" says the constable, eyeing him aside with ineffable disdain.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: This was not the discomposure of last night; that had quite passed—such discomposures were a detail; the real coercion was to see a man ineffably adored.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: Not producing any or the desired effect; lacking the ability to fulfill a role.

examples.text: Muttering, after an ineffectual call to his lodger, that he will go downstairs and bring a lighted candle from the shop, the old man departs.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: As old chess-players open every game with established gambits, they opened with a thrust and parry, orthodox and even frankly ineffectual.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: Strong as is the tie of interest, it has been often found ineffectual.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Having or showing no skill; clumsy; not suitable to the occasion.
etymology: From Latin ineptus "unsuited, foolish," from in- "not" + aptus "fitted."

examples.text: Controversy was in no short supply, with racist abuse of England's black players, Wayne Rooney's petulance and England's inept performance.
This stupid repetition was too incongruous in its ineptitude with the serious, brooding and enigmatic glance he turned upon his visitor.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The life which had been so charming that he could not bear to leave it now seemed inept; he was seized with a distaste for the cafes, the restaurants with their ill-cooked food, the shabby way in which they all lived.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Lacking the ability or strength to move; sluggish; chemically inactive.
etymology: From Latin iners "unskilled, idle," from in- "without" + ars "skill."

examples.text: London, which had gone to bed on Sunday night oblivious and inert, was awakened, in the small hours of Monday morning, to a vivid sense of danger.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: I sprang to my feet, my inert hand grasping my pistol, my mind paralyzed by the dreadful shape which had sprung out upon us from the shadows of the fog.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: As it sank he became less and less frenzied; and just as it dipped he slid from the hands that held him, an inert mass, on the floor.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Impossible to stop or prevent; (of a person) impossible to persuade.
etymology: From Latin inexorabilis, from in- "not" + exorare "to prevail upon by entreaty," from orare "to pray."

examples.text: The proliferation of gadgets in our homes is inexorably altering the role of the high street in our lives thinks Mr Vaughan.
examples.source: BBC News, “Sony PSP tipped as a 'must-have'”

examples.text: If he was by an inexorable logic to pay for it he was literally impatient to know the cost, and he held himself ready to pay in instalments.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: A third challenge we have is to keep this inexorable march of technology from giving terrorists and potentially hostile nations the means to undermine our defenses.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: Incapable of making mistakes or being wrong; never failing.
etymology: From Medieval Latin infallibilis, from in- "not" + fallere "to deceive."

examples.text: "I profoundly believe in the market system as the best way for securing economic prosperity (but) that does not mean to say the markets are infallible."
examples.source: Reuters, “Lawson Says Bp Share Offer Going Ahead”

examples.text: If Kostya did not agree with her, he almost always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and his verdict was regarded as infallible by both of them.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It is only as the temporary representatives and servants of the people that we meet here, we bring no hereditary status or gift of infallibility, and none follows us from this place.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: The state of being well known for some bad quality or deed; an evil or wicked act.
etymology: From Latin infamia, from in- "not" + fama "reputation."

examples.text: Then, also, the blameless purity of her life during all these years in which she had been set apart to infamy was reckoned largely in her favour.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: The poet did as she bade him, and left her without a shred of reputation, and she was satisfied by getting fame though it was infamy.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: Franklin Delano Roosevelt spoke of a day of infamy and summoned a nation to arms.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Extremely small.
etymology: From Modern Latin infinitesimus, formed from Latin infinitus "infinite."

examples.text: As a philosopher he knew that at the termination of any allotted life only an infinitesimal part of any person's desires has been realised.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Eleanor returned the pressure of the other's hand with an infinitesimal soupcon of a squeeze.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: These infinitesimal distinctions between man and man are too paltry for an Omnipotent Being.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Innocent, unsuspecting, and candid. (Do not confuse with ingenious, "clever.")
etymology: From Latin ingenuus "native, freeborn," hence "noble, frank."

examples.text: It would be a unique delight to wait and watch for the melodious fragments in which her heart and soul came forth so directly and ingenuously.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He rose with a start, his ingenuous face looking as though it had been dipped in crimson: even the reddish tint in his beard seemed to deepen.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Nor did his blushes and awkwardness take away from it: she was pleased with these healthy tokens of the young gentleman's ingenuousness.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Of a habit or belief, firmly fixed or established and difficult to change.

examples.text: Such expectations are now ingrained, which was partly the fault of Nakasone, who heralded Maekawa's report as a sea of change in Japanese affairs, said U.S. Officials.
examples.source: Reuters, “Japan Isolated, Yen Rises, World Feels Cheated”

examples.text: The idea of absolute financial probity as the first law of a gentleman's code was too deeply ingrained in him for sentimental considerations to weaken it.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: He attributed the tragic crime to the habits that had become ingrained by ages of serfdom and the distressed condition of Russia, due to the lack of appropriate institutions.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To bring oneself into favor with someone by flattering or trying to please them.
etymology: From Latin in gratiam "into favor," from gratia "grace, favor."

examples.text: Makar Alexeevich came twice that evening shuffling along in his galoshes as far as the door and stopped and looked ingratiatingly at Pierre.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Indeed, it was remarkable how well he bore these slights and with what unwearying politeness he kept on trying to ingratiate himself with all.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

examples.text: The pedlar's smile grew more ingratiating, though he understood no word of what Cronshaw said, and like a conjurer he produced a sandalwood box.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Tending to obstruct or harm; unfriendly or hostile.
etymology: From Latin inimicalis, from inimicus "enemy," from in- "not" + amicus "friend."

examples.text: When a wife's relations interpose against a husband who is a gentleman, who is proud, and who must govern, the consequences are inimical to peace.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Nor was Miss Briggs, although forced to adopt a hostile attitude, secretly inimical to Rawdon and his wife.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Wealth is not inimical to welfare; it ought to be its friendliest agency.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: Immoral or grossly unfair behavior; wickedness; a sinful act.
etymology: From Latin iniquitas "unfairness," from iniquus, from in- "not" + aequus "equal, just."

examples.text: He said a residency criteria would end "at a stroke this fundamental iniquity".
He did not trouble his friend Mr. Towers with any written statement of the iniquity of Mrs. Proudie, or the imbecility of her husband.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Come, straggling lights into the windows of the ugly houses; and you who do iniquity therein, do it at least with this dread scene shut out!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Inborn; natural; existing in someone or something from the start rather than acquired.
etymology: From Latin innatus, past participle of innasci "to be born in," from in- "in" + nasci "to be born."

examples.text: Among other surprises from the project were that researchers found sea urchins have the most sophisticated innate immune system of any animal studied to date.
She really did hope he liked her face as it was now, but it was simply the rising again of her innate delight in admiration and love.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: We of the Republic sensed the truth that democratic government has innate capacity to protect its people against disasters once considered inevitable, to solve problems once considered unsolvable.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: Not harmful or offensive; inoffensive and unlikely to provoke strong feelings.
etymology: From Latin innocuus, from in- "not" + nocuus "harmful," from nocere "to hurt."

examples.text: The England international, 24, was hurt in an innocuous challenge with Alan Shearer during the Londoners' FA Cup defeat at Newcastle on Sunday.
examples.source: BBC News, “Bridge could miss rest of season”

examples.text: Dynamite was milky and innocuous beside that report of C25; and even an Oriental, with an Oriental's views of the value of time, could see that the sooner it was in the proper hands the better.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: The mere statement of the fact would have rendered it innocuous.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: An indirect or subtle remark, typically suggestive or disparaging.
etymology: From Latin innuendo "by nodding at, by intimating," ablative gerund of innuere "to nod to."

examples.text: The marathon world record holder believes more needs to be done to rid athletics of the "suspicions and innuendoes" which greet any fast time.
examples.source: BBC News, “Radcliffe eyes hard line on drugs”

examples.text: He read another article, too, a financial one, which alluded to Bentham and Mill, and dropped some innuendoes reflecting on the ministry.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: So doing, we must use language to enlighten the mind, not as the instrument of the studied innuendo and distorter of truth.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Unusually or disproportionately large; excessive.
etymology: From Latin inordinatus "disordered," from in- "not" + ordinare "to arrange."

examples.text: He said the March drop in industrial activity "is a reasonable response in light of the inordinate contribution inventory accumulation made to GNP."
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Jobs Data Said To Rule Out Fed Tightening”

examples.text: He never used to swear, though, at his men, they said; but somehow he got an inordinate quantity of cruel, unmitigated hard work out of them.
examples.author: Herman Melville
