examples.text: If in lifting burdens from the daily life of our people we reduce inordinate and unequal advantages too long enjoyed, this is but a necessary incident of our return to right and justice.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Impossible to satisfy.
etymology: From Latin insatiabilis, from in- "not" + satiare "to satisfy," from satis "enough."

examples.text: Australian marine scientists are trying to farm tropical lobsters, in a bid to meet the insatiable appetite of the Chinese.
In her home she had a habit of being invisible, sometimes through insatiable domesticity, sometimes through an equally insatiable solitude.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: When this corrupting passion once takes possession of the human mind, like the love of gold it becomes insatiable.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Impossible to understand or interpret; mysterious.
etymology: From Late Latin inscrutabilis, from in- "not" + scrutari "to search, examine."

examples.text: It came at the end of his speeches like a seal applied on the words to make the meaning of the commonest phrase appear absolutely inscrutable.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: I still stood absolutely dumfoundered at what appeared to me her miraculous self-possession and most inscrutable hypocrisy, when the cook entered.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: For, it inscrutably appeared to stand to reason, in the minds of the whole company, that I was an excrescence on the entertainment.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Proceeding in a gradual, subtle way but with harmful effects.
etymology: From Latin insidiosus "cunning," from insidiae "ambush," from insidere "to sit in, lie in wait."

examples.text: At a time when negative stereotypes of Muslims are on the increase we feel that Sky - as a major UK broadcaster - has a responsibility to challenge these insidious views, not help to reinforce them.
examples.source: BBC News, “Muslim group attacks TV drama 24”

examples.text: As he had often done before, he pulled his hat over his face and watched the sun peering insidiously at him through the interstices of the straw.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: The strong man must at all times be alert to the attack of insidious disease.
examples.author: Herbert Hoover

definition: To suggest or hint something bad in an indirect way; to work oneself into favor or a position by subtle means.
etymology: From Latin insinuare "to bring in by winding," from in- "in" + sinus "curve, fold."

examples.text: This was addressed to the brown setter, who had jumped up at the sound of the voices and laid her nose in an insinuating way on her master's leg.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: It was in vain that the archdeacon tried to insinuate, though he could not plainly declare, that there were no new duties to perform.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: We reject any insinuation that one race or another, one people or another, is in any sense inferior or expendable.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Lacking flavor; lacking vigor or interest.
etymology: From Late Latin insipidus, from in- "not" + sapidus "tasty," from sapere "to taste, be wise" (also in "sapient").

examples.text: The eaters of the dinner, like the dinner itself, were lukewarm, insipid, overdone—and all owing to this poor little dull Young Barnacle.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The waves were colourless, and the Bournemouth steamer gave a further touch of insipidity, drawn up against the pier and hooting wildly for excursionists.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: The news that "Bony" was come back from Egypt was comparatively insipid, and the repulse of the French in Italy was nothing to Mrs. Poyser's repulse of the old squire.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Showing a rude and arrogant lack of respect.
etymology: From Latin insolens "unaccustomed, arrogant," from in- "not" + solere "to be accustomed."

examples.text: Well sped, my boy, before the world had dubbed your ambition insolence, had held your ideals unattainable, and taught you to cringe and bow.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: Dolokhov with a cold smile and a gleam in his handsome insolent eyes looked at him—evidently wishing to get some more amusement out of him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: No weak nation that acts manfully and justly should ever have cause to fear us, and no strong power should ever be able to single us out as a subject for insolent aggression.
examples.author: Theodore Roosevelt

definition: Ignorant of or uninterested in cultures, ideas, or people outside one's own experience; relating to an island.
etymology: From Late Latin insularis, from insula "island."

examples.text: There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Both preferred a continental to an insular manner of life, a cisatlantic to a transatlantic place of residence.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: So much of my early life has been passed abroad, that I have quite cast my insular skin in that respect.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Too great to be overcome.

examples.text: Some analysts believe Icahn's proposed three-way airline combination might face insurmountable regulatory hurdles, but others believe it could be cleared if the companies are acquired separately.
When he found the old woman he had felt an insurmountable repulsion for her at the first glance, though he knew nothing special about her.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In justly balancing the powers of the Federal and State authorities difficulties nearly insurmountable arose at the outset and subsequent collisions were deemed inevitable.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: To intervene on behalf of another; to mediate in a dispute.
etymology: From Latin intercedere "to come between," from inter- "between" + cedere "to go."

examples.text: But the ladies interceded, and when it had been made clear that it was a very great favour, the goddess was allowed to mount beside the god.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: Kolya's mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intercession by a suggestion of hope.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It does not say, "Intercede for us, through the Saviour, with the Father, for this boon," but "Blessed Peter, give it us."
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Endless or apparently endless, often tediously so.
etymology: From Late Latin interminabilis, from in- "not" + terminare "to limit," from terminus "boundary."

examples.text: Instead, the worst die-offs happen when some sort of interminable, multi-generational pressure on life is combined with a few powerful blows.
I heard your father and mine talking about it a little while ago, after dinner, in one of their interminable discussions about business.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Then, after an interminable time, as it seemed to us, crouching and peering through the hedge, came a sound like the distant concussion of a gun.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: Occurring at irregular intervals; not continuous or steady.
etymology: From Latin intermittere "to leave off, interrupt," from inter- "between" + mittere "to let go."

examples.text: Cargo handling companies said they were hiring twice the usual number of dockers to offset an intermittent strike in Spanish ports.
examples.source: Reuters, “Spain Cargo Firms Hire Dockers To Offset Strike”

examples.text: The kitchens were cupboards each containing an electric range, a copper sink, a glass refrigerator, and, very intermittently, a Balkan maid.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: In the past decade we have intermittently considered a variety of programs, but we have never adopted a consistent policy.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: Hard to control, deal with, or solve; stubborn.
etymology: From Latin intractabilis, from in- "not" + tractabilis "manageable," from tractare "to handle."

examples.text: He said the buyer would also have to deal with "the intractable problems" Tenneco faces with its farm equipment unit and energy businesses.
When he looked about him for another and a less intractable damsel to immortalize in melody, memory produced one with the most obliging readiness.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: All of us know the depth of bitterness that has made the dispute between Israel and its neighbors so painful and intractable.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: Unwilling or refusing to change one's views or to agree about something.
etymology: From Spanish los intransigentes, the name of an extreme republican party in the 1870s, from Latin in- "not" + transigere "to come to an agreement."

examples.text: Employers organization chairman, Jacques Schoufour, accused the FNV of intransigence in refusing to alter its stance at all over the past two months.
examples.source: Reuters, “Neither Side Optimistic On Rotterdam Port Issues”

examples.text: Jorge Cardenas, manager of the national federation and head of his nation's delegation in London, has blamed the intransigence of some big countries, without naming them.
examples.source: Reuters, “Colombia Coffee Exporters Believe In Pragmatism”

examples.text: Tesfay accused the West of intransigence in the negotiation of recent commodity agreements.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ethiopia Minister Sees Africa Debt Payment Problem”

definition: Fearless; adventurous.
etymology: From Latin intrepidus, from in- "not" + trepidus "alarmed" (compare "trepidation").

examples.text: Not only do mythical figures like the Amazons, the god Apollo or the sirens of Homeric lore appear in space, but Star Trek contains the sweeping themes of intrepid adventure and bold exploration that lie at the heart of classical mythology.
She had thought that of course Tom had deserted long ago, and she wondered at seeing him place himself in her power again in this intrepid way.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: It spoke in a voice harsh and lugubrious but intrepid, and little by little it dawned upon Archie that this was a development of the Patna case.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Very complicated or detailed, with many interrelated parts.
etymology: From Latin intricatus "entangled," from intricare, from in- "in" + tricae "perplexities."

examples.text: The finding may help explain some whale behaviours, such as intricate communication skills, the formation of alliances, cooperation, cultural transmission and the use of tools, the researchers report in journal The Anatomical Record.
This man carved the walls of his prison house from floor to roof with all manner of figures of men and animals grouped in intricate designs.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: The economic mechanism is intricate and its parts interdependent, and has suffered the shocks and jars incident to abnormal demands, credit inflations, and price upheavals.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: Belonging naturally; essential to the nature of a thing.
etymology: From Latin intrinsecus "inwardly, on the inside."

examples.text: It's so contentious that earlier this year Professor Lawrence Summers resigned as president of Harvard University amid an uproar after he suggested that women have less intrinsic ability in maths and science than men.
A man's estimates of value betray something of the STRUCTURE of his soul, and wherein it sees its conditions of life, its intrinsic needs.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: It is no paradox to say that although comparatively weak the new-born nation was intrinsically strong.
examples.author: Franklin Pierce

definition: To flood; to overwhelm someone with things to be dealt with.
etymology: From Latin inundare, from in- "onto" + unda "a wave."

examples.text: The barring of non-US visitors has led to the campaign being inundated with calls and forced it to make a statement about why the blocking was taking place.
examples.source: BBC News, “Attack prompts Bush site block”

examples.text: "We have the beer, but distribution and sales is the important point," van Schaik said, adding that since the ruling Heineken had been inundated by German traders seeking joint ventures.
examples.source: Reuters, “Heineken Sees Higher Profits, Wider Penetration”

examples.text: Here and there, especially at first, the inundation started on them and swept by; but when they had done descending, and were winding and climbing up a tower, they were alone.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To accustom someone to something, especially something unpleasant, so they cease to be affected.

examples.text: Many moderns, inured to a weak worship of intellect and force, might have wavered in their allegiance under this oppression of a great personality.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: Eleanor's countenance was dejected, yet sedate; and its composure spoke her inured to all the gloomy objects to which they were advancing.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: "However, it is so sometimes, and nothing happens that we expect," he added, with the repose of a man whom misfortune had inured rather than subdued.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Insulting, abusive, or highly critical language.
etymology: From Late Latin invectivus "abusive," from invehi "to attack with words," the same source as "inveigh."

examples.text: The former Dundee United and Dumbarton full-back is from the managerial old school - straight talking and never slow to let players know when he expects better (often with the use of some colourful invective).
examples.source: BBC News, “Can Smith work Scottish wonders?”

examples.text: I now related my history briefly but with firmness and precision, marking the dates with accuracy and never deviating into invective or exclamation.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: The opening was a sound piece of slashing invective about the evil secrets of princes, and despair in the high places of the earth.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Having a particular habit or quality that is long established and unlikely to change.
etymology: From Latin inveteratus "made old," from in- "into" + vetus, veter- "old."

examples.text: But, imbued from her childhood with a brooding sense of wrong, and an inveterate hatred of a class, opportunity had developed her into a tigress.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Though one of the most inveterate smokers I ever met with, he gave up his cigar, because she said, one day, she hated the stale smell of it in his clothes.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: The gentleman with the gray whiskers was obviously an inveterate adherent of serfdom and a devoted agriculturist, who had lived all his life in the country.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Likely to arouse resentment or anger in others; unfairly discriminating.
etymology: From Latin invidiosus, from invidia "envy, ill will."

examples.text: But all suppositions of this kind are invidious, and ought to be banished from the consideration of the great question before the people.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Had what now really prevailed with Strether been but a dread of that thump—a dread of wincing a little painfully at what it might invidiously demonstrate?
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: It will be understood that the food and champagne were of the best—the talk and laughter too, in the sense of belonging to the best society, where no one makes an invidious display of anything in particular, and the advantages of the world are taken with that high-bred depreciation which follows from being accustomed to them.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Too powerful to be defeated or overcome.
etymology: From Latin invincibilis, from in- "not" + vincere "to conquer."

examples.text: These sentences, and those to follow, should send a message to others entertaining similar beliefs of invincibility.
examples.source: BBC News, “The pirates with no profit motive”

examples.text: Mr Dorrit, still panting under his injury, saluted the gentleman, and saluted the lady, in a distant, final, and invincible manner.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The legend that they were invincible — above and beyond the processes of a democracy — has been shattered.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: Never to be broken, infringed, or dishonored.
etymology: From Latin inviolabilis, from in- "not" + violare "to violate."

examples.text: Formerly they believed themselves sprung from Jupiter, and shielded by their birth; but nowadays they are not inviolable.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The one would be amenable to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: The credit of the Government, the integrity of its currency, and the inviolability of its obligations must be preserved.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Having or showing a tendency to be easily angered.
etymology: From Late Latin irascibilis, from irasci "to grow angry," from ira "anger."

examples.text: It is true that he was irascible by nature, "of an unstable and unbalanced mind," as our justice of the peace, Katchalnikov, happily described him.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But Vronsky was startled and annoyed by the nervous irascibility with which Golenishtchev talked of the subject that engrossed him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: They spoke of the sayings and doings of their commander, the Grand Duke, and told stories of his kindness and irascibility.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Showing luminous colors that seem to change when seen from different angles.
etymology: From Latin iris, irid- "rainbow," from Greek iris "rainbow."

examples.text: These tints of feeling indeed were doubtless but the iridescence of his idleness, and they were presently lost in a new light from Maria.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: Well, all that was clear to him amounted to this, that the whole scheme had burst up, like an iridescent soap-bubble, under the touch of a reasoned inquiry.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: He played with the idea and grew wilful; tossed it into the air and transformed it; let it escape and recaptured it; made it iridescent with fancy and winged it with paradox.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

definition: To irritate or annoy.

examples.text: Firstly, the carefully-scripted way that you progress through each level might irk some people.
examples.source: BBC News, “No half measures with Half-Life 2”

examples.text: It irks me, nevertheless, that the partner of her iniquity should not at least, stand on the scaffold by her side.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: He was tired of having to do things because he was told; and the restrictions irked him, not because they were unreasonable, but because they were restrictions.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Representing findings or views so opposed that they cannot be made compatible; of people, implacably hostile.

examples.text: The company cited "irreconcilable differences" in the financial structure of the deal.
It is likely that these occupations are irreconcilable with home enjoyment, but it is certain that Mr. Bucket at present does not go home.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Even among the zealous patrons of a council of state the most irreconcilable variance is discovered concerning the mode in which it ought to be constituted.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Impossible to deny or disprove.
etymology: From Late Latin irrefutabilis, from in- "not" + refutare "to repel, refute."

examples.text: There is irrefutable proof that foxes are alive and thriving in Tasmania after the discovery of a still warm carcass by a farmer in the Northern Midlands yesterday.
The theory seems irrefutable just because the act of transference of the people's will cannot be verified, for it never occurred.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: I should like to make a chain of evidence such as twice two are four, it ought to be a direct, irrefutable proof!
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Showing a lack of respect for people or things generally taken seriously.

examples.text: But there was no sign of reawakening courage in his followers, rather, indeed, of growing terror at the irreverence of his words.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

examples.text: She drove into town for the purpose in a one-horse carriage irreverently called at that period of English history, a pill-box.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The merits of all these candidates were discussed and somewhat irreverently disposed of, and then "The Jupiter" declared that Dr. Proudie was to be the man.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Not able to be changed, reversed, or recovered; final.
etymology: From Latin irrevocabilis, from in- "not" + revocare "to call back."

examples.text: He hurried downstairs and left poor Maggie to that bitter sense of the irrevocable which was almost an every-day experience of her small soul.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: A deed done is irrevocable, and its result coinciding in time with the actions of millions of other men assumes an historic significance.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: To avoid misconstruction of what I have said, I depart from my purpose not to speak of particular amendments so far as to say that, holding such a provision to now be implied constitutional law, I have no objection to its being made express and irrevocable.
examples.author: Abraham Lincoln

definition: Traveling from place to place, especially for work; a person who travels in this way.
etymology: From Late Latin itinerari "to travel," from Latin iter, itiner- "journey."

examples.text: Vilbert was an itinerant quack-doctor, well known to the rustic population, and absolutely unknown to anybody else, as he, indeed, took care to be, to avoid inconvenient investigations.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: They were Levantines, itinerant vendors of cheap rugs, and each bore on his arm a bundle.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The one called Lucas was a mild and meek-looking little gentleman of clerical aspect; he had been an itinerant evangelist, it transpired, and had seen the light and become a prophet of the new dispensation.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

definition: Tired, bored, or lacking enthusiasm, typically after having had too much of something.

examples.text: Early in the forenoon parties of jaded men began to straggle into the village, but the strongest of the citizens continued searching.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: A knowledge of its faded and jaded condition made the charge appear like a paroxysm, a display of the strength that comes before a final feebleness.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

examples.text: I had had a hard day's work, and was pretty well jaded when I came climbing out, at last, upon the level of Blackheath.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Fond of or characterized by joking; humorous or playful.
etymology: From Latin jocularis, from joculus "little joke," diminutive of jocus "joke."

examples.text: I was quite unprepared for the rapid manner in which Mrs. Guppy's power of jocularity merged into a power of taking the profoundest offence.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There was some speculation at the dinner-table about the Time Traveller's absence, and I suggested time travelling, in a half-jocular spirit.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: When they did venture, tables got in their way, and they sought to cover embarrassment by heavy jocularity at the coatroom.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Having, showing, or done with good judgment or sense.
etymology: From French judicieux, from Latin judicium "judgment."

examples.text: It is not easy, therefore, to commend too highly the judicious attention which has been paid to this subject in the proposed Constitution.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: When these had been judiciously distributed in the various rooms she would be likely to occupy, I considered that my preparations were complete.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: When judiciously and properly exercised, the Constitution itself may be saved from infraction and the rights of all preserved and protected.
examples.author: James K. Polk

definition: Praise and honor received for an achievement.
etymology: From Greek kudos "glory, renown"; it is singular in origin, though often treated as plural.

examples.text: But it was not only the senior squad that brought kudos to Ireland, the youngsters strutted their stuff on the big stage as well.
examples.source: BBC News, “A year to remember for Irish”

examples.text: Their motivation was the kudos which surrounded being able to crack sophisticated software.
examples.source: BBC News, “The pirates with no profit motive”

examples.text: She was equally irritated, when the motor returned through Gopher Prairie, to find that she was proud of sharing in Bresnahan's kudos as people waved, and Juanita Haydock leaned from a window.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Lacking enthusiasm and determination; carelessly lazy.
etymology: From the archaic exclamation "lackaday," a shortening of "alack the day."

examples.text: A senior Tory MP has criticised agriculture department Defra's "lackadaisical" approach to planning for a future foot and mouth outbreak.
examples.source: BBC News, “New foot and mouth action urged”

examples.text: She is but a poor lackadaisical creature, and it is my belief has no heart at all.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: There is no doubt whatever that I was a lackadaisical young spooney; but there was a purity of heart in all this, that prevents my having quite a contemptuous recollection of it, let me laugh as I may.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Using very few words.
etymology: From Greek Lakōnikos "of Laconia," the region around Sparta. Spartans were famed for curt speech; when Philip II of Macedon threatened "If I invade Laconia...," they reportedly replied, "If."

examples.text: Jude did not pause to remember that, in the laconic words of the historian, "insulted Nature sometimes vindicated her rights" in such circumstances.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: But their father, though very laconic in his expressions of pleasure, was really glad to see them; he had felt their importance in the family circle.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Mr Plornish, as being of a more laconic temperament, embraced this opportunity of interposing with the suggestion that she should now leave Mr Clennam to himself.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Displaying or having a disinclination for physical exertion; relaxed and slow; weak or faint.
etymology: From Latin languidus "faint, weak," from languere "to be weak."

examples.text: It was not a scorching, hard, dusty day like the treacherous intruder of a week before, but soaked with languor, softened with a milky light.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The wind shook some blossoms from the trees, and the heavy lilac-blooms, with their clustering stars, moved to and fro in the languid air.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

examples.text: Yet, in spite of all this, Anne had reason to believe that she had moments only of languor and depression, to hours of occupation and enjoyment.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: To lose or lack vitality; to grow weak; to be forced to remain in an unpleasant place or situation.
etymology: From Old French languir, from Latin languere "to be faint, weak."

examples.text: Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger has admitted he is at a loss to explain why Newcastle are languishing in the bottom half of the table.
examples.source: BBC News, “Wenger shock at Newcastle dip”

examples.text: He was silent and sensitive, and ready to sigh and languish ponderously (as only fat men CAN sigh and languish) on the smallest provocation.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: It is tough on criminals and supportive of police, and it has been languishing in these hallowed halls for years now.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: A state of physical or mental weariness; lack of energy.
etymology: From Latin lassitudo, from lassus "weary."

examples.text: Despite that pernicious assumption of lassitude and indifference, which had become his second nature, he was strongly attached to his friend.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Kutuzov still in the same place, his stout body resting heavily in the saddle with the lassitude of age, sat yawning wearily with closed eyes.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: At length lassitude succeeded to the tumult I had before endured, and I threw myself on the bed in my clothes, endeavouring to seek a few moments of forgetfulness.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: Existing but not yet developed, manifest, or active; hidden.
etymology: From Latin latens, present participle of latere "to lie hidden."

examples.text: Will saw that she was offended, but this only gave an additional impulse to the new irritation of his latent dislike towards Mr. Casaubon.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: I have still a latent belief that she must have been Mrs. Crupp's daughter in disguise, we had such an awful time of it with Mary Anne.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He had detected the latent sensuality, which unfolded under his delicate sense of her nature's requirements like a torpid, torrid, sensitive blossom.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

definition: Deserving praise and commendation.
etymology: From Latin laudabilis, from laudare "to praise," from laus, laud- "praise."

examples.text: A visitor coming with such laudable intentions might be received with more attention and consideration than if he came from simple curiosity.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In a word, no great improvement or laudable enterprise can go forward which requires the auspices of a steady system of national policy.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: It had the best of taste, the best of inexpensive rugs, a simple and laudable architecture, and the latest conveniences.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Not sufficiently strict, severe, or careful; loose or slack.
etymology: From Latin laxus "loose."

examples.text: Regulations designed to ensure energy-efficient buildings are too lax, and builders routinely flout them anyway, it said.
examples.source: BBC News, “Housing plans criticised by MPs”

examples.text: He disliked having anything to do with the domestic serfs—the "drones" as he called them—and everyone said he spoiled them by his laxity.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: It was one thing to look back on forgiven sins, nay, to explain questionable conformity to lax customs, and another to enter deliberately on the necessity of falsehood.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Affected by a lack of energy or enthusiasm; sluggish.
etymology: From Greek lēthargos "forgetful," from lēthē "forgetfulness." Lethe was the river of forgetting in the underworld.

examples.text: Indeed, it was the visitors who looked likelier to enliven a drab opening played at a lethargic pace.
examples.source: BBC News, “Chelsea denied by James heroics”

examples.text: The gaunt rooms, deserted for years upon years, seemed to have settled down into a gloomy lethargy from which nothing could rouse them again.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The lethargy grows upon her, and though she seems strong and well, and is getting back some of her colour, Van Helsing and I are not satisfied.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Humor or frivolity, especially the treatment of a serious matter with inappropriate lightness.
etymology: From Latin levitas "lightness," from levis "light."

examples.text: Is any man insane enough to imagine that this picnic of patriarchs sang, made love, danced, laughed, told anecdotes, dealt in ungodly levity?
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: In the very act of calling this tone of levity to his aid, he felt it to be profligate and worthless, and asserted her against it.

examples.text: "Such immediate expectation of something extraordinary," he said, "shows a levity, possible to worldly people but unseemly in us."
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: A person, especially a man, who behaves without moral principles, especially in sexual matters; freethinking or dissolute.
etymology: From Latin libertinus "freedman," from libertus "made free," from liber "free."

examples.text: So did a man with the air of an emaciated beau or worn-out libertine, who looked at life through one eye-glass, and held out his hand tremulously when he asked for change.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: And so the young man passes out of his original nature, which was trained in the school of necessity, into the freedom and libertinism of useless and unnecessary pleasures.

examples.text: Now he did not try; he merely made love; and Louetta dropped her head on his shoulder, told him what a nagger Eddie was, and accepted Babbitt as a decent and well-trained libertine.

definition: Promiscuous and unprincipled in sexual matters; disregarding accepted rules or conventions.
etymology: From Latin licentiosus, from licentia "freedom, license."

examples.text: He could not have thought worse of the document had he read it and discovered it to be licentious and atheistical.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: My mind shudders when I think of her awful, awful situation, and that, near as she is to the grave, she should be so given up to vanity, licentiousness, profaneness, and folly.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: During this course of administration, and in order to disturb it, the artillery of the press has been leveled against us, charged with whatsoever its licentiousness could devise or dare.
examples.author: Thomas Jefferson

definition: Of a liquid, completely clear and transparent; of writing or music, clear and easily understood.
etymology: From Latin limpidus "clear."

examples.text: Here he sees a brook whose limpid waters, like liquid crystal, ripple over fine sands and white pebbles that look like sifted gold and purest pearls.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: Her large eyes were limpid and almost colourless; they seemed to be very little affected by light, and to stand unnaturally still.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: From a little mound here in the plain issues a broad stream of limpid water and forms a large shallow pool, and then rushes furiously onward, augmented in volume.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Lacking energy or enthusiasm.

examples.text: I passed whole days on the lake alone in a little boat, watching the clouds and listening to the rippling of the waves, silent and listless.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: He thought of it with such a passionate desire, all through May and June, that, when at length the time came for him to go, he was listless.

examples.text: It seems hardly real when I find myself leaning for a moment on a ruined wall and looking listlessly down into the historic pool of Bethesda.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Furiously angry; dark bluish-gray in color, like a bruise.
etymology: From Latin lividus "bluish, envious," from livere "to be bluish."

examples.text: England coach Andy Robinson said he was "livid" after his side were denied two tries in Sunday's 19-13 Six Nations loss to Ireland in Dublin.
The other convict was livid to look at, and, in addition to the old bruised left side of his face, seemed to be bruised and torn all over.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: His face was livid, large drops rolled down his face, and in his fingers he held the fragments of a quill pen which he had torn to atoms.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Reluctant; unwilling.
etymology: From Old English lath "hostile, hateful."

examples.text: Understandably, they want more and until they do, both they and others are loath to continue lending.

examples.text: Dealers here were loath to quantify the scale of Bank of Japan action this morning.

examples.text: When they drew near he motioned them away with an expressive action of the foot, loath to disturb the fixed lines of his countenance, his arms, or his rigid shoulders.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

definition: Tending to talk a great deal; talkative.
etymology: From Latin loquax "talkative," from loqui "to speak."

examples.text: Pedestrians are also out in force, and are a loquacious bunch.
examples.source: BBC News, “GTA sequel is criminally good”

examples.text: Uncle Glegg stood open-mouthed with astonishment at this unembarrassed loquacity, with which his understanding could hardly keep pace.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; showing an ability to think clearly.
etymology: From Latin lucidus "bright," from lux "light."

examples.text: But he rode home with a terribly lucid vision of the difficulty there would be in arranging any result that could be permanently counted on with this man.

examples.text: Mr Plornish amiably growled, in his philosophical but not lucid manner, that there was ups you see, and there was downs.

definition: So foolish, unreasonable, or out of place as to be amusing; absurd.
etymology: From Latin ludicrus "sportive," from ludus "play, game."

examples.text: Tony Blair has launched an attack on Conservative spending plans, saying they are a "ludicrous improbability".
examples.source: BBC News, “Blair blasts Tory spending plans”

examples.text: "It is ludicrous for the nations of the world to plough immense amounts of financial resources into the production of items that nobody wants to buy," he said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Yeutter Sees Gatt Consensus On Farm Trade Reform”

examples.text: Most terrible of all had been his ludicrous, shameful position when Alexey Alexandrovitch had pulled his hands away from his humiliated face.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal, often exaggeratedly so.
etymology: From Latin lugubris "mournful," from lugere "to mourn."

examples.text: Cecil and Lucy turned up at four o'clock, and these, with little Minnie Beebe, made a somewhat lugubrious sextette upon the upper lawn for tea.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: All through the meal Gunch watched them, while Babbitt watched himself being watched and lugubriously tried to keep from spoiling Tanis's gaiety.

examples.text: How does that little old song go, which, under pretence of being cheerful, is by far the most lugubrious I ever heard in my life?

definition: Very vivid in color, especially unpleasantly so; presented in a sensational, shocking way with gruesome details.
etymology: From Latin luridus "pale yellow, wan."

examples.text: Then it was withdrawn as suddenly as it appeared, and all was dark again save the single lurid spark which marked a chink between the stones.

examples.text: It was whispered by those who peered after her that the scarlet letter threw a lurid gleam along the dark passage-way of the interior.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: The sun, shining through the smoke that drove up from the tops of the trees, seemed blood red, and threw an unfamiliar lurid light upon everything.

definition: Growing thickly and abundantly; lush; richly ornate or profuse.
etymology: From Latin luxuriare "to grow rank, be excessive," from luxuria "excess."

examples.text: Therefore she did as she was told, and did it with such nervous hands that her hair (which was luxuriant and beautiful) fell all about her face.

examples.text: The draperies and fluttering things which she wore suited her rich, luxuriant beauty as a greater severity of line could not have done.

examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: A crafty scheme or plot intended to achieve a sinister end.
etymology: From Latin machinatio, from machinari "to contrive, plot," from machina "device."

examples.text: "None of the 10 former directors was a direct participant in the accounting machinations of the WorldCom fraud," said the Wall Street Journal (WSJ).
They knew that, and their machinations were conducted in secret; consequently, Madame Rigaud and I were brought into frequent and unfortunate collision.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, against whom your evil machinations avail not nor have any power.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: Very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
etymology: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus "great" + animus "soul."

examples.text: I regard you in any case as a man of noble character and not without elements of magnanimity, though I don't agree with all your convictions.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In spite of this magnanimity Dorothea was still smarting: perhaps as much from Celia's subdued astonishment as from her small criticisms.

examples.text: They have claims on the magnanimity and, I may add, on the justice of this nation which we must all feel.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: A disease or ailment; a serious problem afflicting a society or institution.
etymology: From Old French maladie, from malade "sick," from Latin male habitus "in poor condition."

examples.text: Many, already smitten, went home only to die: some died at the school, and were buried quietly and quickly, the nature of the malady forbidding delay.

etymology: From Latin malevolens, from male "badly" + volens "wishing."

examples.text: Cornelius would keep on slinking through the doorways, across the verandah and back again, as mute as a fish, and with malevolent, mistrustful, underhand glances.

definition: The intention or desire to do harm or evil; ill will.
etymology: From Old French malice, from Latin malitia "badness," from malus "bad."

definition: To speak harmful untruths about; slander; (as adjective) evil in nature or harmful in effect.
etymology: From Latin malignus "evil-disposed," from malus "bad."

examples.text: At its most malign, spyware watches everything that people do with their PC and steals login information and other personal data.
examples.source: BBC News, “Microsoft sets sights on spyware”

examples.text: Can it be that there is a malign influence of the sun at periods which affects certain natures—as at times the moon does others?

examples.text: His look went from brooder's beard to carper's skull, to remind, to chide them not unkindly, then to the baldpink lollard costard, guiltless though maligned.

definition: Clear or obvious to the eye or mind; to show or display plainly.
etymology: From Latin manifestus "palpable, evident."

examples.text: She adds that many other animals possess self-awareness, a multi-faceted, complex phenomenon, which seems to manifest itself at different levels.

definition: Many and various; having many different forms or elements.
etymology: From Old English manigfeald "many-fold."

examples.text: No one who has not had a hand in the preparation of such an affair can understand the manifold difficulties which Miss Thorne encountered in her project.

definition: Self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental, often from drunkenness.
etymology: From Middle English Maudelen, Mary Magdalene, who was commonly depicted weeping.

examples.text: Some stagger about in each other's arms, whispering maudlin words—others start quarrels upon the slightest pretext, and come to blows and have to be pulled apart.

examples.text: Still: but an itch of death is in them, to tell me in my ear a maudlin tale, urge me to wreak their will.

examples.text: He burst into tears of maudlin pity for himself, and at length suffering her to embrace him and take charge of him, let his grey head rest against her cheek, and bewailed his wretchedness.

definition: Excessively or falsely sentimental; sickly or feeble in sentiment.
etymology: From obsolete mawk "maggot"; the word originally meant "nauseated" or "nauseating."

examples.text: It would have been good-natured except for a look in the eyes, which shone with a watery, mawkish light under almost white, blinking eyelashes.

examples.text: At Heidelberg I met a fat veterinary surgeon whose voice broke with sobs as he repeated some mawkish poetry.

examples.text: He was astonished at its religious tone, which seemed to him neither mawkish nor sentimental.

definition: A short statement expressing a general truth or rule of conduct.
etymology: From Medieval Latin maxima, as in maxima propositio "greatest premise."

examples.text: His hope must be that voters watching him on the rack will bear out for Labour the old maxim: "No pain, no gain."

examples.text: Having now seen that the maxims relied upon will not bear the use made of them, let us endeavor to ascertain their proper use and true meaning.

examples.text: Some of our best political maxims and opinions have been drawn from our parent isle.

definition: Lacking in quantity or quality; deficient or scanty.
etymology: From Old French maigre "thin," from Latin macer "lean."

definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
etymology: From Latin mel "honey" + fluere "to flow."

examples.text: Just as I moved the Count's persuasive hand was laid on his shoulder, and the Count's mellifluous voice interposed to quiet him.

definition: A beggar; given to begging, especially as a member of a religious order living on alms.
etymology: From Latin mendicare "to beg," from mendicus "beggar."

examples.text: In that country the preachers are not like our mendicant orders of friars—they have two or three suits of clothing, and they wash sometimes.

examples.text: Thy face and thy walk and thy fashion of speech put me in mind of my Sahib, though thou art only a wandering mendicant to whom I give a dole.

examples.text: I may feel—nay, know—that in uniting herself to Mr Rokesmith she has united herself to one who is, in spite of shallow sophistry, a Mendicant.

definition: Motivated primarily by money or gain; a soldier hired to fight for a foreign army.
etymology: From Latin mercenarius "hireling," from merces "wages."

examples.text: Then she tried a child's story, which she could easily have disposed of if she had not been mercenary enough to demand filthy lucre for it.

examples.text: I say, therefore, that the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or they are mercenaries, auxiliaries, or mixed.

examples.text: Believe that they are not all mercenary, although I have, through a series of strange fatalities, faded out of my place in life.

definition: Subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or mind.
etymology: From Latin mercurialis "of Mercury," the swift messenger god whose name was also given to the volatile metal.

examples.text: But before that game in Cardiff, Wales must get past Scotland at Murrayfield, while Ireland face the not insignificant task of a home fixture with the mercurial French.

examples.text: He wanted no confidence in return, but seemed to take Deronda as an Olympian who needed nothing—an egotism in friendship which is common enough with mercurial, expansive natures.

definition: Deserving reward or praise.
etymology: From Latin meritorius, from mereri "to earn, deserve."

examples.text: Such behaviour as this, so exactly the reverse of her own, appeared no more meritorious to Marianne, than her own had seemed faulty to her.

definition: To have a strong influence or effect, especially against something; to weigh heavily against.
etymology: From Latin militare "to serve as a soldier," from miles "soldier."

definition: A difficult situation from which it is hard to escape; swampy ground; to entangle in difficulty.
etymology: From Old Norse mýrr "bog."

examples.text: In Germany, industry is exporting more these days, but the economy as a whole is once again mired in slow growth and high unemployment.

examples.text: Yet it was not a common passage through common rain, and mire, and noise, to Clennam, having this little, slender, careful creature on his arm.

examples.text: You may grow fond of that mire of crawling, cowardly morals, and you may come to think a blow bad, because it hurts, and not because it humiliates.

definition: A person who dislikes humankind and avoids human society.
etymology: From Greek misanthrōpos, from misein "to hate" + anthrōpos "human being." Popularized by Molière's play Le Misanthrope (1666).

examples.text: Like a plethoric burning martyr, or a self-consuming misanthrope, once ignited, the whale supplies his own fuel and burns by his own body.

examples.text: A perfect misanthropist's heaven: and Mr. Heathcliff and I are such a suitable pair to divide the desolation between us.

examples.text: All the world used her ill, said this young misanthropist, and we may be pretty certain that persons whom all the world treats ill, deserve entirely the treatment they get.

definition: To interpret wrongly; misunderstand.
etymology: From mis- "wrongly" + construe, from Latin construere "to build up, construct."

examples.text: "We knew when we did it that it could be misconstrued, and that people almost inevitably would say (the acquisition was) defensive, but it never was," Holden-Brown told reporters.

examples.text: Still, when I reached my chamber, I felt a pang at the idea she should even temporarily misconstrue what she had seen.

examples.text: My own position upon this subject was clear and unequivocal, upon the record of my words and my acts, and it is only recurred to at this time because silence might perhaps be misconstrued.

definition: A person who behaves badly or unlawfully; a wrongdoer or villain.
etymology: From Old French mescreant "unbelieving," from mes- "wrongly" + creant "believing."

definition: To make something bad less severe, serious, or painful.
etymology: From Latin mitigare, from mitis "mild, soft" + agere "to make."

examples.text: We have not failed, nor shall we fail to respond, whenever necessary to mitigate human suffering and assist in the rehabilitation of distressed nations.

definition: To appease the anger or anxiety of someone.
etymology: From Latin mollificare "to soften," from mollis "soft."

examples.text: But some analysts said Japan's attempt to mollify the U.S. was a double edged sword, and might be read at a subtle form of trade retaliation for the tariffs proposed by the U.S.

definition: Sullen and ill-tempered.
etymology: From Latin morosus "peevish, fastidious," from mos "custom, manner." Being set in one's ways became being sour about it.

etymology: From Latin munificus, from munus "gift" + facere "to make."

examples.text: He made a great resolve that he would atone to Eleanor for all the injury he had done her by the munificence of his future treatment.
