definition: Liable to change; inconstant.
etymology: From Latin mutabilis, from mutare "to change."

examples.text: By necessitating a change of men, in the first office of the nation, it would necessitate a mutability of measures.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: This ice is not made of such stuff as your hearts may be; it is mutable and cannot withstand you if you say that it shall not.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: This outward mutability indicated, and did not more than fairly express, the various properties of her inner life.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

definition: Vague, unclear, or ill-defined; cloudy or hazy.
etymology: From Latin nebulosus "misty," from nebula "mist, cloud."

examples.text: They were like the tiniest grains of dust, and they whirled round and gathered in clusters in a nebulous sort of way.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: There actually rose the faint halo, a small dim nebulousness, hardly recognizable save by the eye of faith.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: A sick-bed could recall Helen, but she was deaf to more human calls; after a glimpse at her aunt, she would retire into her nebulous life behind some poste restante.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: A person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief; a beginner.
etymology: From Greek neophytos "newly planted," from neos "new" + phyton "plant."

examples.text: He placed himself in front of Sergeant Cuff, and put his hands behind him, after the approved fashion of a neophyte who is examined in his catechism.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: Her whole soul was possessed by the fact that a fuller life was opening before her: she was a neophyte about to enter on a higher grade of initiation.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: "You have no right to preach to me, you neophyte, that have not passed the porch of life, and are absolutely unacquainted with its mysteries."
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Having an extremely offensive smell; disagreeable or harmful.
etymology: From Middle English noy "harm," a shortening of "annoy," + -some; it is unrelated to "noise."

examples.text: His blind and aged father and his gentle sister lay in a noisome dungeon while he enjoyed the free air and the society of her whom he loved.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: He who should have been our shield against all harm, hath kept us shut within the noisome caverns of his donjon-keep for lo these thirty years.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: Extraordinary how soon the noisome flavour of imprisoned sleep, becomes manifest in all such places that are ill cared for!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Feeling or appearing casually calm and relaxed; not displaying anxiety, interest, or enthusiasm.
etymology: From French nonchalant, from non- "not" + chaloir "to concern," from Latin calere "to be warm."

examples.text: Wolzogen, nonchalantly stretching his legs, approached Kutuzov with a half-contemptuous smile on his lips, scarcely touching the peak of his cap.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The red-haired detective who had masqueraded as Gogol rose to his feet without a word, and walked out of the room with an air of perfect nonchalance.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: They followed him up the bank attempting the tense yet nonchalant expression that is suitable for ladies on such occasions.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Lacking distinctive or interesting features or characteristics; unremarkable.
etymology: From non- + Latin descriptus "described"; it first named species not yet scientifically described.

examples.text: Such a senseless lie, too, yet it shattered her nerves and made her connect these Emersons, friends of Cecil's, with a pair of nondescript tourists.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: There was a string of people already straggling in, whom it was not difficult to identify as the nondescript messengers, go-betweens, and errand-bearers of the place.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I was now, it seemed, cut off upon both sides; behind me the murderers, before me this lurking nondescript.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

definition: Harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin noxius, from noxa "harm," related to nocere "to hurt."

examples.text: Depleted coastal ecosystems are vulnerable to invasive species, disease outbreaks, coastal flooding and noxious algae blooms, they report.
That small relative of the elephant has no harm in him; but what great mental or social type is free from specimens whose insignificance is both ugly and noxious?
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: It was very bitter, but they wandered about the fields seeking it and dug it out with their sabers and ate it, though they were ordered not to do so, as it was a noxious plant.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action.
etymology: From Latin obdurare "to harden," from ob- "against" + durus "hard."

examples.text: This old man wears a hat, a thumbed and napless and yet an obdurate hat, which has never adapted itself to the shape of his poor head.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: May I die if the enchanters that persecute me are not trying to entangle me in them and delay my journey, by way of revenge for my obduracy towards Altisidora.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: She came, but refused to kiss them: it was such hard luck on the little things, she said, and though Dolly proffered Chorly-worly and Porgly-woggles in turn, she was obdurate.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Not explicit or done directly; indirect; slanting, neither parallel nor perpendicular.
etymology: From Latin obliquus "slanting, sidelong."

examples.text: They note that Mars often has changed its tilt so that the poles face the Sun and the equator gets only oblique sunlight.
I suppose he made straight enough for the place where he wanted to get to, but his progress with one shoulder carried forward seemed oblique.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The rain stretched obliquely through the dull atmosphere in liquid spines, unbroken in continuity between their beginnings in the clouds and their points in him.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To destroy utterly; wipe out; to cause to become invisible or indistinct.
etymology: From Latin obliterare "to strike out, erase," from ob- + littera "letter."

examples.text: Mr Bloom, without evincing surprise, unostentatiously turned over the card to peruse the partially obliterated address and postmark.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: But this discovery was so great and overwhelming that all the steps by which I had been progressively led to it were obliterated, and I beheld only the result.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: The recent election not only most fortunately demonstrated the obliteration of sectional or geographical lines, but to some extent also the prejudices which for years have distracted our councils and marred our true greatness as a nation.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree.
etymology: From Latin obsequiosus "compliant," from obsequi "to comply," from ob- "toward" + sequi "to follow."

examples.text: Philip flushed, all the more because the surgeon spoke obviously with a humorous intention, and his brow-beaten dressers laughed obsequiously.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The cavalcade passed out by the lower gate of Phoenix park saluted by obsequious policemen and proceeded past Kingsbridge along the northern quays.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Whenever Mr. Snagsby and his conductors are stationary, the crowd flows round, and from its squalid depths obsequious advice heaves up to Mr. Bucket.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or chosen course of action, despite attempts to persuade.
etymology: From Latin obstinatus "determined," from obstinare "to persist."

examples.text: The money market head said the unions' humiliation by the protracted financial problems of the Neue Heimat cooperative housing venture would contribute to union obstinacy.
examples.source: Reuters, “German Wage Round Said To Limit Monetary Options”

examples.text: With regard to a large number of matters about which other men are decided or obstinate, he was the most easily manageable man in the world.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He always took her hand as though with repugnance, always seemed vexed to meet her and was sometimes obstinately silent throughout her visit.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Noisy and difficult to control; unruly.
etymology: From Latin obstreperus "clamorous," from obstrepere "to make a noise against."

examples.text: The liquor soon mounted into their heads, as it generally does even with the arrantest topers newly landed from sea, and they began capering about most obstreperously.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: He was catching fire from the flame he was partly simulating, and at tea-time he was obstreperously merry.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Mamma was an abject slave to their caprices, but Papa was not so easily subjugated, and occasionally afflicted his tender spouse by an attempt at paternal discipline with his obstreperous son.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: Noticeable or prominent in an unwelcome or intrusive way.
etymology: From Latin obtrudere "to thrust upon," from ob- + trudere "to push."

examples.text: Less-obtrusive means, such as using a video to monitor gestures or a recorder to analyse voice, allow the user to behave more naturally.
There was an obtrusive show of compassionate zeal in his voice and manner, more intolerable—at least to me—than any demeanour he could have assumed.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: To enter on this occasion into a further or more minute exposition of my views on the various questions of domestic policy would be as obtrusive as it is probably unexpected.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: Annoyingly insensitive or slow to understand; (of an angle) more than 90 degrees.
etymology: From Latin obtusus "blunted, dull," from obtundere "to beat against."

examples.text: For there was one quality in Henry for which she was never prepared, however much she reminded herself of it: his obtuseness.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: When the elder Osborne gave what he called "a hint," there was no possibility for the most obtuse to mistake his meaning.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: She liked their elegance, their lightness, their lack of emphasis: even the self-assurance which at times was so like obtuseness now seemed the natural sign of social ascendency.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To remove a need or difficulty; to avoid or prevent.
etymology: From Late Latin obviare "to meet in the way, prevent," from ob viam "in the way."

examples.text: "These technological advances could potentially obviate the need for geological repositories altogether."
The propositions which have been made for supplying the omission have rather served to illustrate than to obviate the difficulty of the thing.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: In order to obviate any delays possible through any routine requirements as to payment in your departments, we enclose cheque herewith for ten pounds (L10), receipt of which please acknowledge.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Of or connected with the eyes or vision; perceived by sight.
etymology: From Latin ocularis, from oculus "eye."

examples.text: Only, of course, the belief in their truth is necessary, as plausible belief and ocular evidence belonging to the perspective view of life.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: He then asked Mrs Tickit how long a space of time she supposed there might have been between the two sets of ocular quiverings she had experienced?
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Into the principal parlour of this place entered two strangers, who found themselves, as is always the case in such hostels, the object, not of fluttered curiosity or pert inquiry, but of steady, ceaseless, devouring ocular study.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Extremely unpleasant; repulsive and deserving hatred.
etymology: From Latin odiosus, from odium "hatred."

examples.text: The game's rather odious gangland lowlifes swagger and mouth off in a way that rings very true indeed.
examples.source: BBC News, “GTA sequel is criminally good”

examples.text: Would his aunt relent towards him now that he was a Lieutenant-Colonel and a C.B.? and would that odious Rebecca once more get into favour?
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: But totalitarianism is no less odious to us because we are able to reach some accommodation that reduces the danger of world catastrophe.
examples.author: Lyndon B. Johnson

definition: Assertive of authority in an annoyingly domineering way, especially about trivial matters; meddlesome.
etymology: From Latin officiosus "obliging, dutiful," from officium "service, duty." Being eager to serve tipped into meddling.

examples.text: Margaret Schlegel has been officious and tiresome during this terrible week, and we have all suffered under her, but upon my soul she's honest.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: You don't know how the cursed carelessness that is over-officious in helping me at every other turning of my life, WON'T help me here.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: How this charmingly convenient obstacle could have escaped the officious penetration of the Count, it was impossible to conceive—but it HAD escaped him.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Giving the impression that something bad or unpleasant is going to happen; threatening.
etymology: From Latin ominosus, from omen "portent."

examples.text: Baker also said he still sees "ominous" signs of pressure for protectionist trade legislation "and this pressure for protectionism is coming from new areas of society."
examples.source: Reuters, “Baker Says G-6 Pact Just A Start”

examples.text: There was none the less for him, in the very manner of his host's allusion to satiety as a thinkable motive, a slight breath of the ominous.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: The situation at this time last year was truly ominous.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Involving a great deal of effort, trouble, or difficulty; burdensome.
etymology: From Latin onerosus, from onus "a load, burden."

examples.text: The SEC said it had taken into consideration the fact that foreign companies were already working to meet more onerous financial reporting rules in their home countries.
examples.source: BBC News, “US gives foreign firms extra time”

examples.text: I think on the whole the bishop was right, for though the services required will not be of a very onerous nature, they will be more so than they were before.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: The appointing power vested in the President imposes delicate and onerous duties.
examples.author: Zachary Taylor

definition: Well-chosen or particularly favorable for a purpose; timely.
etymology: From Latin opportunus, from ob portum "toward the harbor," originally describing a wind blowing toward port.

examples.text: But it said it would be opportune to look in depth at the role and the procedures of G-7 in relation to those of G-5.
examples.source: Reuters, “Italy Says G-7 Gives Chance To Verify Tokyo Accord”

examples.text: Although in one instance the bearers of not good tidings, Mr. and Mrs. Weston's visit this morning was in another respect particularly opportune.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Something always drew him toward those richer and more powerful than himself and he had rare skill in seizing the most opportune moment for making use of people.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Harsh criticism or public disgrace arising from shameful conduct.
etymology: From Latin opprobrium "infamy, reproach," from opprobrare "to reproach."

examples.text: I am content to suffer alone while my sufferings shall endure; when I die, I am well satisfied that abhorrence and opprobrium should load my memory.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: If an ill appointment should be made, the Executive for nominating, and the Senate for approving, would participate, though in different degrees, in the opprobrium and disgrace.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: By such methods we will make our contribution to the world's peace, which no nation values more highly, and avoid the opprobrium which must fall upon the nation that ruthlessly breaks it.
examples.author: Benjamin Harrison

definition: Ostentatiously rich and luxurious; wealthy; abundant.
etymology: From Latin opulentus "wealthy," from opes "wealth, resources."

examples.text: The world will think you abandoned and poor, for the wife of a bankrupt would never be forgiven, were she to keep up an appearance of opulence.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The light in which they stood made a dense blackness all round, and only above their heads there was an opulent glitter of stars.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Yet, in spite of this, nowhere in all America will you find more patrician-like houses; parks and gardens more opulent, than in New Bedford.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Elaborately or excessively decorated; (of style) using unusual words and complex constructions.
etymology: From Latin ornatus "adorned," from ornare "to adorn."

examples.text: But as he passed under the shadow of one handsome villa with verandas and wide ornate gardens, he heard a noise that made him almost involuntarily stop.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: He had made a toilet of a nicely-adjusted kind—of a nature between the carefully neat and the carelessly ornate—of a degree between fine-market-day and wet-Sunday selection.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: The flats, their only outlook, hung like an ornate curtain between Margaret and the welter of London.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Conforming to established or traditional beliefs, standards, or doctrines.
etymology: From Greek orthodoxos, from orthos "right, straight" + doxa "opinion."

examples.text: However, Mr da Silva has stuck to an orthodox monetary policy inherited from his predecessor even in the face of last year's economic crisis.
But it is not the minds of heretics that are deteriorated most, by the ban placed on all inquiry which does not end in the orthodox conclusions.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: He would never, Carol fancied, be one of the town pillars, because he was not orthodox in hunting and motoring and poker.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To waver between opinions, feelings, or courses of action; to swing back and forth.
etymology: From Latin oscillare "to swing."

examples.text: This says that everything from the vibration of violin strings to the spread of heat through a metal bar can be viewed as sums of simple wave patterns, oscillating sine and cosine waves.
Have Shares enough to be on Boards of Direction in capital letters, oscillate on mysterious business between London and Paris, and be great.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: We can no longer afford to oscillate from year to year in so vital a matter; indeed, we have a duty to look beyond the immediate question of budgets and to examine the nature of the problem we will face over the next generation.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: Stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so; apparent.
etymology: From French, from Latin ostendere "to show."

examples.text: "It's a very complex transaction, but basically what happens is they ostensibly put up money but the fees recapture any investment they might have once the merger takes place," Gardner said.
He had already hovered more than once about that possibility, been aware of it, in the course of ostensible strolls, as lurking but round the corner.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: And what is a still greater novelty, the mass do not now take their opinions from dignitaries in Church or State, from ostensible leaders, or from books.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

definition: Characterized by vulgar or pretentious display, designed to impress.
etymology: From Latin ostentare "to display," frequentative of ostendere "to show."

examples.text: However, the ostentation of some of the items on sale painted a picture of the eccentricity that endeared him to the British public in shows such as Channel 4's gameshow Don't Forget Your Toothbrush.
examples.source: BBC News, “Chris Evans back on the market”

examples.text: He carried his fat paunch with ostentation on his short legs, and during the time his gang infested the station spoke to no one but his nephew.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Our honesty, we free spirits—let us be careful lest it become our vanity, our ornament and ostentation, our limitation, our stupidity!
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

definition: Peaceful in character or intent; tending to bring about peace.
etymology: From Latin pacificus "peacemaking," from pax "peace" + facere "to make."

examples.text: It is doubtful whether our soldiers would be maintained if there were not pacific people at home who like to fancy themselves soldiers.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: The friend arose and went over to them, making pacific motions with his arms.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

examples.text: But its full realization also implies a greater and greater perfection in the instrumentalities for pacific settlement of controversies between nations.
examples.author: Herbert Hoover

definition: Acceptable or satisfactory to the mind; pleasant to taste.
etymology: From palate, from Latin palatum "roof of the mouth," + -able.

examples.text: The water membrane technology is already being used in other countries to recycle waste, make bore water palatable and desalinate salty water.

More recently, less palatable concerns - at least in liberal European circles - have been voiced, with senior EU or member state officials talking darkly of a "river of Islam", an "oriental" culture and a threat to Europe's "cultural richness".
examples.source: BBC News, “Turkey turns on the economic charm”

examples.text: "I do not know if the result will be as agreeable as you describe, but the thing does not appear to me as palatable as you say."
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Pale, typically because of poor health; lacking vigor, color, or interest.
etymology: From Latin pallidus, from pallere "to be pale."

examples.text: Captain Wentworth, who had caught her up, knelt with her in his arms, looking on her with a face as pallid as her own, in an agony of silence.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Monte Cristo took off the wig which disfigured him, and let fall his black hair, which added so much to the beauty of his pallid features.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The nearer houses still stood intact, awaiting their fate, shadowy, faint and pallid in the steam, with the fire behind them going to and fro.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: So intense or obvious as to be almost felt; able to be touched.
etymology: From Late Latin palpabilis, from palpare "to touch gently."

examples.text: Mr Gupta says the power of Morquendi's text message blogs was palpable.
examples.source: BBC News, “Web logs aid disaster recovery”

examples.text: But Newland Archer was too imaginative not to feel that, in his case and May's, the tie might gall for reasons far less gross and palpable.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: To persons standing alone on a hill during a clear midnight such as this, the roll of the world eastward is almost a palpable movement.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Small or meager; petty or trivial.

examples.text: If that was a paltry reward for their early pressure, Scotland got the try they deserved when Paterson's searing break and Andy Craig's pass sent Southwell streaking to the right corner.
'Now,' said he, with curbed ferocity, 'I'm getting angry and if you don't command that paltry spirit of yours—damn you! get up directly!'
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: Bitter memories were more and more covered up by the incidents—paltry in his eyes, but really important—of his country life.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: A solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases.
etymology: From Greek panakeia, from panakēs "all-healing," from pan "all" + akos "remedy."

examples.text: And other experts warn against thinking such technology can be a panacea for traffic jams.
The use of ink and readers by itself is not a panacea for election ills.
examples.source: BBC News, “Ink helps drive democracy in Asia”

examples.text: Then she met Champ Perry in the post-office—and decided that in the history of the pioneers was the panacea for Gopher Prairie, for all of America.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To gratify or indulge an immoral or distasteful desire, or a person with such desires.
etymology: From Pandarus, who acts as go-between for the lovers in Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.

examples.text: The Liberal Democrats have warned Labour and the Tories they were "in danger of pandering to prejudice rather than challenging it".
examples.source: BBC News, “At a glance: Tory health checks”

examples.text: But he hasn't borne the Roman yoke as I have, nor yet he hasn't been required to pander to your depraved appetite for miserly characters.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And this is not all; for the servants and panders of the parasites are also parasites, the milliners and the jewelers and the lackeys have also to be supported by the useful members of the community.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

definition: A public speech or published text in praise of someone or something; an elaborate encomium.
etymology: From Greek panēgyrikos "for a public assembly," from panēgyris "general assembly."

examples.text: The painter's absurd fits of jealousy, his wild devotion, his extravagant panegyrics, his curious reticences—he understood them all now, and he felt sorry.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

examples.text: This naturally introduced a panegyric from Jane on his diffidence, and the little value he put on his own good qualities.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Catherine assented—and a very warm panegyric from her on that lady's merits closed the subject.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: A person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality.
etymology: From Italian paragone "touchstone," a stone used to test the purity of gold, from Greek parakonan "to sharpen against."

examples.text: Down in Bleeding Heart Yard, where there was not one unappropriated halfpenny, as lively an interest was taken in this paragon of men as on the Stock Exchange.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: From heaven the hero must be smiling down upon that paragon of a boy whom he had left to comfort and console her.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: The suggestion, it is true, was a faint one, but then Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that it was enough for the time being to make him perfectly happy.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: More important than anything else; supreme.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman paramont "above," from Old French par "by" + amont "above."

examples.text: He said his Budget struck a balance "between tax cuts that are affordable, investments that are essential and stability that is paramount".
examples.source: BBC News, “Brown targets OAPs and homebuyers”

examples.text: Kitty felt a peculiar pleasure in being able now to talk to her mother on equal terms about those questions of such paramount interest in a woman's life.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The paramount duty of Congress is to stop deficiencies by the restoration of that protective legislation which has always been the firmest prop of the Treasury.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: The state or condition of being equal, especially in status or pay.
etymology: From Late Latin paritas, from par "equal."

examples.text: And Poehl noted that the dollar/mark parity was unchanged since February 22 without the Bundesbank having had to sell marks to support the dollar.
examples.source: Reuters, “Stoltenberg Sees Moves To Strengthen Paris Accord”

examples.text: But there is no parity between the feeling of a person for his own opinion, and the feeling of another who is offended at his holding it; no more than between the desire of a thief to take a purse, and the desire of the right owner to keep it.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: Our aim should be economic stability and full parity of income for American farmers.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Having a limited or narrow outlook or scope; relating to a church parish.
etymology: From Late Latin parochialis, from parochia "parish."

examples.text: He had never looked for parochial duty, and his career at Oxford was utterly incompatible with such domestic joys as a wife and nursery.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Formerly Caroline Jellyby, spinster, then of Thavies Inn, within the city of London, but extra-parochial; now of Newman Street, Oxford Street.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It's time to rise above the parochial and the pork barrel, to do what is necessary, what's right, and what will enable this nation to play the leadership role required of us.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: A sudden attack or violent outburst of a particular emotion or activity.
etymology: From Greek paroxysmos, from paroxynein "to exasperate," from oxynein "to sharpen."

examples.text: The Irving economist noted that three times last year, in a similar "paroxysm of pessimism," the key bonds reached a similar closing yield high.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Credit Market Outlook - Cautious Trading”

examples.text: She broke from me with hysterical vehemence, and threw herself on the sofa in a paroxysm of sobs and tears that shook her from head to foot.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: Claudia recovered from her fainting fit, but not so Don Vicente from the paroxysm that had overtaken him, for his life had come to an end.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: To ward off a weapon or attack; to evade an awkward question or criticism skillfully.
etymology: Probably from French parez, imperative of parer "to ward off," from Italian parare.

examples.text: Scholes' free-kick took a deflection, and Martyn could only parry the ball out for Ronaldo, who reacted first to score easily.
examples.source: BBC News, “Man Utd stroll to Cup win”

examples.text: Montano also had his cutlass unsheathed, and Muscari, without further speech, sent a slash at his head which he was compelled to catch and parry.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: Over and over again had she thrown out her "Surely, surely," at Mr. Harding's devoted head, and ill had that gentleman been able to parry the attack.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Unwilling to spend money or use resources; extremely frugal.
etymology: From Latin parsimonia "frugality," from parcere "to be sparing."

examples.text: This work has led to the creation of the Mobile PC Extended Battery Life (EBL) Working Group that shares information about building notebooks that are more parsimonious with power.
examples.source: BBC News, “Long life promised for laptop PCs”

examples.text: He had not come to stay with him on his arrival in Petersburg simply from parsimony, though that had been perhaps his chief object.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious public.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Prejudiced in favor of a particular cause or party; a strong, often uncritical supporter of one.
etymology: From French partisan, from Italian partigiano, from parte "part."

examples.text: Masters Cup champions Mike and Bob Bryan thrashed Juan Carlos Ferrero and Tommy Robredo 6-0 6-3 6-2 in front of a partisan crowd in Seville.
examples.source: BBC News, “Bryan twins keep US hopes alive”

examples.text: He had proposed for Miss Swartz, but had been rejected scornfully by the partisans of that lady, who married her to a young sprig of Scotch nobility.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: But we have to move ahead with courage and honesty, because our children's retirement security is more important than partisan politics.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: A quality, as in speech, art, or life, that evokes pity or sadness.
etymology: From Greek pathos "suffering, experience."

examples.text: Like all other music, it breathed passion and pathos, and emotions high or tender, in a tongue native to the human heart, wherever educated.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: Helen was telegraphed for, and that spring party that after all gathered in that hospitable house had all the pathos of fair memories.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: And Mrs. Gummidge took his hand, and kissed it with a homely pathos and affection, in a homely rapture of devotion and gratitude, that he well deserved.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To treat with an apparent kindness that betrays a feeling of superiority; to be a regular customer of.
etymology: From Medieval Latin patronizare, from patronus "protector, patron."

examples.text: She nodded twice or thrice patronizingly to the little boy, who looked up from his dinner or from the pictures of soldiers he was painting.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: I will not allow you to utter in my presence the absurd suspicion that any strangers—I care not what their names—can patronize my child.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I reject the patronizing idea that government in Washington, D.C., is inevitably more wise, more honest, and more efficient than government at the local or State level.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: The presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities.
etymology: From Latin paucitas, from paucus "few" (related to "paltry" and "poor").

examples.text: "With the paucity of contrary evidence, the hills are presumed to be anthropogenic structures of potentially colossal proportions," says Bosnian geophysicist Dr Amer Smailbegovic.

Nashashibi said lack of experience among Arab banks, a paucity of financial instruments and a legal framework that often does not recognise the western banking concept of interest have hampered the growth of Arab markets.
examples.source: Reuters, “Arab Banker Says Too Soon For Single Currency”

examples.text: Any inward debate Lydgate had as to the consequences of this engagement which had stolen upon him, turned on the paucity of time rather than of money.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Relating to or consisting of money.
etymology: From Latin pecuniarius, from pecunia "money," from pecus "cattle."

examples.text: "My pecuniary interest has been on the public register now for almost three years for anyone to see," he said.
The most unpleasant thing of all was that his pecuniary interests should in this way enter into the question of his reconciliation with his wife.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The proposition that business is not a property or pecuniary right which can be protected by equitable injunction is utterly without foundation in precedent or reason.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules; overscrupulous.
etymology: From Italian pedante "teacher, schoolmaster," perhaps from Greek paideuein "to teach."

examples.text: His gentleness was never tinged by dogmatism, and his instructions were given with an air of frankness and good nature that banished every idea of pedantry.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Perhaps it need not be done so pedantically, thought Nicholas, or even done at all, but this untiring, continual spiritual effort of which the sole aim was the children's moral welfare delighted him.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: "He's a cursed white-blooded pedantic coxcomb," said Will, with gnashing impetuosity.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Lacking inspiration or excitement; dull; a person walking rather than traveling in a vehicle.
etymology: From Latin pedester "going on foot, plain," from pes "foot."

examples.text: Northumbria Police said the pedestrian Millennium Bridge, by the demonstration site, will be shut if necessary.
examples.source: BBC News, “Hunt demo at Labour meeting”

examples.text: In Lower Mount street a pedestrian in a brown macintosh, eating dry bread, passed swiftly and unscathed across the viceroy's path.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Bathsheba's nerves were still unstrung: she crouched down out of sight again, and the pedestrian came into view.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Feeling or showing sorrow and regret for having done wrong; repentant.
etymology: From Latin paenitere "to repent."

examples.text: But soon, as Maggie looked, every distinct thought began to be overflowed by a wave of loving penitence, and words burst forth with a sob.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: With tears of penitence and poignant, tender anguish, he will exclaim: 'Others are better than I, they wanted to save me, not to ruin me!
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: When he presented himself again he was racked with a headache—penitent, and volubly afraid that in his drunkenness he might have been indiscreet.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

definition: Engaged in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought.
etymology: From Old French pensif, from penser "to think," from Latin pensare "to weigh, consider."

examples.text: But she certainly did grow a little pale and pensive that spring, lost much of her relish for society, and went out sketching alone a good deal.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: It was dusk when Oak, who had not been far a-field that day, took the same path and met her returning, quite pensively, as he thought.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Anatole lay on the sofa in the study leaning on his elbow and smiling pensively, while his handsome lips muttered tenderly to himself.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: The state of being very poor; extreme poverty.
etymology: From Latin penuria "want, scarcity."

examples.text: He almost regretted the penury which he had suffered during the last two years, since the desperate struggle merely to keep body and soul together had deadened the pain of living.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: It contained but two rooms, and these exhibited all the squalidness of the most miserable penury.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: If there is one measure better calculated than another to produce that state of things so much deprecated by all true republicans, by which the rich are daily adding to their hoards and the poor sinking deeper into penury, it is an exclusive metallic currency.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Having or showing sensitive insight; quick to notice and understand.
etymology: From Latin percipere "to seize, understand," from per- "thoroughly" + capere "to take."

examples.text: Tom had never found any difficulty in discerning a pointer from a setter, when once he had been told the distinction, and his perceptive powers were not at all deficient.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Yet her engaging face, being an open as well as a perceptive one, was not without her husband's latent smile.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The intense excitement of the events had no doubt left my perceptive powers in a state of erethism.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: Insisting on immediate attention or obedience, especially in a brusquely imperious way; not open to debate.
etymology: From Latin peremptorius "deadly, decisive," from perimere "to destroy."

examples.text: He peremptorily denied for example, that any whale could so smite his stout sloop-of-war as to cause her to leak so much as a thimbleful.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Of course, after such a peremptory order as this, Miss Sharp, the governess, received commands to dine with the illustrious company below stairs.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: When, awakened from his sleep, he received that cold, peremptory note from Kutuzov, he felt the more irritated the more he felt himself to blame.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Deceitful and untrustworthy; treacherous.
etymology: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia "faithlessness."

examples.text: On ordinary occasions it might not be exerted with the requisite firmness, and on extraordinary occasions it might be perfidiously abused.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Traitor, cruel, vindictive, and perfidious, wherein had this poor wretch failed in his fidelity, who with such frankness showed thee the secrets and the joys of his heart?
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: I said with every unkind intention; but the perfidious shaft fell harmless—dropped at his feet like a spent arrow, as it were, and he did not think of picking it up.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Deceitfulness; deliberate breach of faith or trust.
etymology: From Latin perfidia, from perfidus "faithless," from per- "away" + fides "faith."

examples.text: "Provided I understand your perfidy, sir, and succeed in making you understand that I will be revenged, I shall be reasonable enough," said Albert furiously.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: By my soul, the countenance of that fellow when he was a boy was the blackest image of perfidy, cowardice, and cruelty ever set up as a scarecrow in a field of scoundrels.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It doubles the security to the people, by requiring the concurrence of two distinct bodies in schemes of usurpation or perfidy, where the ambition or corruption of one would otherwise be sufficient.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Carried out with a minimum of effort or reflection, merely as a routine duty.
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius "careless," from perfungi "to get through with, discharge."

examples.text: Now and again he would emit a bothered perfunctory "Sssh," which neither produced nor was expected to produce the slightest effect.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: She had invented a way of meeting them—as if he had been a polite perfunctory poor relation, of distant degree—that made them almost ridiculous in him.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: Reforms in the civil service must go on; but the changes should be real and genuine, not perfunctory, or prompted by a zeal in behalf of any party simply because it happens to be in power.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Of secondary or minor importance; relating to or situated on the edge.
etymology: From Greek periphereia "circumference," from peri "around" + pherein "to carry."

examples.text: Drinking too much coffee, however, means we're more likely to be distracted by peripheral factors, rather than the strength of the argument.
The rationalisation programme, including sale of the Bahamas oil terminal and all peripheral activities, is now complete.
The sale by Gallaher reflects a decision to dispose of more peripheral businesses.
examples.source: Reuters, “Glynwed Buys Gallaher Units For Around 14 Mln Stg”

definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.
etymology: From Latin perniciosus "destructive," from pernicies "ruin," from per- "completely" + nex "death."

examples.text: The pernicious program opens a backdoor on a computer so it can be controlled remotely by malicious hackers.
examples.source: BBC News, “Beckham virus spotted on the net”

examples.text: Sviazhsky began talking of Levin, describing his strange view that machinery is simply pernicious in its effects on Russian agriculture.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It will furnish absolute security which makes the proposed scheme of government guaranty of deposits so alluring, without its pernicious results.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: A benefit or privilege to which one is entitled because of one's position, beyond regular pay.
etymology: From Medieval Latin perquisitum "thing acquired," from Latin perquirere "to search diligently for."

examples.text: The truth is, he was attached to the lady's maid in question, and indignant that she should have been robbed of her perquisites.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in fobbing his perquisites; which are his chiefly by virtue of that same fobbing of them.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Men began to pride themselves on having nothing to do with their own government, and to agree tacitly with those who regarded public office as a private perquisite.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action; stubbornly persistent.
etymology: From Latin pertinax "very tenacious," from per- "thoroughly" + tenax "holding fast."

examples.text: It was wonderful to see the pertinacity with which the washerwoman from Tooting brought the cart every Saturday, and her bills week after week.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: I couldn't affirm that you are,' observed my young lady, wondering at his pertinacious assertion of what was evidently an untruth.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: Though the bishop had so pertinaciously insisted on giving way to his wife in the matter of the hospital, Mr. Slope did not think it necessary to abandon his object.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: To make anxious or unsettled; to subject a system to a disturbance.
etymology: From Latin perturbare "to throw into confusion," from per- "thoroughly" + turbare "to disturb."

examples.text: He stated that this had greatly perturbed his peace of mind in the other region and earnestly requested that his desire should be made known.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: The question that had perturbed Pierre on the Mozhaysk hill and all that day now seemed to him quite clear and completely solved.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: I walked up and down my room hastily and perturbed, while my imagination conjured up a thousand images to torment and sting me.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: To read or examine with great care and thoroughness; (informally) to scan or browse.

examples.text: I devoured the books they lent me: then it was full satisfaction to discuss with them in the evening what I had perused during the day.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Elizabeth noticed every sentence conveying the idea of uneasiness, with an attention which it had hardly received on the first perusal.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: He had not a correspondent on earth, nor was there a possible letter coming to him whose contents the whole parish would not have been welcome to peruse.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered; peevish.
etymology: From Latin petulans "forward, insolent," from petere "to seek, attack."

examples.text: That was altogether too much from a lad younger than herself, and Meg walked away, saying petulantly, "You are the rudest boy I ever saw."
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: She only felt irritable and petulant, and anxious to do what she was not expected to do, and in this spirit she proceeded with the conversation.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: She had not done this, but had shown herself angry and sore, and was now ashamed of her own petulance, yet unable to discontinue it.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Having an unemotional and stolidly calm disposition.
etymology: From Greek phlegmatikos, from phlegma "phlegm," the bodily humor once believed to cause sluggishness.

examples.text: But that is just how it is, sometimes, especially in cases like the present one, with the decisions of the most precise and phlegmatic people.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: Miss Arrowpoint colored, and Mr. Bult observed, with his usual phlegmatic stolidity, "Your pianist does not think small beer of himself."
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: She said "Good morning, Miss," in her usual phlegmatic and brief manner; and taking up another ring and more tape, went on with her sewing.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: The quality of being religious or reverent; a conventional belief or standard accepted unthinkingly.
etymology: From Latin pietas "dutifulness," from pius "dutiful."

examples.text: It was written with a plain, unaffected, homely piety that I knew to be genuine, and ended with 'my duty to my ever darling'—meaning myself.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And there have always been enough of his kidney, whose piety lies in punishing who can see the justice of grudges but not of gratitude.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But she half-permitted his adoration, and that half-permission added such fuel to his fire that all the fountain of his piety could not quench it.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: To rob a place using violence, especially in wartime; plunder.
etymology: From Old French pillage, from piller "to plunder."

examples.text: Since the battle of Borodino and the pillage of Moscow it had borne within itself, as it were, the chemical elements of dissolution.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Otherwise, good heavens! otherwise they would swarm over the river in their multitude to the side where those great buildings were, secure and stately, and they would pillage, burn, and sack.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: But these unfortunate persons frequently found their houses had been pillaged by robbers, who, in these moments of general confusion, enrich themselves with the spoils of their fellow-creatures.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

definition: Devoutly religious; making a hypocritical display of virtue.
etymology: From Latin pius "dutiful, devout."

examples.text: With you to guide him I hope that he will become a soldier in Christ's Faith and be all the days of his life God-fearing, humble, and pious.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Esther was truly pious, and quite sincere in her advice, for she had an affectionate heart, and felt much for the sisters in their anxiety.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: The pia fraus is still more repugnant to the taste (the "piety") of the free spirit (the "pious man of knowledge") than the impia fraus.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

definition: Concise and forcefully expressive; brief but full of meaning.
etymology: From pith, the spongy core of a plant stem, from Old English pitha.

examples.text: Then, his preaching was ingenious and pithy, like the preaching of the English Church in its robust age, and his sermons were delivered without book.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: They could always talk; and their discourse, witty, pithy, original, had such charms for me, that I preferred listening to, and sharing in it, to doing anything else.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: For I am a plodding kind of fellow, Copperfield, and had learnt the way of doing such things pithily.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: A very small or inadequate amount of money.
etymology: From Old French pitance "pious donation," ultimately from Latin pietas "pity, piety."

examples.text: Amelia thinks, and thinks, and racks her brain, to find some means of increasing the small pittance upon which the household is starving.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Robert is very well in a way, to give up all the money he can earn to the family, and keep the barest pittance for himself.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: She procured plain work; she plaited straw and by various means contrived to earn a pittance scarcely sufficient to support life.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: To make someone less angry or hostile.
etymology: From Latin placare "to soothe," related to placere "to please."

examples.text: They say Mr Ellison may be trying to placate Peoplesoft customers riled by Oracle's determined takeover strategy.
examples.source: BBC News, “Jobs go at Oracle after takeover”

examples.text: But today's smaller than expected rate cut appeared to have placated markets for now, analysts said.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.K. Base Rates Will Fall Again Soon, Say Analysts”

examples.text: His manner of sneering at what he called "parlor socialists" (though the phrase was not overwhelmingly new) had a power which made her wish to placate his company of well-fed, speed-loving administrators.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Not easily upset or excited; calm and peaceful.
etymology: From Latin placidus "gentle," from placere "to please."

examples.text: Ultraviolet light is used to break open the bonds of some of the rings and let the molecules reform into long, placid chains that behave like viscous oil.
Instantly, Miss Skiffins stopped it with the neatness of a placid boxer, took off that girdle or cestus as before, and laid it on the table.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And so, under pretence of softening the previous outrage, of stroking and soothing me into placidity, you stick a sly penknife under my ear!
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Sounding sad and mournful.
etymology: From Old French plaintif, from plainte "lamentation," from Latin planctus.

examples.text: A pitiful and plaintive look, with which she had begun to regard him when she was still extremely young, was perhaps a part of this discovery.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But after the exclamation of surprise that had escaped from Vereshchagin he uttered a plaintive cry of pain, and that cry was fatal.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: There were signs in him, though none of them plaintive, of always paying for others; and the principal one perhaps was just this failure of type.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: A remark or statement, especially one with a moral content, used too often to be interesting or thoughtful.
etymology: From French platitude, from plat "flat."

examples.text: But then in England a man announcing these platitudes is generally a fool and a frightened fool, announcing them out of mere social servility.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: We call it War, and pass it by—but do not put me off with platitudes and conventions—come with me, come with me—realize it!
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: He uttered some platitude as to his deep obligation for the trouble she had taken, and wondered more and more who she was.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Of or belonging to the common people; lacking refinement, unsophisticated.
etymology: From Latin plebeius, from plebs "the common people" of ancient Rome.

examples.text: The hybrid European—a tolerably ugly plebeian, taken all in all—absolutely requires a costume: he needs history as a storeroom of costumes.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: A more plebeian one will answer my purpose just as well, and the pleasure of knowing whose heart my old one beats against—well, I won't speak of that.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: She was unnaturally pale, and her head was bundled in her borrowed plebeian shawl; but I am certain it was Etta Todd, the millionaire's daughter.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Easily influenced or controlled; easily bent, flexible.
etymology: From French plier "to bend," from Latin plicare "to fold."

examples.text: Exporter Ross Gates says the skin is proving popular because of its strength, repellent nature and pliability.
More pliable under change than her sister, Laura showed more plainly the progress made by the healing influences of her new life.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: She felt an immense need of some one to speak to, and she had never before seen any one who seemed so quick and pliable, so likely to understand everything.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret; deeply affecting.
etymology: From Old French poindre "to prick," from Latin pungere "to prick."

examples.text: The poignant finale was later voted the best farewell episode of a TV series.
examples.source: BBC News, “BBC denies Blackadder TV comeback”

examples.text: There was a look of poignant discomfort in her face, as though Avdotya Romanovna's courtesy and attention were oppressive and painful to her.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: To speak sooth, however, his sufferings on that dreadful night had been so poignant as to leave him little spirit for further rebellion.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: A strong verbal or written attack on someone or something; controversial argument.
etymology: From Greek polemikos "warlike," from polemos "war."

examples.text: She also triggered a storm of dreams, dread and ethical polemic that hasn't abated since.
She had no opinions on anything more polemic than woolen union-suits, a topic on which Mrs. Howland discoursed for five minutes.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: She knew that this man at her side, this accomplished scholar, this practised orator, this great polemical combatant, was striving and striving in vain to tell her that his heart was no longer his own.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Dull, laborious, or excessively solemn; slow and clumsy because of great weight.
etymology: From Latin ponderosus, from pondus "weight."

examples.text: The ponderous stone Bridge of Sighs crosses it at the second story—a bridge that is a covered tunnel —you can not be seen when you walk in it.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: He had scarcely read this note, and frowned at its contents, when he heard below the ponderous tramp of the servants, carrying something heavy.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: He was now in retirement, and hence (in a ponderous white cravat, like a stiff snow-drift) was so obliging as to shade the dinner.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To be a sign or warning that something, especially something momentous or calamitous, is likely to happen.
etymology: From Latin portendere "to foretell," from pro- "forth" + tendere "to stretch."

examples.text: But Stephen Roach of Morgan Stanley and Co Inc was not convinced that the February reports portend economic gains.
examples.source: Reuters, “Fed Seen Content With U.S. February Economy”

examples.text: The locking of the black hole door was a terrible sound—some knew not what it portended, and others knew TOO WELL.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: But had it not been proven at Umballa that his sign in the high heavens portended War and armed men?
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

definition: A sign or warning that a momentous or calamitous event is likely to happen; an omen.
etymology: From Latin portentum "omen, token," from portendere "to foretell."

examples.text: And the equine portent grows again, magnified in the deserted heavens, nay to heaven's own magnitude, till it looms, vast, over the house of Virgo.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Signs and portents of the experience thus in reserve for him had as it happened, multiplied even through the dazzle of Chad's party.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: Such symptoms of prosperity may become portents of disaster!
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: To suggest or assume the existence, fact, or truth of something as a basis for reasoning; such a premise.
etymology: From Latin postulare "to ask, demand."

examples.text: Geometry is an ancient field and Dehaene's team postulated that it may spring from innate abilities.
But to arrive at these laws, resulting from the sum of all those human wills, man's mind postulates arbitrary and disconnected units.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: This, however, is but one yarn, yet with interruptions affording some measure of relief; and in regard to the listeners' endurance, the postulate must be accepted that the story was interesting.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: A monarch or ruler, especially an autocratic one.
etymology: From Latin potentatus "dominion," from potens "powerful."

examples.text: I am told that the old masters had to do these shameful things for bread, the princes and potentates being the only patrons of art.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: I went not into the forest to seek a potentate, neither do I, at any future time, design a visit thither, with a view to gaining the favour of such personage.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: They drove about the chain of garden-circled lakes, and viewed the houses of the millers and lumbermen and real estate peers—the potentates of the expanding city.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically, based on practical rather than theoretical considerations.
etymology: From Greek pragmatikos "relating to affairs," from pragma "deed, thing done."

examples.text: Using Braille for speeches, and briefed by his officials on tape, he also has a sharp tongue at times, and a pragmatic approach to politics.
Liberal Democrat spokesman Mark Oaten called the change pragmatic and argued it gave a better chance of producing a European asylum solution.
examples.source: BBC News, “Tories attack EU asylum moves”

definition: Showing a lack of courage or determination; timid.
etymology: From Late Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus "very small" + animus "mind, spirit."

examples.text: Pusillanimity disposeth men to Irresolution, and consequently to lose the occasions, and fittest opportunities of action.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: The archdeacon was fuming with rage when he got into the drawing-room, and had by this time nearly forgotten the pusillanimity of the bishop in the villainy of the chaplain.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: It puts our Government in a pusillanimous position to make definite engagements to protect aliens and then to excuse the failure to perform those engagements by an explanation that the duty to keep them is in States or cities, not within our control.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: An uneasy feeling of doubt, worry, or fear, especially about one's own conduct; a misgiving.

examples.text: While accepting that people "have to be prepared" for a possible terrorist attack, Mr Solana said he had "qualms" about the home secretary's new plans.
Tasmanian farmer Neil Monks bought the 20-month-old pup sight unseen, and had no qualms at forking out an Australian record amount for the dog, Bagalla Mick.
It is impossible to picture to oneself the shame and moral degradation to which the jealous man can descend without a qualm of conscience.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: A state of perplexity or uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation.

examples.text: This was a quandary but, bringing common sense to bear on it, evidently there was nothing for it but put a good face on the matter and foot it which they accordingly did.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: "Well—the general air, the style, the self-possession, the—the—illusion—you know", laughed Laurie, breaking down and helping himself out of his quandary with the new word.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: 'You'll be the one man that could help me in my quandaries.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

definition: To put an end to a rebellion or disorder, typically by force; to subdue or suppress a feeling.
etymology: From Old English cwellan "to kill."

examples.text: But his admission that he "guessed something like this was going to happen on Saturday", will do little to quell claims of a falling-out with Benitez.
examples.source: BBC News, “Unclear future for striker Baros”

examples.text: "Cancer, for example, is often caused by overactive genes, and quelling their activity could halt the disease," his institute says.
The drawling and the pauses with which this speech was uttered gave time for crowding reflections in Gwendolen, quelling her resistance.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Complaining in a petulant or whining manner.
etymology: From Latin querulus, from queri "to complain" (also the source of "quarrel").

examples.text: Thereafter Cornelius did not open his lips except to ask querulously for somebody to bale out his canoe, which was towing behind the long-boat.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: He was interested in the human side of that struggle to express something which was so obscure in the man's mind that he was become morbid and querulous.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Lisbeth was going on, for she was not at all afraid of Seth, and usually poured into his ears all the querulousness which was repressed by her awe of Adam.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: In a state or period of inactivity or dormancy.
etymology: From Latin quiescere "to become quiet," from quies "rest."

examples.text: In a second study published in the same journal, UK researchers say they found one important protein that keeps stem cells in a quiescent and non-dividing stage.
He never omitted the ceremony afterwards, and the gravity and quiescence with which I underwent it, seemed to invest it for him with a certain charm.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: If Edgar Linton meets me, I shall not hesitate to knock him down, and give him enough to insure his quiescence while I stay.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Exceedingly idealistic; unrealistic and impractical in pursuit of noble but unattainable goals.
etymology: From Don Quixote, the idealistic hero of Cervantes's 1605 novel.

examples.text: The annals of this Ninth Crusade are yet to be written,—the tale of a mission that seemed to our age far more quixotic than the quest of St. Louis seemed to his.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: The pilgrims read "Nomadic Life" and keep themselves in a constant state of Quixotic heroism.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: "Yet it can't be ungenerous to warn you that you are indulging mad, Quixotic expectations."
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: A complex or unwelcome consequence of an action or event; a branching structure.
etymology: From French ramification, from Medieval Latin ramificare "to form branches," from Latin ramus "branch."

examples.text: The prisoners' dilemma and all its ramifications have truly captured economists in the last couple of decades.
The cyclone will have huge ramifications for jobs and local businesses in the affected districts, which heavily rely on the two crops that used to dominate the landscape: sugar and bananas.
This was the ultimate belief on which all the systems elaborated by human thought in almost all their ramifications rested.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Flourishing or spreading unchecked, typically of something unwelcome.
etymology: From Old French rampant "climbing," present participle of ramper "to climb, crawl"; originally a heraldic term for a beast rearing on its hind legs.

examples.text: It is one of a series of proposals designed to tackle corruption, which was rampant during the Shevardnadze era, and boost Georgia's fragile public finances.
examples.source: BBC News, “Georgia plans hidden asset pardon”

examples.text: As the occupants of the carriage changed, he varied this tale, or adorned it with all the shoots of a budding fancy, the more rampant for being held off native speech so long.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: First, a decade of rampant inflation drained its reserves as we tried to protect beneficiaries from the spiraling cost of living.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Bitterness or resentfulness, especially when long-standing.
etymology: From Late Latin rancor "rankness, rancid smell," from rancere "to stink" (compare "rancid").

examples.text: It began with a flood of publicity which helped UKIP into third place in last June's European elections but became dominated by rancour as he tried to take over the party leadership.
He recognises the laws of the state and he can break them without sense of sin, but if he is punished he accepts the punishment without rancour.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: We have to go forward to the era of working together as a community, as a team, as one America, with all of us reaching across these lines that divide us—the division, the discrimination, the rancor—we have to reach across it to find common ground.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: To cause persistent annoyance or resentment.
etymology: From Old French rancler "to fester," from Medieval Latin dracunculus "little dragon," a term for an ulcer.

examples.text: The dimensions of the Brys' ball-room must rankle: you may be sure she knows 'em as well as if she'd been there last night with a yard-measure.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Philip had a fiendish instinct for discovering other people's raw spots, and was able to say things that rankled because they were true.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: And the vain boy began by degrees to have a rankling fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him, and thought he was showing off before him.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Aggressively greedy or grasping; predatory.
etymology: From Latin rapax "grasping," from rapere "to seize."

examples.text: Mr Venus's mouth screwed itself up, as Mr Boffin's face lengthened itself, Mr Venus not having been prepared for such a rapacious demand.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: However, in the town many hoped that the rapacious strangers would be induced, by the sight of so many brave men making ready to fight, to go away.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: To presume a want of motives for such contests as an argument against their existence, would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Esoteric or exclusive, distant from ordinary people's concerns; (of air) of lower pressure than usual; thin.
etymology: From "rarefy," from Latin rarefacere, from rarus "thin, rare" + facere "to make."

examples.text: The sensation reminded me of my only experience of mountaineering, and from that I judged the air to be more rarefied than it is now.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: If we would know why the same Body seems greater (without adding to it) one time, than another; they say, when it seems lesse, it is Condensed; when greater, Rarefied.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: The sun shone somewhat to the left and behind him and brightly lit up the enormous panorama which, rising like an amphitheater, extended before him in the clear rarefied atmosphere.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Acting or done without careful consideration of the possible consequences; impetuous.

examples.text: Mr Clarke said the security services and police backed his measures and it would be "rash and negligent" to ignore their advice.
examples.source: BBC News, “Anti-terror plan faces first test”

examples.text: The overseer of science investigations on NASA's New Horizons mission to Pluto calls the reclassification rash and illogical.
It would not perhaps be rash to predict, that as a mean of influence it will be found to outweigh all the peculiar attributes of the Senate.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Making or constituting a disturbingly harsh and loud noise; boisterous and disorderly.
etymology: From Latin raucus "hoarse."

examples.text: After Moya's win in the opening rubber, a raucous Seville crowd is buoyed by Nadal's impressive start which sees him race into a 30-0 lead.
And high above all the sound of the struggle there broke into the silent evening a bellowing human voice, nasal, raucous, at the highest pitch of pain.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: We have found ourselves rich in goods, but ragged in spirit; reaching with magnificent precision for the moon, but falling into raucous discord on earth.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: To completely destroy a building, town, or other site; to tear down to the ground.
etymology: From Old French raser "to shave close," from Latin radere "to scrape."

examples.text: 'If I had been shut up in any place to pine and suffer, I should always hate that place and wish to burn it down, or raze it to the ground.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The fortifying of the Kremlin, for which la Mosquee (as Napoleon termed the church of Basil the Beatified) was to have been razed to the ground, proved quite useless.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: He slaughtered the people, laid waste their soil, and razed their cities to the ground.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To reject someone or something in an abrupt or ungracious manner; (noun) such a rejection.
etymology: From obsolete French rebuffer, from Italian ribuffare "to reprimand."

examples.text: A U.S. offer last fall to sell the Soviets lower-priced wheat through the export enhancement program, EEP, was also rebuffed due to the price.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Grain Trade Calls Shultz Remark Significant”

examples.text: He says mating in the squid world is forceful on the part of the male but females play a role in choosing to associate with prospective mates or in attempting to rebuff unwanted advances.
Having no excuse for lingering longer, I slipped out, while Linton was engaged in timidly rebuffing the advances of a friendly sheep-dog.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority or discipline.
etymology: From Latin recalcitrare "to kick back," from re- "back" + calx "heel," as a horse kicks.

examples.text: He had often thought of Arabella's remarks that he should have been more severe with Sue, that her recalcitrant spirit would soon have been broken.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Behind her, waiting their turn to name themselves to the Countess, Archer noticed a number of the recalcitrant couples who had declined to meet her at Mrs. Lovell Mingott's.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: They shrank from the master who still strove for their chains; they fled to the friends that had freed them, even though those friends stood ready to use them as a club for driving the recalcitrant South back into loyalty.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

definition: To summarize and state again the main points of something.
etymology: From Late Latin recapitulare "to go over the main points again," from re- "again" + capitulum "chapter, heading."

examples.text: He recapitulated the statements which Becky had made, pointed out the probabilities of their truth, and asserted his own firm belief in her innocence.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: In reality, her thoughts were finding definite utterance in the tranquil recapitulation of the blessings in store for her.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: I claim the right to correct misstatements, and have so corrected the color of the water in the above recapitulation.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Little known; abstruse and understood only by specialists.
etymology: From Latin reconditus "hidden, put away," past participle of recondere "to store away."

examples.text: But to learn all about these recondite matters, your best way is at once to descend into the blubber-room, and have a long talk with its inmates.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: The reason is not recondite; it is simply because the police-court is not such a menacing novelty to the poor ruffian as it is to the rich.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: The Time Traveller (for so it will be convenient to speak of him) was expounding a recondite matter to us.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: A source of help in a difficult situation; the use of someone or something as such a source.
etymology: From Old French recours, from Latin recursus "a running back, return."

examples.text: "The hard part is that when things get tabled in Parliament they can quite easily become law and we have no recourse to change it," he said.
The weaker States or confederacies would first have recourse to them, to put themselves upon an equality with their more potent neighbors.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Equality depends not on the force of arms or tear gas but upon the force of moral right; not on recourse to violence but on respect for law and order.
examples.author: Lyndon B. Johnson

definition: Morally correct behavior or thinking; righteousness.
