etymology: From Late Latin rectitudo, from Latin rectus "straight, right."

examples.text: As far as most commentators are concerned, the state is pursuing Yukos out of a political vendetta, rather than simply to enforce fiscal rectitude.
examples.source: BBC News, “Could Yukos be a blessing in disguise?”

examples.text: Moreover, her capability of rectitude told her again and again that she had no right to complain of her contract, or to withdraw from it.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: This supposition of universal venalty in human nature is little less an error in political reasoning, than the supposition of universal rectitude.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Strongly reminiscent or suggestive of something; fragrant or strongly smelling of something.
etymology: From Latin redolens, present participle of redolere "to emit a scent," from re- + olere "to smell."

examples.text: Must it not be to that famous elephant, with jewelled tusks, and redolent with myrrh, which was led out of an Indian town to do honour to Alexander the Great?
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: There was also, perhaps, a little redolence of port wine, as it were the slightest possible twang, in Mr. Staple's voice.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Stephen, that is when the accosting figure came to close quarters, though he was not in an over sober state himself recognised Corley's breath redolent of rotten cornjuice.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect or fear.
etymology: From Old French redoutable, from redouter "to fear," from re- + douter "to doubt, fear."

examples.text: After which effusion the redoubtable specimen duly arrived on the scene and regaining his seat he sank rather than sat heavily on the form provided.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: He thought he must hasten to produce his tale to protect him from the missiles already on the lips of his redoubtable comrades.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

examples.text: Meanwhile she folds up a cocked hat for that redoubtable old general at Bath, descriptive of her melancholy condition.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To remedy or set right an undesirable situation or wrong; (noun) remedy or compensation for a wrong.
etymology: From Old French redresser "to set upright again," from re- + dresser "to straighten."

examples.text: The three nations, joined by France, Britain and Canada, agree these policies are essential to redress huge global trade imbalances.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Appears To Tolerate Further Dlr Decline”

examples.text: It is for others' good that I ask—to redress great wrong, and to lift much and terrible troubles—that may be more great than you can know.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: Should we persistently fail to discipline ourselves, eventually there will be increasing pressure on government to redress the failure.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Stubborn or unmanageable; resistant to a process, treatment, or stimulus.
etymology: From Latin refractarius "obstinate," from refringere "to break up."

examples.text: Mr Venus took the lead, towing Mr Wegg, in order that his refractory leg might be promptly extricated from any pitfalls it should dig for itself.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He still made a naughty or refractory lad stand with one arm stretched out for anything from ten minutes to half an hour, and he was as violent as before with his tongue.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: So Meg wrestled alone with the refractory sweetmeats all that hot summer day, and at five o'clock sat down in her topsy-turvey kitchen, wrung her bedaubed hands, lifted up her voice and wept.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: To prove a statement or theory to be wrong or false; to deny the accuracy of.
etymology: From Latin refutare "to repel, rebut."

examples.text: Mr Stott refuted Mr Hogan's claim that he had anything to do with the establishment of an incentives scheme through which trucking fees would be paid.
But this hypothesis, such as it is, has already been refuted in the remarks applied to the duration in office prescribed for the senators.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: They refute last week's television commentary downgrading our optimism and our idealism.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: To entertain or amuse someone with talk; to lavishly supply with food or drink.
etymology: From French régaler, from Old French gale "pleasure, merriment."

examples.text: Each stalk served as a perch for a grasshopper, which regaled the passers by through this Egyptian scene with its strident, monotonous note.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: So, with a gulf between him and the good company of about a foot in width, standard measure, Mrs Plornish's father was handsomely regaled.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Who would think, then, that such fine ladies and gentlemen should regale themselves with an essence found in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale!
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: To consign or dismiss to an inferior rank or position.
etymology: From Latin relegare "to send away, banish," from re- "back" + legare "to send."

examples.text: Chester's downturn in form culminated in a 5-0 defeat at Shrewsbury that leaves them hovering just above the League Two relegation zone.
examples.source: BBC News, “Rush future at Chester uncertain”

examples.text: It was Saints' fourth stalemate in succession in all competitions, but didn't lift them out of the relegation zone.
She thought not—time and change seemed so completely to have relegated him to his proper distance.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To abandon or moderate a harsh intention or cruel treatment; to become less severe or intense.

examples.text: When the whole earth is vibrant with life, does it not seem to you, Octavie, that heaven might for once relent and give us back our dead?
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: Peepy retired behind his elbow at first, but relented at the sight of sponge-cake and allowed me to take him on my lap, where he sat munching quietly.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I will not yield; I will not rest; I will not relent in waging this struggle for freedom and security for the American people.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Lacking care or attention to duty; negligent.
etymology: From Latin remissus "slack," past participle of remittere "to send back, slacken."

examples.text: I haven't "fallen victim to a rogue-dialling scam" but I think you're seriously remiss in not pointing out that the vast majority of these scams arise from people trying to access services purporting to provide free pornography.
examples.source: BBC News, “Call for action on internet scam”

examples.text: I don't think he'll find that I have been very remiss or confused in my way of conducting them; but that's for him to say—whoever he is—not for me.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: "Well, Sally, I'm in fault, and I acknowledge it; I've been remiss; but I won't let to-morrow go by without stopping up them holes."
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: To make a forcefully reproachful protest; to argue in protest or objection.
etymology: From Medieval Latin remonstrare "to demonstrate," from re- + monstrare "to show."

examples.text: The first charge relates to his failure to leave the field promptly, pushing referee Alan Wiley and remonstrating with assistant referee Paul Norman.
examples.source: BBC News, “Prutton poised for lengthy FA ban”

examples.text: On her remonstrating against this on the score of his fatigue, he said that something might happen for which he would never forgive himself.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: He has taken the matter so much to heart that he has remonstrated (in my presence he remonstrated) with Mr Eugene Wrayburn, if that be the name.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Money paid for work or a service; payment or compensation.
etymology: From Latin remunerari "to reward," from re- + munus "gift, service."

examples.text: "But ADSS fully supports proper remuneration for valued foster carers and looks forward to working with ministers, local government and the fostering organisations themselves in order to make sure a sensible and practicable policy emerges."
examples.source: BBC News, “Minimum rate for foster parents”

examples.text: The last mile I performed on foot, having dismissed the chaise and driver with the double remuneration I had promised.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: And they employ a moral police, which occasionally becomes a physical one, to deter skilful workmen from receiving, and employers from giving, a larger remuneration for a more useful service.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

definition: A person who deserts and betrays an organization, country, or set of principles; (adjective) having rejected established authority.
etymology: From Spanish renegado, from Medieval Latin renegare "to deny, renounce."

examples.text: The renegade lobby group has failed to win previous resolutions to remove directors from the MLA board and has not submitted any this year.
You are the eponymous renegade spy, an agent who deserts to the Bond world's extensive ranks of criminal masterminds, after being deemed too brutal for MI6.
examples.source: BBC News, “Bond game fails to shake or stir”

examples.text: But for my part I should have been sorry if he had spoken to her, for perhaps it might have alarmed her to find her affairs talked of by renegades.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: The making of amends for a wrong one has done, by paying money or otherwise helping those wronged.
etymology: From Late Latin reparatio, from reparare "to restore, repair."

examples.text: It is easy for him to talk of reparation, fresh from journeying and junketing in foreign lands, and living a life of vanity and pleasure.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: If you but make such reparation as is in your power, by telling us where the beryls are, all shall be forgiven and forgotten.'
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: The Germans and the Japanese cannot be left in doubt and fear as to their future; they must know their national boundaries, their resources, and what reparations they must pay.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Conversation or speech characterized by quick, witty comments or replies.
etymology: From French repartie "a retort," from repartir "to reply promptly, set out again."

examples.text: But, as the repartee did not occur to him, he contented himself with coming in from the balcony and standing at the side of his wife's couch.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There was a gentle play about his mouth which declared that his wit never descended to sarcasm, and that there was no ill-nature in his repartee.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He was not an Italian, still less a Frenchman, in whose blood there runs the very spirit of persiflage and of gracious repartee.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: A meal.
etymology: From Old French repast, from Late Latin repascere "to feed again," from Latin pascere "to feed."

examples.text: Jo moves on, through the long vacation, down to Blackfriars Bridge, where he finds a baking stony corner wherein to settle to his repast.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Sometimes, when nature, overcome by hunger, sank under the exhaustion, a repast was prepared for me in the desert that restored and inspirited me.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Meanwhile his comrades had prepared the repast, had got some water from a spring, spread out the fruit and bread, and cooked the kid.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Expressing or feeling sincere regret and remorse.
etymology: From Old French repentant, present participle of repentir "to repent."

examples.text: Then, whatever inconvenience or distress of mind the deception cost him, it was manful repentantly to accept as among its consequences, and make no complaint.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: "What a good girl you are, Amy!" said Jo, with a repentant glance from her own damaged costume to that of her sister, which was fresh and spotless still.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: She would rather have had him more sorry, she thought, and then was deeply repentant within herself for daring to be so selfish as to wish her own son to be unhappy.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Filled or well supplied with something; very full, especially with food.
etymology: From Latin repletus, past participle of replere "to fill up."

examples.text: This practice in the course of the late war, was found replete with obstructions to a vigorous and to an economical system of defense.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: I was overcome by gloom and misery and often reflected I had better seek death than desire to remain in a world which to me was replete with wretchedness.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: The striking incidents of your history, replete with instruction and furnishing abundant grounds for hopeful confidence, are comprised in a period comparatively brief.
examples.author: Franklin Pierce

definition: Deserving censure or condemnation.
etymology: From Late Latin reprehensibilis, from Latin reprehendere "to hold back, rebuke."

examples.text: Lady Chettam thought that such conduct was very reprehensible, and remembered that Mrs. Truberry's mother was a Miss Walsingham of Melspring.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: At first he saw nothing reprehensible in this, but in the second year of his marriage his view of that form of punishment suddenly changed.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Jo leaned her chin on her knees in a disconsolate attitude and shook her fist at the reprehensible John.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: A cancellation or postponement of a punishment; a temporary relief; (verb) to grant such a delay or relief.

examples.text: Dundee United manager Ian McCall has won a reprieve from the sack, with chairman Eddie Thompson calling for an end to speculation over his future.
Victorian farmers say overnight rain has given dying crops a reprieve and delayed decisions to sell livestock.
Susan resolved to keep the pleasure of telling him of his week's reprieve till he should come home to sup, as he had promised to do, in her mother's room.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

definition: An act of retaliation, especially one done in response to an injury or attack.
etymology: From Anglo-French reprisaille, from Italian ripresaglia, from riprendere "to take back."

examples.text: Some diplomats believe Iran could also consider carrying out reprisals against the United States outside the Gulf.
examples.source: Reuters, “Chances Of Direct U.S.-Iran Gulf Clash Seen Low”

examples.text: There would of course be always danger that the rights of other nations might be infringed by their decisions, so as to afford occasions of reprisal and war.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Many feared that the end of that foreign war of men and machines meant the beginning of a domestic war of recrimination and reprisal.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: To express disapproval of or disappointment in someone's actions; (noun) such an expression of disapproval.
etymology: From Old French reprochier, probably from Vulgar Latin repropiare "to bring back near," from Latin prope "near."

examples.text: My father made no reproach in his letters and only took notice of my silence by inquiring into my occupations more particularly than before.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: He was only twenty-one, and three months ago—nay, much later—he had thought proudly that no man should ever be able to reproach him justly.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: We should rise above bitterness and reproach, and if Americans could come together in a spirit of understanding and helping, then we could find positive solutions to the tragedy of abortion.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: An unprincipled person, especially one who is morally depraved; (adjective) unprincipled.
etymology: From Late Latin reprobatus "disapproved, rejected," from reprobare "to disapprove."

examples.text: For though the Scripture bee clear for an universall Resurrection; yet wee do not read, that to any of the Reprobate is promised an Eternall life.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

examples.text: Frankness and kindness like Amelia's were likely to touch even such a hardened little reprobate as Becky.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: He spits them out with a remorseful air, for he feels that it is in his nature to be an unimprovable reprobate and that it's no good HIS trying to keep awake, for HE won't never know nothink.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: To reprimand or censure someone, often gently.
etymology: From Old French reprover, from Late Latin reprobare "to disapprove."

examples.text: And if he reproved her, even by a look, you would have thought it a heart-breaking business: I don't believe he ever did speak a harsh word to her.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: Jim's voice, suddenly raised with a stern intonation, carried across the courtyard, reproving the carelessness of some dumb sinner by the river-side.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Philip's glance unconsciously went to the absinthe, and Cronshaw, seeing it, gave him the quizzical look with which he reproved the admonitions of common sense.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: To refuse to accept or be associated with; to deny the truth or validity of.
etymology: From Latin repudiare "to divorce, reject," from repudium "divorce."

examples.text: Poor Little Dorrit, not seeing her way to the offering of any soothing words that would escape repudiation, deemed it best to remain quiet.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He could not disavow his actions, belauded as they were by half the world, and so he had to repudiate truth, goodness, and all humanity.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: He would pay for Mrs. Munt's hearth-rug with ostentatious haste, a large claim he would repudiate quietly, and fight court by court.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Extremely distasteful or unacceptable; contrary or incompatible with something.
etymology: From Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare "to fight against."

examples.text: He said revenue should not be raised by taxing the consumer and called the proposal "repugnant."
examples.source: Reuters, “British Minister Criticises Proposed Ec Oils Tax”

examples.text: The little flame under his hand cast a deeper crimson on his puffing face, and Lily averted her eyes with a momentary feeling of repugnance.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Americans have always found the very thought of a Federal police force repugnant, and so do I.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: To drive back an attack or attacker by force; to rebuff or reject; to cause intense distaste.
etymology: From Latin repulsus, past participle of repellere "to drive back."

examples.text: Our fugitives returned, the battalions re-formed, and the French who had nearly cut our left flank in half were for the moment repulsed.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The French had been repulsed certainly, but it was after a severe and doubtful struggle, and with only a division of the French army.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Because peace is the keystone of our national policy, our defense program emphasizes an effective flexible type of power calculated to deter or repulse any aggression and to preserve the peace.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Made necessary by particular circumstances; required; (noun) a thing that is necessary.
etymology: From Latin requisitus, past participle of requirere "to seek, need."

examples.text: "The problem is the players that are around to replace the icons which have been lost because of retirement and injury don't have the requisite experience," Moore added.
It seldom happens in the negotiation of treaties, of whatever nature, but that perfect SECRECY and immediate DESPATCH are sometimes requisite.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: A force adequate to the enemy, collected at that single point, with suitable preparation for such others as might be menaced, is all that would be requisite.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Admirably purposeful, determined, and unwavering.
etymology: From Latin resolutus, past participle of resolvere "to loosen, release."

examples.text: The top-selling Hurriyet topped its front page with: "Our resolute stand made Greece see reason."
examples.source: Reuters, “Turkey Lifts Survey Ship Escort As Tension Abates”

examples.text: For more than a week she lay there, little altered outwardly, with her old handsome resolute frown that I so well knew carved upon her face.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Prices have displayed a welcome stability in recent months and, if we are wise and resolute, we will not tolerate inflation in the years to come.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: A short period of rest or relief from something difficult or unpleasant.
etymology: From Old French respit, from Latin respectus "regard, refuge."

examples.text: Laughter is essential because it provides a cognitive respite, Hales says.
Jos felt that the delay of yesterday had been only a respite, and that his dearly bought horses must of a surety be put into requisition.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: To settle for merely another temporary respite would surely jeopardize the future security of all the world.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: Attractive and impressive through being richly colorful or sumptuous; dazzling.
etymology: From Latin resplendens, present participle of resplendere "to shine brightly."

examples.text: A stout butler, resplendent with a smoothly shaven round chin and a starched white cravat, announced that dinner was ready, and the ladies got up.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The flashing cascade of his mane, the curving comet of his tail, invested him with housings more resplendent than gold and silver-beaters could have furnished him.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: He was so resplendent that I was almost emboldened to confess the abstraction of the lesser gem—, but he bore down all other topics with his over-powering projects.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: The restoration of something lost or stolen to its proper owner; compensation for loss or injury.
etymology: From Latin restitutio, from restituere "to restore."

examples.text: The lawsuit is asking for restitution, damages and other compensation.
examples.source: BBC News, “US woman sues over cartridges”

examples.text: The divine tribunal had changed its aspect for him; self-prostration was no longer enough, and he must bring restitution in his hand.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He accordingly handed her the card as if in restitution, but as soon as she had it she felt the difference and, with her eyes on it, stopped short for apology.
examples.author: Henry James

definition: Unable to keep still or silent and becoming increasingly impatient or unruly; resistant to control.
etymology: From Old French restif "stationary, balky," from rester "to remain"; originally of a horse refusing to move.

examples.text: "In truth," replied he on the mare, "I would not pass you so hastily but for fear that horse might turn restive in the company of my mare."
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: Rostov's horse was also getting restive: it pawed the frozen ground, pricking its ears at the noise and looking at the lights.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Mr Pancks was the third, and carried his hat under his arm for the liberation of his restive hair; the weather being extremely hot.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved.
etymology: From Latin reticere "to keep silent," from re- (intensive) + tacere "to be silent" (compare "tacit").

examples.text: "Although his films vary in style, they all bear his unmistakable stamp: they are forceful and charged cinematographically, as well as reticent, stylised and musical," organisers said in a statement.
examples.source: BBC News, “Berlin honours S Korean director”

examples.text: Mr Inspector replied, with due generality and reticence, that it was always more likely that a man had done a bad thing than that he hadn't.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She showed her usual reticence to her parents, and only said, that if Lydgate had done as she wished he would have left Middlemarch long ago.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Punishment inflicted on someone as vengeance for a wrong or criminal act.
etymology: From Late Latin retributio, from retribuere "to repay," from re- "back" + tribuere "to assign."

examples.text: Garn, a Utah Republican, said "I am talking about specific retribution on a company that endangers the security of their own country and ours."
examples.source: Reuters, “U.S. Senators Propose Ban On Toshiba Imports”

examples.text: The retribution that followed every vengeful success was so sweeping and majestic that the boys always retired from the field badly worsted.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: See ye not, she is the scarlet letter, only capable of being loved, and so endowed with a millionfold the power of retribution for my sin?
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

definition: Directed or moving backward; reverting to an earlier and inferior condition.
etymology: From Latin retrogradus, from retro "backward" + gradi "to step."

examples.text: Triton stands out among all the large moons in the solar system because it orbits Neptune in a direction opposite to the planet's rotation, a so-called retrograde orbit.
The living soul demands life, the soul won't obey the rules of mechanics, the soul is an object of suspicion, the soul is retrograde!
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: "If we believe in Scripture, we can hardly think that mankind in general will now be allowed to retrograde."
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Feeling or showing deep and solemn respect.
etymology: From Latin reverens, present participle of revereri "to stand in awe of."

examples.text: The priest put on a short white lace garment over his black robe, crossed himself, bowed reverently, and began to turn a windlass slowly.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: His last words were inaudible, but he closed the book reverently and, being nearly blind, made a groping movement and gripped the reading-stand.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: My most reverent prayer for America is for industrial peace, with its rewards, widely and generally distributed, amid the inspirations of equal opportunity.
examples.author: Warren G. Harding

definition: To criticize in an abusive or angrily insulting manner.
etymology: From Old French reviler "to treat as vile," from vil "vile."

examples.text: The poor, as we have already said, whom she sought out to be the objects of her bounty, often reviled the hand that was stretched forth to succour them.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: Still, among the various excesses to which human nature is subject, moralists have never numbered that of being too fond of the people who openly revile us.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Referring to sexual matters in an amusingly rude or irreverent way.

examples.text: A ribald face, sullen as a dean's, Buck Mulligan came forward, then blithe in motley, towards the greeting of their smiles.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: He that possesses her must keep her within bounds, not permitting her to break out in ribald satires or soulless sonnets.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: You have told us of their gloating lips; you heard their ribald laugh as they clutched the moving bag that the Count threw to them.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: (Especially of something undesirable) widespread or common; full of something.
etymology: From Old English rife "abundant."

examples.text: It will be the 21st James Bond film to hit the big screen, and speculation has been rife over who will play the lead.
examples.source: BBC News, “Casino Royale is next Bond movie”

examples.text: So rife and potent was the fever in Bleeding Heart Yard, that Mr Pancks's rent-days caused no interval in the patients.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Committee after committee of this Congress has heard witness after witness describe many of these programs as poorly administered and rife with waste and fraud.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: The quality of being extremely thorough and careful; severity or strictness; harsh conditions.
etymology: From Latin rigor "stiffness," from rigere "to be stiff."

examples.text: The Commission will draw up a new system of steel production quotas to protect vulnerable EC firms from the full rigors of open competition.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ec Ministers Announce Plan For Steel Closures”

examples.text: He was nerving himself to this rigor as he rode from Brassing, and meditated on the representations he must make to Rosamond.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: In the preceding inquiries the powers of the convention have been analyzed and tried with the same rigor, and by the same rules, as if they had been real and final powers for the establishment of a Constitution for the United States.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Involving or limited to basic principles; elementary; undeveloped or immature.
etymology: From "rudiment," from Latin rudimentum "first attempt, beginning," from rudis "unformed, rough."

examples.text: Guthrie also determines that several cave art images are incomplete, overlapping, brief and rudimentary, as though the people who created them were still learning to draw.
He realised that the console could be used as a rudimentary synthesizer.
No born gentleman, no-one with the most rudimentary promptings of a gentleman would stoop to such particularly loathsome conduct.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: To think deeply about something; (of an animal) to chew the cud.
etymology: From Latin ruminari "to chew the cud," from rumen "throat, gullet."

examples.text: When we had done, he brought me a pudding, and having set it before me, seemed to ruminate, and to become absent in his mind for some moments.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: At one end a ruminating tar was still further adorning it with his jack-knife, stooping over and diligently working away at the space between his legs.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: "I am sure Mrs. Garth would agree with you there," said Mr. Farebrother, who for some reason seemed more inclined to ruminate than to speak.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: An action intended to deceive someone; a trick.
etymology: From Old French ruser "to drive back," used of a hunted animal doubling back to elude pursuers.

examples.text: It was really a ruse of Lucy's to justify her despondency—a ruse of which she was not herself conscious, for she was marching in the armies of darkness.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: But he was ashamed; he would look such a fool in his own eyes if he gave in now; his uncle would chuckle at the success of the headmaster's ruse.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: It seemed hopeless to pursue the inquiry any farther, but it was clear that in spite of Holmes's ruse we had no proof that Barrymore had not been in London all the time.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Having or showing keen mental discernment and good judgment; wise.
etymology: From Latin sagax "of quick perception," from sagire "to perceive keenly."

examples.text: Besides, hast thou not chosen thy opportunity with wonderful little skill, indeed with no touch of that sagacity for which thou art famous?
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: A succession of adventures, so much glory, such a victorious progress! and the deep sense of his sagacity crowning every day of his inner life.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The sagacious mind of Mr. Jefferson early saw and lamented this error, and attempts have been made, hitherto without success, to apply the amendatory power of the States to its correction.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: (Especially of something unwelcome) producing good effects; beneficial; promoting health.
etymology: From Latin salutaris "healthful," from salus "health."

examples.text: A space probe that arrives at Venus today will yield new insights into what caused the runaway greenhouse effect there and could bring a salutary warning for our own planet, scientists say.
Whether the salutary reform which has been introduced within its walls has been carried as far as could have been desired may be doubtful.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Their physical strength would be more adequate to foreign danger, and the practice of self-government, aided by the light of experience, could not fail to produce an effect equally salutary on all those questions connected with the internal organization.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Making a show of being morally superior to other people; self-righteous.
etymology: From Latin sanctimonia "holiness," from sanctus "holy."

examples.text: She had had almost enough of Mr. Slope, though she could not quite resist the fun of driving a very sanctimonious clergyman to madness by a desperate and ruinous passion.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: What about sanctimonious Cromwell and his ironsides that put the women and children of Drogheda to the sword with the bible text God is love pasted round the mouth of his cannon?
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: He was donned in his Sunday garments, with his most sanctimonious and sourest face, and, holding his hat in one hand, and his stick in the other, he proceeded to clean his shoes on the mat.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Involving or causing much bloodshed; bloodthirsty.
etymology: From Latin sanguinarius, from sanguis "blood."

examples.text: I thought of Elizabeth, of my father, and of Clerval—all left behind, on whom the monster might satisfy his sanguinary and merciless passions.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: For was it not your fatal and sanguinary intention to destroy that son of whom M. de Morcerf was so proud?
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: However, I got dressed, darkly wiping my sanguinary face at intervals, and I said, "Can I help you?" and he said "No thankee," and I said "Good afternoon," and he said "Same to you."
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Optimistic or positive, especially in an apparently bad or difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin sanguineus "of blood," from sanguis "blood." In medieval humoral theory, an excess of blood made a person cheerful and confident.

examples.text: But in the face of the strengthening yen making exports less competitive and indications of weakening economic conditions ahead, observers were less sanguine.

But a Bank of Japan official took a much more sanguine view, telling Reuters that "the exchange market is apparently reacting too much, and anyone who sold the dollar on the Baker comment will regret it later on."
Meanwhile, I must say, I could not agree with my guardian on the subject of the will, and I had some sanguine hopes of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Grimly mocking or cynical.
etymology: From Greek sardanios, used by Homer of bitter laughter; later linked to a Sardinian plant said to contort the face of anyone who ate it.

examples.text: Old Monsieur Farival laughed sardonically at something as he looked at the sails, and Beaudelet swore at the old man under his breath.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: He sat quietly, with a sardonic expression on his gaunt face, and spoke only when the opportunity occurred to throw in a witticism.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The sergeant, taking note of this, gave pause to his elaborate history while he administered a sardonic comment.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: To satisfy a desire or appetite fully, or to excess.
etymology: From Latin satiare "to fill full," from satis "enough."

examples.text: If thou wert yet alive and yet cherished a desire of revenge against me, it would be better satiated in my life than in my destruction.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: When the task was done, Mr Boffin, with his appetite for Misers whetted instead of satiated, began to look out again.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: This shadow looked satiated and calm, as though for the moment it had had its fill of all the emotions.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Slow and gloomy in temperament or mood; dark and brooding.
etymology: From the planet Saturn, which astrologers believed made people born under it gloomy and sluggish.

examples.text: Somehow his words and his look did not seem to accord, or else it was that his cast of face made his smile look malignant and saturnine.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: With Mr. Heathcliff, grim and saturnine, on the one hand, and Hareton, absolutely dumb, on the other, I made a somewhat cheerless meal, and bade adieu early.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: It was not, however, so saturnine a pride! she laughed continually; her laugh was satirical, and so was the habitual expression of her arched and haughty lip.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: A learned person, especially a distinguished scientist or scholar; someone with exceptional ability in a specific field.
etymology: From French savant "knowing," present participle of savoir "to know."

examples.text: Babbitt had a good deal of honest pride in being the neighbor of such a savant, and in Ted's intimacy with Eunice Littlefield.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: His friends who were specialists and savants, occasionally—unmistakably from politeness—alluded to it.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: I thought he was so learned, such a savant, and all of a sudden he behaved so warmly, openly, and youthfully, with such youthful inexperience, and it was all so fine, like you....
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Barely sufficient or adequate; insufficient in amount; (verb) to provide grudgingly or deal with inadequately.
etymology: From Old Norse skamt, neuter of skammr "short."

examples.text: The scientists say the fossil record for gliding mammals is so scant because the small creatures are poorly preserved, particularly their gliding structure.
Although details were scant, Mr Gates, said IE7 would include new protections against viruses, spyware and phishing scams.
examples.source: BBC News, “Security scares spark browser fix”

examples.text: They said it and they wrought it, though often breathing with scant life, as in a coffin, or as lying wounded amid a heap of slain.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Witheringly scornful or severely critical.
etymology: From "scathe" "to harm," from Old Norse skatha "to injure."

examples.text: And he is scathing of the Tory party which he also appears to believe is unreformable.
Without raising her voice, she threw into it an infinity of scathing contempt, bitterness, and despair.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: No doubt you're right logically, and are entitled to say a great many scathing things about Henry.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: To be brilliantly lively, witty, or clever; to emit flashes of light; sparkle.
etymology: From Latin scintillare "to sparkle," from scintilla "spark."

examples.text: Those are the two questions occupying not just Wales supporters but rugby fans as a whole after a scintillating display in Paris.
examples.source: BBC News, “Paris promise raises Welsh hopes”

examples.text: A kind of arm carried a complicated metallic case, about which green flashes scintillated, and out of the funnel of this there smoked the Heat-Ray.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: For it he concocted verses, for it he made speeches, for it he scintillated the brightest sparks of his quiet wit.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: A person or thing that causes great trouble or suffering; a whip; (verb) to cause great suffering to.
etymology: From Old French escorge "whip," from Latin ex- + corrigia "thong."

examples.text: For currency dealers Karl Otto Poehl is the scourge of speculators, for bankers he is the man who has played a key role in shaping the world's financial destiny for the last seven years, and for Germans he is the guardian of the mark.
examples.source: Reuters, “Poehl Looks Set For Eight More Years At Bundesbank”

examples.text: Inquiry was made into the origin of the scourge, and by degrees various facts came out which excited public indignation in a high degree.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: We now have within our reach the goal of insuring that the next generation can be the first generation in this century to be spared the scourges of war.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: Diligent, thorough, and extremely attentive to details; very concerned to avoid doing wrong.
etymology: From Latin scrupulus "a small sharp stone" — a stone in one's shoe, figuratively a small worry that pricks the conscience.

examples.text: He always wore a white neckcloth, clean indeed, but not tied with that scrupulous care which now distinguishes some of our younger clergy.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He hoped to secure the approbation of his mistress by scrupulous obedience to all her commands, and faithful care of all that belonged to her.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: The war has been waged on our part with scrupulous regard to all these obligations, and in a spirit of liberality which was never surpassed.
examples.author: James Madison

definition: Conduct or speech inciting people to rebel against the authority of a state or monarch.
etymology: From Latin seditio "a going apart, civil discord," from sed- "apart" + itio "a going."

examples.text: Not only had ill-conditioned minds become insubordinate by the fruition of a little power, but sedition had been overtly taught and preached.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: They will arrest him yet unless he assumes an expression of countenance that shall have less of carnage, insurrection and sedition in it.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: Men that distrust their own subtilty, are in tumult, and sedition, better disposed for victory, than they that suppose themselves wise, or crafty.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

definition: Showing dedication and diligence; persevering and careful.
etymology: From Latin sedulus "zealous, careful."

examples.text: Miss Bartlett sedulously denied disapproving of any one, and added "I am afraid you are finding me a very depressing companion."
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: It had been her care which provided me a companion in Clerval—and yet a man is blind to a thousand minute circumstances which call forth a woman's sedulous attention.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: We sedulously cultivate the friendship of all nations as the conditions most compatible with our welfare and the principles of our Government.
examples.author: Martin Van Buren

definition: Given to moralizing in a pompous or affected manner; full of terse, pithy maxims.
etymology: From Latin sententiosus "full of meaning," from sententia "opinion, maxim."

examples.text: 'I am not such a fool as I look, quoth Plato to his disciples,' he said sententiously, emptied his glass with great resolution, and we rose.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: "It's the simplest thing in the world to have an affair with a woman," he remarked sententiously, "but it's a devil of a nuisance to get out of it."
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: As was to be expected, however, from the defect of language and the necessarily sententious manner in which the Constitution is written, disputes have arisen as to the amount of power which it has actually granted or was intended to grant.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Able to perceive or feel things; conscious.
etymology: From Latin sentiens, present participle of sentire "to feel."

examples.text: Like sentient things—even like the lords and ladies of creation sometimes—might have done much, but did nothing.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She longed to be to him something more than a piece of sentient prettiness, a passing diversion to his eye and brain; and the longing betrayed itself in her reply.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: The condition of several moved him as he would have been moved by maimed sentient beings.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To isolate or hide away; to take legal possession of assets until a debt is paid; to remove a gas, such as carbon, from the atmosphere.
etymology: From Late Latin sequestrare "to give up for safekeeping," from sequester "trustee, depositary."

examples.text: He says another option is to neutralise the CO2 before sequestering it in the oceans by mixing it with alkaline minerals such as limestone.
The sale was aborted when Diaz's Presidential Commission on Good Government sequestered the shares on suspicion they were owned by Cojuangco, a close associate of former President Ferdinand Marcos.
examples.source: Reuters, “San Miguel Deal Hit By More Lawsuits”

examples.text: When the time comes for Veneering to deliver a neat and appropriate stammer to the men of Pocket-Breaches, only Podsnap and Twemlow accompany him by railway to that sequestered spot.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Having or showing an excessive willingness to serve or please others; of or like a slave.
etymology: From Latin servilis, from servus "slave."

examples.text: But what they want though it smells of death and can be made of India-rubber, at least is not alive, has no will, is servile and won't revolt!
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In the most cultured sections and cities of the South the Negroes are a segregated servile caste, with restricted rights and privileges.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: Philip looked at his own portrait of Ruth Chalice, and now that three months had passed he realised that it was no more than a servile copy of Lawson.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: To avoid or neglect a duty or responsibility.

examples.text: The best performing police services would get more cash and extra freedoms, he said, but he would not shirk from stepping in where the public was being failed.
Old Gibbons don't say nothing about it—just shirks it complete—Gibbons always done that when he got stuck —but there is Rolampton, what does he say?
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: Let us remember that America was built not by government, but by people — not by welfare, but by work — not by shirking responsibility, but by seeking responsibility.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

definition: Reluctance to work or make an effort; laziness; also a slow-moving tropical mammal.
etymology: From Middle English slouthe, from slow + -th.

examples.text: I have had unformed ideas of striving afresh, beginning anew, shaking off sloth and sensuality, and fighting out the abandoned fight.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: How strange that Georgia, the world-heralded refuge of poor debtors, should bind her own to sloth and misfortune as ruthlessly as ever England did!
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: There were other signs of removal about, with queer narrow footprints like those I could imagine made by a sloth.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: The state of being sober; the quality of being staid, serious, or sensible.
etymology: From Latin sobrietas, from sobrius "sober."

examples.text: Jo had sudden fits of sobriety, and was seen to shake her fist at Mr. Brooke's umbrella, which had been left in the hall.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: "I certainly agree with Mr. MacIan," said Turnbull with sobriety and perfect respectfulness, "that you had better let us see the head of the institution."
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: Yet, for all his hardy sobriety and fortitude, there were certain qualities in him which at times affected, and in some cases seemed well nigh to overbalance all the rest.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: To ask for or try to obtain something from someone; to request earnestly.
etymology: From Latin sollicitare "to agitate, disturb," from sollicitus "anxious."

examples.text: Harper also said that New World Pictures, a shareholder, has requested a copy of Harper's shareholder list to be used in soliciting proxies.
Last night, on being childishly solicited for twopence, to buy 'lemon-stunners'—a local sweetmeat—he presented an oyster-knife at the twins!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Fellow citizens, without solicitation on my part, I have been chosen by the free and voluntary suffrages of my countrymen to the most honorable and most responsible office on earth.
examples.author: James K. Polk

definition: Characterized by showing interest or concern; eager or anxious to do something.
etymology: From Latin sollicitus "anxious, troubled."

examples.text: These points formed her chief solicitude in anticipating her removal from Uppercross, where she felt she had been stationed quite long enough.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: This was said with a careless, abstracted indifference, which showed that my solicitude was, at least in his opinion, wholly superfluous.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: But this is still the Government of all the people, and it should be none the less an object of their affectionate solicitude.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: An act of speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone, especially by a character in a play.
etymology: From Late Latin soliloquium, from solus "alone" + loqui "to speak."

examples.text: This woman was not given to soliloquy; but extremity of feeling lessens the individuality of the weak, as it increases that of the strong.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: "I'll answer by doing the Highland fling or the sailor's hornpipe; and you—well, let me see—oh, I've got it—you can do Hamlet's soliloquy."
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: To mend the matter, Hamlet's aunt had the family failing of indulging in soliloquy, and held forth in a desultory manner, by herself, on every topic that was introduced.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Sleepy or drowsy; causing or suggestive of sleep.
etymology: From Latin somnolentus, from somnus "sleep."

examples.text: Onward to the dead sea they tramp to drink, unslaked and with horrible gulpings, the salt somnolent inexhaustible flood.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: He was again painfully aware of a somnolent tendency in Frederick (which had no existence out of his own imagination), and after dinner, when Frederick had withdrawn, privately apologised to Mrs General for the poor man.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Nevertheless, there can be but few of us who had never known one of these rare moments of awakening when we see, hear, understand ever so much—everything—in a flash—before we fall back again into our agreeable somnolence.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: (Of a sound) imposingly deep and full; (of speech) using imposing language.
etymology: From Latin sonorus "resounding," from sonor "sound."

examples.text: There was the Odeon quite near them, and Philip soon shared his friend's passion for the tragedians of Louis XIV and the sonorous Alexandrine.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The magnificent melody of the Prayer in Rossini's Moses, sung in a sonorous bass voice, rose grandly through the suburban silence of the place.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: This was said in excellent Tuscan, and with that soft Roman accent which makes the language of Dante as sonorous as that of Homer.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: The use of clever but false arguments, especially with the intention of deceiving.
etymology: From "sophist," from Greek sophistes "expert, wise man," later applied to paid teachers of rhetoric criticized for specious reasoning.

examples.text: Sophistry may reply, that sovereigns are equal, and that a majority of the votes of the States will be a majority of confederated America.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: But I saw on your mouth the twitch of your infernal sophistry; I knew that something was wrong with you and your cathedrals.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: Then, after hours of clear reasoning and firm conviction, we snatch at any sophistry that will nullify our long struggles, and bring us the defeat that we love better than victory.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Involving ignoble actions and motives; morally vile; dirty or squalid.
etymology: From Latin sordidus "dirty, foul," from sordes "dirt."

examples.text: Sordid in my grief, sordid in my love, sordid in my miserable escape from the darker side of both, oh see the ruin I am, and hate me, shun me!'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: What wonder that the sordid lights of work-day prudence should pale before the glory of a hope like theirs in the full splendor of its fruition?
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: It perverts the patriotic sentiments of our countrymen and tempts them to pitiful calculation of the sordid gain to be derived from their Government's maintenance.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Superficially plausible but actually wrong; misleadingly attractive.
etymology: From Latin speciosus "fair, beautiful," from species "appearance."

examples.text: This argument presents itself under a very specious and seducing form; and is well calculated to lay hold of the prejudices of those to whom it is addressed.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: She had held herself for months with a firm hand; she hadn't interfered on any chance—and chances were specious enough—that she might interfere to her profit.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: He then, by a specious argument, prevented her from going, and so had the chance for which he had waited.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Occurring at irregular intervals or only in a few places; scattered.
etymology: From Greek sporadikos "scattered," from speirein "to sow" (also in "spore").

examples.text: There was only sporadic activity for spot material, which was mainly requirement buying, they said, adding that pre-registered coffees were no longer available.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ico Quota Talks Failure Paralyse Hamburg Market”

examples.text: It has an active and smoke-misted billiard room, it is represented by baseball and football teams, and in the pool and the gymnasium a tenth of the members sporadically try to reduce.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The threat we face is not sporadic or dated: It is continuous.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Not being what it purports to be; false or fake; (of reasoning) apparently but not actually valid.
etymology: From Latin spurius "illegitimate, false."

examples.text: A carriage at the gate, and Mortimer's man arrives, looking rather like a spurious Mephistopheles and an unacknowledged member of that gentleman's family.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: When all men flinched, then—he felt sure—he alone would know how to deal with the spurious menace of wind and seas.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: That institution is reserved for men like Kennicott who, after devoting fifty years to "putting aside a stake," incontinently invest the stake in spurious oil-stocks.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To reject with disdain or contempt.
etymology: From Old English spurnan "to kick, reject."

examples.text: As a member of a new-look England side on the long road to World Cup glory - a journey not without mishaps as a succession of Grand Slams opportunities were spurned - Dallaglio emerged as a key performer once again.
examples.source: BBC News, “Dallaglio his own man to the end”

examples.text: The young girl spoke in high and enthusiastic terms of her mother, who, born in freedom, spurned the bondage to which she was now reduced.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: How is it that Amelia, who had such a number of friends at school, and was so beloved there, comes out into the world and is spurned by her discriminating sex?
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Extremely dirty and unpleasant, especially from neglect or poverty; morally degraded or sordid.
etymology: From Latin squalidus "rough, dirty," from squalere "to be stiff with dirt."

examples.text: In both, there were several knots of loungers, squalid and miserable, but now with a manifest sense of power enthroned on their distress.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But the drivers, through miles of dark squalid road, poured out their souls to the dryads and the saints, and Lucy poured out hers to her cousin.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: She pictured herself leading such a life as theirs—a life in which achievement seemed as squalid as failure—and the vision made her shudder sympathetically.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Sedate, respectable, and unadventurous; dull and conventional.
etymology: An old past participle of "stay," in the sense "fixed, settled."

examples.text: The panorama of Delft is a little staid in contrast to the dramatic rockscape captured in Mr Lyons' image.
examples.source: BBC News, “How to make a gigapixel picture”

examples.text: For Michel Develle, Director of Economic Studies at newly-privatised Banque Paribas, the government's outstanding achievement has been to launch "a veritable intellectual revolution" breaking the staid habits formed by centuries of state control.
If that staid old house near the Green at Richmond should ever come to be haunted when I am dead, it will be haunted, surely, by my ghost.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Loyal, reliable, and hardworking; strongly built; a loyal, steadfast supporter of a cause or organization.
etymology: From Old English stælwierthe "serviceable," a Scots variant of "stalworth."

examples.text: As the summer ended, stalwarts Catherina McKiernan and Dermot Donnelly hung up their competitive spikes.
examples.source: BBC News, “2004: An Irish Athletics Year”

examples.text: There was one thing that much aided me in renewing and re-creating the stalwart soldier of the Niagara frontier—the man of true and simple energy.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: Troy heard the dull determination in Boldwood's voice, looked at his stalwart frame, then at the thick cudgel he carried in his hand.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: Stiff, artificial, and unnatural in manner or language; overly formal.
etymology: From "stilt," originally meaning raised on stilts, hence pompous or elevated.

examples.text: This notion of shuffling the player along a studiously pre-determined path, forcibly witnessing a series of pre-set moments of action, is a perilous business which can make the whole affair feel stilted rather than organic.
examples.source: BBC News, “Big war games battle it out”

examples.text: Without understanding when or how, without a tangible change in the stilted intoning of the stage-puppets, she was conscious of another time and place.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Then he wondered whether what she said had any meaning for her: perhaps she knew no other way to express her genuine feelings than the stilted language of The Family Herald.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Unwilling to give or spend money; mean and ungenerous; scanty or meager.

examples.text: For though she could filch a lot of money from the papa he wouldn't marry her, and maybe he'll turn stingy in the end, and keep his purse shut.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: To her other defects (as most people thought them, but which to Pierre were qualities) of untidiness and neglect of herself, she now added stinginess.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Bound to happen to a good-looking girl with stingy relatives, I suppose; anyhow, they DID happen, and she found the ground prepared for her.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To demand or specify as a requirement, especially as part of an agreement or contract.
etymology: From Latin stipulari "to demand a formal promise," a term of Roman contract law.

examples.text: The accord stipulated that current rates reflect fundamentals of the six nations - Britain, Canada, France, Japan, the U.S. And West Germany.
examples.source: Reuters, “Miyazawa Says Present Yen Not Necessarily Ideal”

examples.text: This business-like obstacle surmounted, he then stipulated that before resuming with you I should look over the books and form my own opinion.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: To protect the national honor, every dollar of Government indebtedness should be paid in gold, unless otherwise expressly stipulated in the contract.
examples.author: Ulysses S. Grant

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining.
etymology: From Greek Stōikos, from Stoa Poikilē, the "Painted Porch" in Athens where Zeno of Citium taught his philosophy around 300 BC.

examples.text: The suppression of grief was also helped by a decline in religious ritual and by a period of major wars in which soldiers, and by implication all of us, were expected to bear death with stoicism, says Jalland.
Every truck that made its way from the factories to the freight-stations was guarded by a policeman, trying to look stoical beside the scab driver.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The men, pitching forward insanely, had burst into cheerings, moblike and barbaric, but tuned in strange keys that can arouse the dullard and the stoic.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: Calm, dependable, and showing little emotion or animation; impassive.
etymology: From Latin stolidus "dull, stupid, slow."

examples.text: Next the Scotchman was the place assigned to Costello, the eccentric, while at his side was seated in stolid repose the squat form of Madden.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: You and I know that he died of sheer fright, and we know also what frightened him, but how are we to get twelve stolid jurymen to know it?
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: They passed within view of a stolid white house, and saw in front of it groups of their comrades lying in wait behind a neat breastwork.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: Loud and harsh, grating; presenting a point of view forcefully and aggressively.
etymology: From Latin stridere "to creak, make a harsh noise."

examples.text: "I consider the strident tone of US declarations on Airbus ill-advised, and the EC fats and oils tax proposal a dangerous provocation," he said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Dutch Official Warns Of More Trade Conflicts”

examples.text: It was a landscape of Bocklin's beside a landscape of Leader's, strident and ill-considered, but quivering into supernatural life.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: There was a long pause, which the inner devils filled with strident laughter; then May freed herself from his arms and stood up.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To make someone unable to think or feel properly; to astonish or shock greatly.
etymology: From Latin stupefacere, from stupere "to be stunned" + facere "to make."

examples.text: The judges themselves appeared to be stupefied, and the jury manifested tokens of disgust for cynicism so unexpected in a man of fashion.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The scream had been heard but a few seconds when it was followed by sudden deafening report that echoed through the room and stupefied them all.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: It stifles the spirit of true Americanism and stupefies every ennobling trait of American citizenship.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: A state of near-unconsciousness or greatly dulled senses.
etymology: From Latin stupor "numbness, astonishment," from stupere "to be stunned."

examples.text: The grating against the library-door aroused the young girl from the stupor in which she was plunged, and which almost amounted to insensibility.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: All that they knew was, that after what seemed a mighty stretch of time, both awoke out of a dead stupor of sleep and resumed their miseries once more.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: Jo is in a sleep or in a stupor to-day, and Allan Woodcourt, newly arrived, stands by him, looking down upon his wasted form.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Charming, confident, and elegant, typically of a man; smoothly polite, sometimes superficially so.
etymology: From French suave, from Latin suavis "agreeable, sweet."

examples.text: She was for the first time invited up-stairs, and found the suave old woman sewing in a white and mahogany room with a small bed.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: 'There is a little business where he would be most useful—in the South,' said Lurgan, with peculiar suavity, dropping his heavy blued eyelids.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: "You can understand," said Holmes suavely, "that I extend to the affairs of my other clients the same secrecy which I promise to you in yours."
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: To bring under domination or control, especially by conquest.
etymology: From Latin subjugare "to bring under the yoke," from sub- "under" + jugum "yoke."

examples.text: The bold and reckless young blood of ten-years back was subjugated and was turned into a torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: But gradually the sense of complete subjugation came over her, and she wondered languidly what had made her feel so uneasy and excited.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Also at this moment, massive Soviet troops are attempting to subjugate the fiercely independent and deeply religious people of Afghanistan.
examples.author: Jimmy Carter

definition: Of such excellence, grandeur, or beauty as to inspire great admiration or awe.
etymology: From Latin sublimis "uplifted, lofty."

examples.text: Wright-Phillips' sublime skill and pace took him past Brown and he delivered a pin-point centre to the feet of McManaman.
Is it not, by its noble cares and sublime results, the one best calculated to fill the void left by uptorn affections and demolished hopes?
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: I wish to be providence myself, for I feel that the most beautiful, noblest, most sublime thing in the world, is to recompense and punish.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Excessively willing to obey others; less important, subordinate.
etymology: From Latin subservire "to be subject to, comply with," from sub- "under" + servire "to serve."

examples.text: It is observed that select corps may be formed, composed of the young and ardent, who may be rendered subservient to the views of arbitrary power.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: The words, and the movement which accompanied them, combined to startle Lily out of the state of tranced subservience into which she had insensibly slipped.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: For it is a thing that dependeth not on Nature, but on the scope of the Writer; and is subservient to every mans proper method.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

definition: To become less intense, violent, or severe; to sink to a lower level.
etymology: From Latin subsidere "to settle, sink," from sub- "down" + sidere "to settle."

examples.text: It's just that their blushing takes longer to subside so it's more obvious to them and others, Australian research suggests.
That Lily was a star fallen from that sky did not, after the first stir of curiosity had subsided, materially add to their interest in her.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Fear of external Communist conquest in many Asian nations is already subsiding—and with this, the spirit of hope is rising.
examples.author: Lyndon B. Johnson

definition: To provide evidence to support or prove the truth of a claim.
etymology: From Latin substantia "substance, being."

examples.text: But there's no evidence for humans and "there's nothing to substantiate claims that wheatgrass can help dissolve tumours", the report says.
But the diplomats said they had seen no reports in the state press and heard no comments from officials to substantiate them.
examples.source: Reuters, “No Proof Of More Chernobyl Grain Damage-Diplomats”

examples.text: Some were perusing the article, others making comments and recalling circumstances which substantiated the charges still more.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Deceit used in order to achieve one's goal; a trick or deceptive stratagem.
etymology: From Late Latin subterfugium, from Latin subterfugere "to escape secretly," from subter- "beneath" + fugere "to flee."

examples.text: I admit that our meeting as strangers prevented a sense of relationship, and that it was a sort of subterfuge to avail myself of it.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Maggie felt her heart leap at this subterfuge of Philip's, and there passed over her face that almost imperceptible shock which accompanies any relief.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: There is a belief abroad that by invoking technicalities, subterfuge, and delay, the ends of justice may be thwarted by those who can pay the cost.
examples.author: Herbert Hoover

definition: Seeking or intended to undermine an established system or institution; a person who does so.
etymology: From Latin subvertere "to overturn," from sub- "from below" + vertere "to turn."

examples.text: But there was something new and subversive of the universe in the combination of so much cheerful decision with a body without a brain.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: The subversive character of the Communist Party in the United States has been clearly demonstrated in many ways, including court proceedings.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

examples.text: Nevertheless it is hard for any nation to focus on an external or subversive threat to its independence when its energies are drained in daily combat with the forces of poverty and despair.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: Assistance and support in times of hardship and distress; to give such help.
etymology: From Old French socours, from Latin succurrere "to run to the help of," from sub- "up to" + currere "to run."

examples.text: Turning to critics' fears that the US was poised for further military action, Mr Blair refused to give succour to suggestions it was preparing for strikes against Iran.
examples.source: BBC News, “Blair sees greater Bush consensus”

examples.text: Those were the knightly days of our profession, when we only bore arms to succor the distressed, and not to fill men's lamp-feeders.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: "Yes, I need your help: that is I thought like a madman that you could lend me your assistance in a case where God alone can succor me."
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: To gradually spread through or over, as with a color, light, liquid, or feeling.
etymology: From Latin suffundere "to pour beneath," from sub- "under" + fundere "to pour."

examples.text: She could not herself have explained the sense of buoyancy which seemed to lift and swing her above the sun-suffused world at her feet.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: A flash of eagerness suffused the face of Alexey Alexandrovitch as he rapidly wrote out a synopsis of these ideas for his own benefit.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: And the feeling even suffused itself over his face so as to attract his mother's notice, while she was drinking her tea.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Splendid and expensive-looking; lavish.
etymology: From Latin sumptuosus, from sumptus "expense," from sumere "to take, spend."

examples.text: It certainly was agreeable to fare sumptuously, drive in a fine carriage, wear her best frock every day, and do nothing but enjoy herself.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: A sumptuous breakfast of bacon and fish was shortly provided, and as the boys set to work upon it, Tom recounted (and adorned) his adventures.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: A few sumptuously-cloaked ladies were already gathered in the marble vestibule, and in the coat-room he found Van Alstyne and Gus Trenor.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Behaving or looking as though one thinks one is superior to others; haughtily disdainful.
etymology: From Latin supercilium "eyebrow," evoking a raised, scornful brow.

examples.text: A distant supercilious air makes a cold atmosphere about her, and there is nothing in her bearing, as there was before, to encourage openness.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He did not go, because he was afraid to seem supercilious, and he talked with the girls and laughed, but in his heart was unhappiness.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: "I am told, on excellent authority, that her father keeps an American dry-goods store," said Sir Thomas Burdon, looking supercilious.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

definition: Unnecessary, especially through being more than enough.
etymology: From Latin superfluus "overflowing," from super- "over" + fluere "to flow."

examples.text: Farmer Oak had one-and-a-half Christian characteristics too many to succeed with Bathsheba: his humility, and a superfluous moiety of honesty.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Touched by such superfluity of simple confidence in a woman of her mature years, I opened the ample reservoirs of my nature and absorbed it all.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: We are determined to make every American citizen the subject of his country's interest and concern; and we will never regard any faithful law-abiding group within our borders as superfluous.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: Lying face upward; failing to act or protest out of moral weakness or indolence.
etymology: From Latin supinus "bent backward, lying on the back."

examples.text: She lay supine, and straight as an arrow, on the sloping sod of this hill-top, gazing up into the blue miles of sky, and still retaining her warm hold of Jude's hand.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Susan was only acting on the same truths, and pursuing the same system, which her own judgment acknowledged, but which her more supine and yielding temper would have shrunk from asserting.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Oh, merciful heavens, was I not accessory to his death by my supine insensibility, by my contempt for him, not remembering, or not willing to remember, that it was for my sake he had become a traitor and a perjurer?
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: To supersede and replace, often by force or scheming.
etymology: From Latin supplantare "to trip up," from sub- "under" + planta "sole of the foot."

examples.text: She emphasized, however, that "if some charter arrangement could be worked out, it would not supplant the reflagging arrangement that we worked out with the Kuwaitis."
examples.source: Reuters, “Kuwait Seen Wanting To Lease Some U.S. Tankers”

examples.text: To him, even in his poverty, the thought that he was supplanting a brother clergyman so kind and courteous as Mr. Harding had been very bitter.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: At this hour the animosities of political strife, the bitterness of partisan defeat, and the exultation of partisan triumph should be supplanted by an ungrudging acquiescence in the popular will and a sober, conscientious concern for the general weal.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Bending and moving easily and gracefully; flexible; adaptable in mind or behavior.
etymology: From Old French souple, from Latin supplex "submissive, bending under."

examples.text: Natasha rose slowly and carefully, crossed herself, and stepped cautiously on the cold and dirty floor with her slim, supple, bare feet.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Twilight phantoms are they, yet moulded in prophetic grace of structure, slim shapely haunches, a supple tendonous neck, the meek apprehensive skull.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: The little procession then moved forward—the man in front bearing the light, the two bony women next, supporting between them the small and supple one.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To ask or beg for something earnestly or humbly.
