etymology: From Latin supplicare "to kneel down, beg humbly," from supplex "kneeling in entreaty."

examples.text: The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes, or of supplicating the aid of Macedon, its former oppressor.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: She passed five hours by her friend's side, sometimes in remonstrance, sometimes talking cheerfully, oftener in silence and terrified mental supplication.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: She stopt, felt herself getting into a puzzle, and could not be prevailed on to add another word, not by dint of several minutes of supplication and waiting.

examples.text: Whether unbridled curiosity, or ungovernable dread, dictated Miss Verinder's questions I do not presume to inquire.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: He was not to blame for having been born with his unbridled temperament and his somehow limited intelligence.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Strange or mysterious, especially in an unsettling way; beyond what is normal or expected.

examples.text: The researchers found the women were uncannily accurate in guessing which men liked children and which men were less interested or indifferent to kids.
The sound of his voice echoed uncannily through the homelike hush, and he repeated: "There is something I've got to tell you... about myself..."
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: The man in whose breast that faith has been darkened is naturally the subject of dangerous and uncanny suggestions.
examples.author: Benjamin Harrison

definition: Not right or reasonable; unreasonably excessive; not guided by conscience.

examples.text: Mr Blandois, in his most gentlemanly manner, was afraid he had disturbed her by unhappily presenting himself at such an unconscionable time.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He held it for the tenth part of a second, for three strides of the man—an unconscionable time.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: If we don't, the recovery will be too short, unemployment will remain too high, and we will leave an unconscionable burden of national debt for our children.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Lacking good manners, refinement, or grace.
etymology: From Old English uncuth "unknown, strange," from un- "not" + cuth "known."

examples.text: Originally dubbed "Jerry's Guide to the World Wide Web" the firm adopted the moniker Yahoo because the founders liked the dictionary definition of a yahoo as a rude, unsophisticated, uncouth person.
examples.source: BBC News, “Yahoo celebrates a decade online”

examples.text: With a cry John seized the branch of a tree, whipped the crutch out of his armpit, and sent that uncouth missile hurtling through the air.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

examples.text: From Icelandic, Dutch, and old English authorities, there might be quoted other lists of uncertain whales, blessed with all manner of uncouth names.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Excessively or ingratiatingly flattering; oily, greasy.
etymology: From Medieval Latin unctuosus, from Latin unctus "anointed," from unguere "to anoint."

examples.text: Mr Kibble, an unctuous broad man of few words and many mouthfuls, said, more briefly than pointedly, raising his ale to his lips: 'Same to you.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: In a word, after being tried out, the crisp, shrivelled blubber, now called scraps or fritters, still contains considerable of its unctuous properties.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Lush's tone had gradually become more and more unctuous in its friendliness of remonstrance, and he was almost in danger of forgetting that he was merely gambling in argument.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: To move with a smooth wavelike motion; to have a wavy form or outline.
etymology: From Late Latin undulatus "wavy," from Latin unda "wave."

examples.text: It is also not the kind of fast course that tends to suit Radcliffe better, with the undulating finish through the park testing the legs' final reserves.
Here and there water shone like silver, and beyond, the land rose into blue undulating hills, and so faded into the serenity of the sky.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: For leagues and leagues it undulated round us, so that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe and golden wheat.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Leaving no doubt; unambiguous.
etymology: From un- "not" + "equivocal," from Latin aequivocus "of identical sound," from aequus "equal" + vox "voice."

examples.text: On 10 March, military chiefs reportedly asked for an unequivocal statement about the legality of the war to make sure troops could be defended in a court of law.
examples.source: BBC News, “Iraq advice claim sparks new row”

examples.text: And it appears yet more unequivocally, that there is no pretense for the parallel which has been attempted between him and the king of Great Britain.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: The vast majority of scientists have concluded unequivocally that if we don't reduce the emission of greenhouse gases, at some point in the next century, we'll disrupt our climate and put our children and grandchildren at risk.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: Incapable of being fully explored or understood; too deep to measure.
etymology: From "fathom," a unit of depth equal to six feet, originally the span of outstretched arms.

examples.text: They leave Mr. Tulkinghorn, without a ruffle on the surface of his unfathomable depths, drinking his old wine, and go down into the streets.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: I thought of their unfathomable distance, and the slow inevitable drift of their movements out of the unknown past into the unknown future.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: Evening passed, night came, and the feeling of suspense and softening of heart in the presence of the unfathomable did not lessen but increased.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Released from restraint or inhibition; free.

examples.text: "It is no longer appropriate for a government minister to have such unfettered discretion in the appointment of judges."
examples.source: BBC News, “'Best person' for top legal job”

examples.text: She is what we call in England a tomboy, with a strong nature, wild and free, unfettered by any sort of traditions.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: But, as I have said before, the most powerful force we can enlist against the Federal deficit is an ever-expanding American economy, unfettered and free.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Awkward and clumsy; lacking grace in movement or posture; unwieldy.

examples.text: The ungainly piece of honesty beamed and blushed as he said it, quite enraptured with the remembrance of having been serviceable.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He was much below the middle height, but his large head, which seemed to hang loosely on his body, gave him an odd ungainliness.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: "You are driving nobly," said MacIan, and his words (which had no meaning whatever) sounded hoarse and ungainly even in his own ears.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Not able to be doubted, questioned, or discredited; entirely trustworthy.

examples.text: The last thing at night my wife returned to Blackwater, having followed her instructions with the most unimpeachable accuracy.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: If by good and sufficient reason Mr Boffin meant honest and unimpeachable reason, that might weigh with Mr Venus against his personal wishes and convenience.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: One of our most lucrative means of laying out money is in the shape of loans, where the security is unimpeachable.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Having an untidy or disheveled appearance; not maintained.
etymology: From un- "not" + kempt "combed," past participle of dialectal kemb "to comb."

examples.text: Sinister police patrol the unkempt streets, and the oppressive atmosphere clobbers you like a sledgehammer.
examples.source: BBC News, “No half measures with Half-Life 2”

examples.text: There was a movement and an exclamation from my right, and peering through the gloom, I saw Whitney, pale, haggard, and unkempt, staring out at me.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: He was unkempt, uncombed, and clad in the same old ruin of rags that had made him picturesque in the days when he was free and happy.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Absolute; unqualified (usually of something bad); not lessened or softened.

examples.text: The door, however, proved not to be locked, and they were all agreed in turning joyfully through it, and leaving the unmitigated glare of day behind.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: The verdict must have been of unmitigated guilt, and he took the secret of the evidence with him in that leap into the sea.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: What he dreaded above all was meeting that man again; he hated him with an intense, unmitigated hatred and was afraid his hatred might betray him.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Not proper or appropriate; indecorous.

examples.text: The bears rolled on the ground at last in the most unseemly fashion, amid roars of laughter from the closely-packed crowd of men and women.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: A painstaking police officer, considering the presence of a corpse in his excellency's courtyard unseemly, told the dragoons to take it away.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Levin felt that it was unpardonable to eat, to sleep, to talk even now, and it seemed to him that every movement he made was unseemly.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Not able to be maintained or defended against attack or objection.
etymology: From un- "not" + "tenable," from French tenir "to hold," from Latin tenere.

examples.text: He says a permanent ban on hand luggage would be untenable, not least because of the risk of theft from luggage carousels.

Nevertheless, that a male dissembler who by deluging her with untenable fictions charms the female wisely, may acquire powers reaching to the extremity of perdition, is a truth taught to many by unsought and wringing occurrences.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Of the different grounds which have been taken in opposition to the plan of the convention, there is none that was so little to have been expected, or is so untenable in itself, as the one from which this particular provision has been attacked.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Not justified or authorized; unnecessary.

examples.text: He refused to comment directly on the current yen/dollar rate but said flatly that foreign exchange markets recently tended "to draw unwarranted inferences from what I say."
examples.source: Reuters, “Baker Says He Stands By Paris Currency Agreement”

examples.text: At two in the morning they routed us out of bed—another piece of unwarranted cruelty—another stupid effort of our dragoman to get ahead of a rival.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: While meeting all these needs, we intend to plug unwarranted tax loopholes and strengthen the law which requires all large corporations to pay a minimum tax.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

definition: Difficult to carry or move because of size, shape, or weight; too large or complex to manage efficiently.
etymology: From un- "not" + obsolete wieldy "active, nimble," from "wield."

examples.text: Others poured scorn on Farrell's bleached hair and Angelina Jolie's unwieldy accent, which Variety called "a combination of Mata Hari and Count Dracula".
examples.source: BBC News, “Box office blow for Alexander”

examples.text: A robot with a flexible, trunk-like arm could one day work like an elephant to grasp unwieldy loads, say its developers.
'The unwieldy old man, lowering his big forehead like an ox under a yoke, made an effort to rise, clutching at the flintlock pistols on his knees.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: Not aware of the full facts; not done on purpose, unintentional.
etymology: From Old English unwitende, from un- "not" + witan "to know."

examples.text: People can have CJD before they know it and in a few suspected cases, blood and organ donors may have unwittingly infected others.
Soon after being discovered the file is thought to have been removed from the sites that were unwittingly harbouring it.
Raskolnikov had unwittingly worked a revolution in his brain on a certain point and had made up his mind for him conclusively.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To find fault with someone; to scold or reproach sharply.

examples.text: She did not sit there inwardly upbraiding her husband, lamenting at Fate, which had directed her footsteps to the path which they had taken.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: It was part of her creed that the head of the family should never be upbraided in his own house, and Miss Thorne had lived up to her creed.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: She even upbraids herself—most undeservedly, poor thing!—for not having divined at the time what the true solution of the mystery might really be.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Courteous and refined in manner, especially in a smooth, sophisticated way.
etymology: From Latin urbanus "of the city, refined," from urbs "city."

examples.text: With that he rubbed his hands as if the interview had been very satisfactory to him, panted away to the door, and urbanely nodded himself out again.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: He was of a gracious presence, and he welcomed men with such urbanity that those who spoke with him rarely left him displeased.
examples.author: Niccolò Machiavelli (tr. W. K. Marriott)

examples.text: She had him painted in a brooch and wore it—indeed she amused and somewhat pestered her acquaintance with her perpetual talk about his urbanity and beauty.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: To take a position of power or importance illegally or by force; to take the place of wrongfully.
etymology: From Latin usurpare "to seize for use," probably from usus "use" + rapere "to seize."

examples.text: Work and pensions minister Alan Johnson said it was wrong to suggest the chancellor would usurp Mr Milburn, adding they would "work as a team".
examples.source: BBC News, “Brown's poll campaign move denied”

examples.text: Projects of usurpation cannot be masked under pretenses so likely to escape the penetration of select bodies of men, as of the people at large.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Nor can any ecclesiastical organization be safely permitted to usurp in the smallest degree the functions and powers of the National Government.
examples.author: James A. Garfield

definition: Designed to be useful or practical rather than attractive; of utilitarianism, the doctrine that right actions maximize overall happiness.
etymology: From "utility," from Latin utilitas, from utilis "useful"; popularized in the philosophical sense by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

examples.text: Ye Utilitarians—ye, too, love the UTILE only as a VEHICLE for your inclinations,—ye, too, really find the noise of its wheels insupportable!
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: It is possible that there was this golden legend under the utilitarian one: "I will help to my last effort the woman I have loved so dearly."
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: The jolly tombstone-yard, where a utilitarian sculptor in a red calfskin overcoat whistled as he hammered the shiniest of granite headstones.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To alternate or waver between different opinions or actions; to be indecisive.
etymology: From Latin vacillare "to sway, totter."

examples.text: He honestly mistook his sensuality for romantic emotion, his vacillation for the artistic temperament, and his idleness for philosophic calm.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: However much of vacillating whim there might have been in his entrance on matrimony, there was no vacillating in his interpretation of the bond.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: We must avoid extremes, for vacillation between extremes is inefficient, costly, and destructive of morale.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Having or showing a lack of thought or intelligence; mindless; empty.
etymology: From Latin vacuus "empty," from vacare "to be empty."

examples.text: The Tory co-chairman attacked Labour's six new pledges as "vacuous" and said Mr Blair was very worried voters would take revenge for his failure to deliver.
For all the preposterous hat and the vacuous face, there was something noble in the simple faith of our visitor which compelled our respect.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: Two young men in brown robes like furniture-covers were gesturing vacuously and droning cryptic sentences full of repetitions.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: An unexpected and inexplicable change in a situation or in someone's behavior; a whim.
etymology: From Latin vagari "to wander."

examples.text: He admits it has not been an easy job to forecast the vagaries of Australian agriculture, but says it has been important to give farmers the most up-to-date information available.
There was a madman in Seville who took to one of the drollest absurdities and vagaries that ever madman in the world gave way to.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: He held the knife in his hand, and pushed its point between my teeth: but, for my part, I was never much afraid of his vagaries.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: A person without a settled home or regular work who wanders from place to place; wandering, roaming.
etymology: From Anglo-French vagaraunt "wandering about," probably influenced by Latin vagari "to wander."

examples.text: But her husband was rough on me—many times he was rough on me—and mainly he was the justice of the peace that jugged me for a vagrant.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: One hour I'll give you to recollect yourself, and if you don't give up this idle story, I'll—I'll commit you as a vagrant—that's poz!
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: For us that movement of the peoples from west to east, without leaders, with a crowd of vagrants, and with Peter the Hermit, remains incomprehensible.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Possessing or showing courage or determination.
etymology: From Old French vaillant, from valoir "to be worth," from Latin valere "to be strong."

examples.text: He thought of how valiant a companion she would be on a long motor tour, exploring mountains, picnicking in a pine grove high above a valley.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: And I who am here beside thee, may I not put myself on a par with the valiant Pierres, who pressed this very spot that I now press?
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: If we lose that sacred fire—if we let it be smothered with doubt and fear — then we shall reject the destiny which Washington strove so valiantly and so triumphantly to establish.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging; bland and lifeless.
etymology: From Latin vapidus "flat, flavorless," used of wine that had lost its life; related to vapor.

examples.text: Such stale vapid rejected cabbage-leaf and cabbage-stalk dress, such damaged-orange countenance, such squashed pulp of humanity, are open to the day nowhere else.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: "Sacrifice the world for love!" she said in answer to some renewed vapid declaration of his passion.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Much did she censure the attenuated Cupids who encircle the ceiling of the Queen's Hall, inclining each to each with vapid gesture, and clad in sallow pantaloons, on which the October sunlight struck.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Exhibiting different colors, especially as irregular patches or streaks; marked by variety, diverse.
etymology: From Late Latin variegare "to make varied," from Latin varius "various" + agere "to make."

examples.text: Not long ago you were so variegated, young and malicious, so full of thorns and secret spices, that you made me sneeze and laugh—and now?
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: The inside of the great mosque is very showy with variegated marble walls and with windows and inscriptions of elaborate mosaic.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: I have already spoken of the great palaces dotted about among the variegated greenery, some in ruins and some still occupied.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: Showing strong feeling; forceful, passionate, or intense.
etymology: From Latin vehemens "impetuous, violent."

examples.text: Neil Nichols said he was surprised at the vehemence of Dome's statement and denied that TransCanada was trying to usurp other bids.
examples.source: Reuters, “Takeover Battle For Dome Petroleum Begins”

examples.text: He would naturally say to himself, it is impossible that all this vehement and pathetic declamation can be without some colorable pretext.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: Saying these words, with great vehemence he seized hold of Piedro, and in the very midst of the little fruit-market gave him a severe beating.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

definition: Showing or motivated by susceptibility to bribery; corrupt. (Not "venial," which means pardonable.)
etymology: From Latin venalis "for sale," from venum "sale."

examples.text: This peculiar felicity of situation has, in a great degree, contributed to preserve the liberty which that country to this day enjoys, in spite of the prevalent venality and corruption.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

examples.text: There was another attraction in his profession: it wanted reform, and gave a man an opportunity for some indignant resolve to reject its venal decorations and other humbug, and to be the possessor of genuine though undemanded qualifications.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: If that solitary suffrage can be obtained by foreign nations by flattery or menaces, by fraud or violence, by terror, intrigue, or venality, the Government may not be the choice of the American people, but of foreign nations.
examples.author: John Adams

definition: Accorded great respect because of age, wisdom, or character.
etymology: From Latin venerabilis, from venerari "to revere, worship."

examples.text: For many years the venerable IBM operating system, known as OS/2, has been the staple software used to power many of the 1.4m cash machines in operation around the world.
He's too proud a chap to eat it!' and, coming out of her chair, shook her venerable fist so very close to his nose as to tickle the surface.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: A very merry lunch it was, for everything seemed fresh and funny, and frequent peals of laughter startled a venerable horse who fed near by.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: To regard with great respect; to revere.
etymology: From Latin venerari "to adore, revere," related to Venus.

examples.text: It was not the most promising party to travel with and hope to gain a higher veneration for religion through the example of its devotees.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: For forty or fifty years past, from the times of former elders, no visitors had entered that cell without feelings of the profoundest veneration.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The most respectful deference is due to doubts originating in pure patriotism and sustained by venerated authority.
examples.author: John Quincy Adams

definition: Speaking or representing the truth; truthful, accurate.
etymology: From Latin verax "truthful," from verus "true."

examples.text: It is to be observed, that on coming to this passage, the author of this veracious history breaks out into exclamations.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: Albeit it was heard of afterwards, as will afterwards be read in this veracious register of marriage.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: My Lord Dives's remains are in the family vault: the statuaries are cutting an inscription veraciously commemorating his virtues, and the sorrows of his heir, who is disposing of his goods.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Conformity to facts; accuracy; habitual truthfulness.
etymology: From Medieval Latin veracitas, from Latin verax "truthful," from verus "true."

examples.text: "We still want to believe the veracity of the stem cell lines, which we hope will be verified by a world-renowned lab, not some incompetent committee from Seoul National University," Hwang said.
Benedetto maintained the truth of what he had said, and accompanied it with details that did more honor to his imagination than to his veracity.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Nature, he knows, has a language of her own, which she uses with strict veracity, and he considers himself an adept in the language.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: In exactly the same words as were used originally; word for word.
etymology: From Medieval Latin verbatim "word for word," from Latin verbum "word."

examples.text: I rang the bell and called for the weekly county paper, which contained a verbatim account of the inquest.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: 'I'd give a shilling a line for a verbatim note,' said the Editor.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: Here was a rare interview; I shall try to record it verbatim.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Using or expressed in more words than are needed.
etymology: From Latin verbosus, from verbum "word."

examples.text: The persecutors denied that there was any particular gift in Mr. Chadband's piling verbose flights of stairs, one upon another, after this fashion.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There was evidently not space enough for his drunken verbosity and Mitya not only filled the margins but had written the last line right across the rest.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: What he had to say was confused, halting, and verbose; but Philip knew the words which served as the text of his rambling discourse.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Green with grass or other rich vegetation; inexperienced or naive.
etymology: From Old French verdoyant, from Latin viridis "green."

examples.text: From the verdant undulations and the spreading oaks of the Dedlock property, Mr. Tulkinghorn transfers himself to the stale heat and dust of London.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: They were just abreast of Mareciana, and beyond the flat but verdant Island of La Pianosa.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: For as this appalling ocean surrounds the verdant land, so in the soul of man there lies one insular Tahiti, full of peace and joy, but encompassed by all the horrors of the half known life.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Used as an intensifier, often to qualify a metaphor; real, genuine, true.
etymology: From Old French veritable, from Latin veritas "truth."

examples.text: We visited a Jesuit cathedral nearly two hundred years old and found in it a piece of the veritable cross upon which our Saviour was crucified.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: In some instances, to the quick, observant eye, those linear marks, as in a veritable engraving, but afford the ground for far other delineations.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Strange to say, he stood up for her as if she were in earnest his veritable born lady; to such a pass had his unholy books brought him.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: A trace of something that is disappearing or no longer exists; the smallest amount.
etymology: From Latin vestigium "footprint, trace."

examples.text: Only ragged vestiges of glass remained in its windows, and great sheets of the green facing had fallen away from the corroded metallic framework.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: This is how I looked at it that morning—and even now I seem to see an undeniable vestige of truth in that exaggerated view of a common occurrence.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: One would have warning signs: increasing layoffs, rising energy prices, too many failing schools, persistent poverty, the stubborn vestiges of racism.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: Experienced in the imagination through the feelings or actions of another person; acting or done for another.
etymology: From Latin vicarius "substitute," from vicis "change, turn, place."

examples.text: So Eppie was reared without punishment, the burden of her misdeeds being borne vicariously by father Silas.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: My sister, having so much to do, was going to church vicariously, that is to say, Joe and I were going.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She supposed that these were unpunctual guests, who would have to be content with vicarious civility, since Evie and Charles were gone, Henry tired, and the others in their rooms.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: A change of circumstances or fortune, typically one that is unwelcome or unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin vicissitudo, from vicissim "in turn," from vicis "change, turn."

examples.text: Not long after this, Jurgis, wearying of the risks and vicissitudes of miscellaneous crime, was moved to give up the career for that of a politician.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

examples.text: Only the vicissitudes of life can show us its vanity and develop our innate love of death or of rebirth to a new life.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Among the vicissitudes incident to life no event could have filled me with greater anxieties than that of which the notification was transmitted by your order, and received on the 14th day of the present month.
examples.author: George Washington

definition: To clear someone of blame or suspicion; to show to be right or justified.
etymology: From Latin vindicare "to lay claim to, avenge, set free," from vindex "claimant, avenger."

examples.text: The Federal Government says it has been vindicated by the ruling.
Once again, Lily had withdrawn from an ambiguous situation in time to save her self-respect, but too late for public vindication.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: The State of the Union, at the opening of the 85th Congress, continues to vindicate the wisdom of the principles on which this Republic is founded.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: Bitterly hostile or spiteful; extremely severe or harmful, especially of a disease or poison.
etymology: From Latin virulentus "poisonous," from virus "poison, slimy liquid."

examples.text: "The reason for the high mortality probably is not high replication rates per se, but high replication rates of an extremely virulent virus," he says.
The State Department renewed its warning to Americans not to travel to Iran because of what spokeswoman Phyllis Oakley called, "its virulent anti-American policies and support for terrorism."
examples.source: Reuters, “Us Diplomatic Missions On High Alert Over Gulf”

examples.text: These two clauses have been the source of much virulent invective and petulant declamation against the proposed Constitution.
examples.author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John Jay

definition: Attractively lively and animated, especially of a person.
etymology: From Latin vivax "lively, long-lived," from vivere "to live."

examples.text: Free-thought may be suggestive, it may be inspiriting, it may have as much as you please of the merits that come from vivacity and variety.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: Her spirits even were good, and she was full of a happy vivacity, but I could see evidences of the absolute prostration which she had undergone.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: That evening he had the peculiar light in the eyes and the unusual vivacity which had been once noticed in him by Mr. Farebrother.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Expressing opinions or feelings in a loud, forceful, and insistent way.
etymology: From Latin vociferari "to shout," from vox "voice" + ferre "to carry."

examples.text: It may have to go the whole way and have NFL-style video cameras all over the field, or slap the vociferous perpetrators over the knuckles.
At a table, somewhat vociferously buying improbable "soft drinks" for two fluffy girls, was a man with a large familiar back.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance.
examples.author: Stephen Crane

definition: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse; (of a substance) easily evaporated.
etymology: From Latin volatilis "flying," from volare "to fly." First used of birds, then of substances that "fly off" as vapor.

examples.text: The measure, confirmed by a brokerage firm here, has effectively cut off all foreign participation in Venezuela's volatile currency market.
She did not, indeed, expect Lily to remain equally immovable: she had all the American guardian's indulgence for the volatility of youth.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Towering over this volatile, changing world, like a thundercloud on a summer day, looms the awesome power of nuclear weapons.
examples.author: Jimmy Carter

definition: The faculty or power of using one's will; a conscious choice or decision.
etymology: From Medieval Latin volitio, from Latin volo "I wish."

examples.text: Dart said this payment was intended for the three officers' severance agreements, although there was an implication that Lieberman and Dougherty would be leaving the company of their own volition.
examples.source: Reuters, “Dart Group Flexible On Supermarkets ≪Sgl> Bid”

examples.text: "Trust, plain-speaking and straight talking is something which matters so much to me as a politician and as a man that I have decided, of my own volition, to request an independent review of the allegations that I misused my position."
Almost simultaneously, with a mighty volition of ungraduated, instantaneous swiftness, the White Whale darted through the weltering sea.
examples.author: Herman Melville

definition: Speaking or spoken incessantly and fluently.
etymology: From Latin volubilis "rolling, turning," from volvere "to roll." Words that roll off the tongue.

examples.text: The poor girl spoke these words with a spirit and volubility which Rebecca had never before seen in her, and before which the latter was quite dumb.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: So situated, she was powerless to check Jo, who seemed possessed by a spirit of mischief, and talked away as volubly as the lady.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: All of this, however, did not chill their ardor as much as might have been expected, because of the volubility of the agent.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

definition: Occupying much space; very lengthy or full; producing or containing much writing.
etymology: From Late Latin voluminosus, from Latin volumen "a roll of writing, a book."

examples.text: "Well, Blacas, what think you of this?" inquired the king triumphantly, and pausing for a moment from the voluminous scholiast before him.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: In these voluminous notes Toll suggested another scheme, totally different from Armfeldt's or Pfuel's plan of campaign.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: He presented his idols diffidently, but he expanded in Carol's bookishness, in Miss Sherwin's voluminous praise, in Kennicott's tolerance of any one who amused his wife.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Wanting or devouring great quantities of food; very eager in some activity.
etymology: From Latin vorax "greedy," from vorare "to devour."

examples.text: Parker says the latest results provide a smoking gun for the argument that the Milky Way is a voracious cannibal that devours its neighbours.
He walked up to the sideboard, and tearing a piece from the loaf he devoured it voraciously, washing it down with a long draught of water.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: The man's voracious vanity devoured this implied tribute to his local and critical supremacy with an appearance of the highest relish.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: To decrease in vigor, power, or extent; to become weaker; of the moon, to show a decreasing lit surface.
etymology: From Old English wanian "to lessen."

examples.text: It also said there was evidence that manufacturers' confidence may be waning as the outlook for the world economy becomes more uncertain.
examples.source: BBC News, “UK interest rates held at 4.75%”

examples.text: I cannot doubt that Stapleton recruited his waning resources in this fashion, and that for years he has been a desperate and dangerous man.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: And 8 years ago, I sat in that very chair as President Reagan spoke of punishing inflation and devastatingly high interest rates and people out of work — American confidence on the wane.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

definition: Deliberate and unprovoked, especially of cruelty or damage; sexually immodest; growing luxuriantly.
etymology: From Middle English wantowen "undisciplined," from wan- "not" + towen "trained, brought up."

examples.text: He had swept it out of existence, as it seemed, without any provocation, as a boy might crush an ant hill, in the mere wantonness of power.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: Do not think yourself excused by any weakness, any natural defect of understanding on her side, in the wanton cruelty so evident on yours.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: The picture I present to you is peaceful and human, and you must feel that you could deny it only in the wantonness of power and cruelty.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: Skilled at gaining an advantage, especially deceitfully; cunning.

examples.text: And the coxswain, Israel Hands, was a careful, wily, old, experienced seaman who could be trusted at a pinch with almost anything.
examples.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

examples.text: The undesigning Boffin had become so far immeshed by the wily Wegg that his mind misgave him he was a very designing man indeed in purposing to do more for Wegg.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: So wily was he that he had not trusted himself upon foot, but he had availed himself of a cab so that he could loiter behind or dash past them and so escape their notice.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

definition: Attractive or appealing in appearance or character; charmingly engaging.
etymology: From Old English wynsum "pleasant," from wynn "joy."

examples.text: But Harry is no longer the winsome hero, he is a moody teenager and Daniel Radcliffe pulls it off very well.
examples.source: BBC News, “DVD review: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban”

examples.text: She went into the house, a frail small woman, still winsome but hopeless of eye as she staggered with the weight of the drowsy boy in her arms.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Tears came to his eyes as he remembered her childlike look, and winsome fanciful ways, and shy tremulous grace.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

definition: Having or showing a feeling of vague or regretful longing.

examples.text: She looked wistfully at her baby's eyes, saw that they were lost in the deepest slumber, and then made a sort of couch for him on the sofa.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Glancing wistfully around, Eugene saw Miss Jenny at the foot of the bed, looking at him with her elbows on the bed, and her head upon her hands.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But her heart was very heavy, she longed to be at home, and every day looked wistfully across the lake, waiting for Laurie to come and comfort her.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: Using or expressing dry, especially mocking, humor; of a facial expression, twisted in disgust or disappointment.
etymology: From Old English wrigian "to turn, bend."

examples.text: "I should be knighted for this," he adds, with a wry chuckle, "People are going to be so happy to sit at home, make their podcast, and make a little money."
examples.source: BBC News, “'Podcasters' look to net money”

examples.text: But she made a wry face at the prospect, and scratched away at her palette as if bent on vigorous measures before she gave up her hopes.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: I'm not an envious man, and if anybody offered to set up Mordecai in a shop of my sort two doors lower down, I shouldn't make wry faces about it.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Having or showing great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause or objective.
etymology: From Greek zēlos "ardor, jealousy." "Jealous" comes from the same word by way of French.

examples.text: His friend, Saxon Spence, leader of Devon county Labour group, lays the blame for any lack of campaigning zeal on one issue above all others.
examples.source: BBC News, “Labour's core support takes stock”

examples.text: This icon of the Venerable Sergius, the servant of God and zealous champion of old of our country's weal, is offered to Your Imperial Majesty.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: But pride of service and mistaken zeal in promoting particular doctrine has more than once occasioned the kind of difficulty of which I have just spoken.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: The time at which something is most powerful or successful; the point in the sky directly overhead.
etymology: From Arabic samt ar-ra's "path over the head," via Medieval Latin cenit, a misreading of samt.

examples.text: Their parent stars are so nearby they fill up one-third of the sky from the horizon to the zenith, Sahu says.
It was the time when the youthful Speranski was at the zenith of his fame and his reforms were being pushed forward with the greatest energy.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The shadow of the silent cloud had fallen upon the ship from the zenith, and seemed to have extinguished every sound of her teeming life.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

definition: A soft, gentle breeze; literary name for the west wind.
etymology: From Greek Zephyros, the god of the west wind.

examples.text: Euroclydon, nevertheless, is a mighty pleasant zephyr to any one in-doors, with his feet on the hob quietly toasting for bed.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: A delicious zephyr played along the coasts of the Mediterranean, and wafted from shore to shore the sweet perfume of plants, mingled with the fresh smell of the sea.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Spring had come, clad in no classical garb, yet fairer than all springs; fairer even than she who walks through the myrtles of Tuscany with the graces before her and the zephyr behind.
examples.author: E. M. Forster
